cocktails.name: 100 Year Old Cigar
cocktails.shortDescription: A stirred late-night sipper of aged rum, Bénédictine, Cynar and a touch of peated whisky in an absinthe-rinsed glass.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Rinse the chilled glass with absinthe and discard the excess.
Stir the other ingredients with ice.
Strain into the absinthe-rinsed glass.
Serve without garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the 100 Year Old Cigar was created in 2015 or 2016 by bartender Maks Pazuniak at the Counting Room in Brooklyn, New York City. The drink moved with him in 2016 when he opened Jupiter Disco in Bushwick, Brooklyn, with business partner Al Sotack. His original used Ron Zacapa 23, Cynar, Bénédictine and Laphroaig 10 in an absinthe-rinsed Nick & Nora glass. It was first published in Carey Jones's 2016 book Brooklyn Bartender.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dark, smoky and contemplative. Aged rum gives caramel, dried fruit and oak, Bénédictine adds honey and baking spice, and Cynar contributes a bittersweet, vegetal edge. A small dose of peated whisky and the absinthe rinse bring smoke and anise to the aroma, echoing the cigar of the name. Stirred and spirit-forward, it is a late-night sipper, ideally beside an actual cigar.

cocktails.shortDescription: Mezcal, cognac, maraschino, Punt e Mes and Peychaud's stirred: Ezra Star's smoky 2014 Martinez riff from Boston.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The 1910 was created in 2014 by Ezra Star at Drink, the Boston cocktail bar, and Difford's Guide describes it as a riff on the Martinez. The name refers to 1910, the year the Mexican Revolution began. That decade-long conflict transformed both Mexican culture and its government, and the drink nods to it by splitting its base between Mexican mezcal and French cognac, with Italian vermouth and maraschino completing the Martinez template.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, smoky and bittersweet. Mezcal brings earthy smoke and roasted agave, while cognac softens it with dried fruit and vanilla. Punt e Mes adds a bold bitter-sweet vermouth character, maraschino a floral cherry sweetness, and Peychaud's bitters a light anise and red-fruit spice. Silky and strong, it is a contemplative evening drink for fans of the Manhattan and Martinez.

cocktails.name: Adonis
cocktails.shortDescription: Sherry and sweet vermouth stirred with a touch of bitter: a low-strength aperitif named after an 1880s Broadway hit.
cocktails.garnish: Orange zest twist (discarded) and a skewered green olive
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Throw (or stir) all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a skewered green olive.
cocktails.history:
The Adonis is named after a Broadway musical that opened in Chicago in the summer of 1884 and moved to New York's Bijou Theatre that September, where it ran for more than 600 performances. Difford's Guide finds the first mention of the cocktail in an 1887 column in New York's The Sun, where a bartender cheerfully admits he had no idea what an Adonis was but served one anyway. The first printed recipe comes from Jacques Straub's 1913 manual.

Early recipes favour sweet vermouth over sherry, but Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book reversed the ratio, and the sherry-led version is now considered standard. Albert Stevens Crockett's 1931 Old Waldorf Bar Days offered equal parts and confirmed the theatrical link, naming the show's stars Henry E. Dixey and Fanny Ward. Some older books even called the sherry-heavy version a Harvard, a name now used for a quite different cognac drink.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A light, nutty and savoury aperitif. Sherry provides dry walnut, almond and salty notes, while sweet vermouth adds dark fruit, gentle spice and sweetness. A small amount of red bitter gives a faint bitter-orange edge. The drink is silky and low in alcohol, finishing dry and appetising. With the olive garnish, it suits a pre-dinner glass with salted nuts or tapas.

cocktails.name: Affinity
cocktails.shortDescription: Equal parts Scotch, sweet and dry vermouth with aromatic bitters: a stirred, early-1900s New York relative of the Rob Roy.

ingredients.note: vermouth amaro, e.g. Cocchi Vermouth Amaro

instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir the Scotch, both vermouths and the bitters with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide traces the Affinity to a 1907 item in The New York Sun announcing a new Broadway cocktail of that name, though that early version was a shaken mix of Scotch, Italian vermouth, sugar and orange bitters. William Boothby printed a quite different Affinity in 1908, and Jacques Straub's 1913 manual gave a near match under the name Express Cocktail.

The equal-parts version that survives today, with French and Italian vermouth, Scotch and aromatic bitters, is credited to Jacob A. Didier's bartenders' pocket guide of 1909. Hugo Ensslin reprinted it in 1917 and Harry Craddock included it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930, dropping the cherry garnish that modern recipes also leave out.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A smooth, medium-bodied stirred drink in which Scotch shares the stage equally with sweet and dry vermouth. Malty grain and light smoke meet herbal, bittersweet vermouth and a dry, winey edge, while a dash of aromatic bitters adds spice and the lemon oils lift the nose. Less sweet than a Rob Roy and lower in strength than a straight whisky drink, it works as an aperitif or as a gentle after-dinner sipper.

cocktails.name: Air Mail
cocktails.shortDescription: A rum highball of aged rum, lime and honey topped with brut sparkling wine, popular in the 1940s.
cocktails.garnish: Lime zest twist (not expressed) or a mint sprig tip
instructions: Shake the rum, lime juice and honey syrup with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled highball glass.
Top with sparkling wine and stir briefly.
Garnish with a lime zest twist or a mint sprig tip.
cocktails.history:
The Air Mail's name probably refers to airmail as the fastest way to send a letter, and it may date from the early days of the service, which began in May 1918 between New York and Washington. However, the earliest known reference is a 1930s Bacardi promotional pamphlet, Bacardi and Its Many Uses.

The drink appears in W. C. Whitfield's 1941 book Here's How with the note that it "ought to make you fly high", and later in Embury's 1948 Fine Art of Mixing Drinks and Esquire's Handbook for Hosts. These early recipes all specify a highball glass with ice.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Lively, honeyed and effervescent. Lightly aged rum provides soft vanilla and cane sweetness, honey syrup adds floral richness, and lime juice brings a bright citrus snap. Brut sparkling wine tops it with crisp bubbles and a dry, toasty finish. Often described as a rum French 75, it is best served long over ice, perfect for brunch or a celebration.

cocktails.name: Alaska
cocktails.shortDescription: Old tom gin stirred with Yellow Chartreuse and orange bitters: a golden, herbal Martini-style drink from Jacques Straub's 1913 manual.

ingredients.note: chilled; omit if using wet ice

instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Stir the old tom gin, Yellow Chartreuse, water and orange bitters with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide adapts the Alaska from Jacques Straub's Manual of Mixed Drinks, keeping his proportions of two parts old tom gin to one of yellow Chartreuse with a dash of orange bitters. Straub shook the drink, so Difford's stirs it with a splash of water for similar dilution. The name is thought to refer to its golden colour and the gold rushes of the late 1890s, when prospectors moved from the Klondike to Nome in Alaska.

In 1948 David Embury described the Alaska as a Dry Martini with Chartreuse in place of vermouth, also known as the Oriental, and suggested using less Chartreuse plus a little dry sherry to make a variation called the Nome. Embury preferred a lemon twist and a much higher proportion of gin than Straub's original recipe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A spirituous, golden and complex sipper. Old tom gin provides a rounded juniper and botanical base, while Yellow Chartreuse brings honey, saffron, citrus and a gentle alpine-herb sweetness. A dash of orange bitters and the expressed orange zest lift the aroma and sharpen the finish. With the right dilution it is smooth yet assertive, best enjoyed as a pre-dinner aperitif or a herbal nightcap.

cocktails.name: Alexander
cocktails.shortDescription: A rich, creamy after-dinner classic of cognac, brown crème de cacao and fresh cream, finished with grated nutmeg.
instructions: Add the cognac, brown crème de cacao and cream to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Grate fresh nutmeg over the top.
cocktails.history:
The first Alexander was made with gin rather than brandy. Difford's Guide notes that an equal-parts gin, crème de cacao and cream recipe was printed in Hugo Ensslin's 1916 Recipes for Mixed Drinks, and cites competing origin stories: a 1915 Philadelphia newspaper linking it to a bartender honouring pitcher Grover Cleveland Alexander, and a 1929 Walter Winchell column crediting a New York bartender named Troy Alexander.

The brandy version, which the IBA now lists simply as the Alexander, is credited to Harry MacElhone, who printed it in his 1923 ABC of mixing cocktails while working at Ciro's in London. By 1930 Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book listed both the gin and brandy versions.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smooth, rich and dessert-like. Cognac gives warmth and dried-fruit depth, brown crème de cacao adds chocolate sweetness, and the cream turns it into a silky, almost milkshake texture. Shaking hard aerates the cream so the drink feels lighter than its ingredients suggest. A dusting of nutmeg adds a warm, spicy aroma. Sweet but not cloying when made with equal parts, it works best after dinner or as a festive winter treat.

cocktails.name: Algonquin
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey, dry vermouth and pineapple juice shaken: a 1930s classic attributed to New York's Algonquin Hotel.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Algonquin is one of several 1930s drinks attributed to New York City's Algonquin Hotel. Difford's Guide adapts its recipe from G. Selmer Fougner's 1935 anthology Along the Wine Trail, which gives a "New Algonquin" of two parts rye to one part each of French vermouth and pineapple juice. Stanley M. Jones repeated that formula in his 1977 Complete Barguide.

The method has been argued over. Jones and Ted Haigh, who revived it in his 2004 Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails, call for shaking, but Gary Regan's 2003 Joy of Mixology said to stir, and many bartenders followed him. Difford's prefers shaking, which gives a light foam.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry, fruity and quietly complex. Spicy rye whiskey leads, dry and bianco vermouths add herbal and floral notes, and pineapple juice brings tropical sweetness and a gentle acidity. Shaking gives the drink a light, frothy head and a softer texture. Peychaud's bitters add a hint of anise and cherry. Balanced and approachable, it makes a good aperitif or an introduction to rye.

cocktails.name: Amaretto Sour
cocktails.shortDescription: Amaretto shaken with lemon juice, egg white and a dash of bitters: a frothy, almond-scented sour from the 1970s.

ingredients.note: plus extra atomised over the foam

cocktails.garnish: Aromatic bitters sprayed over the foam, lemon wheel and maraschino cherry
instructions: Shake the amaretto, lemon juice, bitters and egg white with ice.
Strain back into the shaker and dry shake without ice.
Fine strain into an ice-filled old fashioned glass.
Spray a little aromatic bitters over the foam and garnish with a lemon wheel and cherry.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide reports that the Amaretto Sour is thought to have been devised in 1974 at the request of the US importer of Amaretto di Saronno, originally as two parts liqueur to one part lemon juice. It is missing from the big 1970s bar encyclopaedias, however, and only turns up in print in the 1980s, for example in Mark Torre's 1987 The Bartender's Cherry, by which time commercial sour mix had replaced fresh lemon.

That sour-mix version earned the drink a reputation as a "disco drink" during the cocktail revival of the 1990s and 2000s, when it was rarely taken seriously by craft bartenders. Difford's Guide credits Jeffrey Morgenthaler with rescuing its image in 2012, when he published a version that adds bourbon alongside the amaretto.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet and sour in roughly equal measure, with marzipan-like almond and apricot-kernel flavour from the amaretto cut by sharp fresh lemon. The egg white gives a thick, silky foam and a soft, rounded texture, while a few drops of aromatic bitters add spice and stop the sweetness from cloying. Fairly light in alcohol, it is an easy, crowd-pleasing drink for an evening aperitif or a relaxed nightcap.

cocktails.name: Amaretto Sour (Morgenthaler)
cocktails.shortDescription: Jeffrey Morgenthaler's 2012 upgrade of the Amaretto Sour with bourbon, fresh lemon and egg white.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist (discarded) and skewered maraschino cherries
instructions: Shake all ingredients with ice, then strain back into the shaker.
Dry shake without ice to emulsify.
Fine strain into an ice-filled old fashioned glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with skewered cherries.
cocktails.history: This version of the Amaretto Sour comes from Jeffrey Morgenthaler, who created it in 2012 in Oregon, USA, according to Difford's Guide. His formula is dominated by amaretto, balanced with fresh lemon juice and given body by egg white and a slug of bourbon for backbone. Morgenthaler's original called for cask-strength bourbon and more lemon juice than Difford's adaptation, which uses standard bourbon, slightly less lemon and a rich demerara syrup.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Nutty, sweet-sour and silky. Amaretto dominates with marzipan and cherry-stone flavours, bourbon adds vanilla, oak and a firmer alcoholic backbone, and lemon juice supplies the sour balance. Egg white gives a smooth, foamy texture and a thick white head. Sweeter than most sours but still well balanced, it is a crowd-pleaser for any evening.

cocktails.name: American Trilogy
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey and applejack stirred with brown sugar syrup and orange bitters: a 2006 Milk & Honey apple-tinged Old Fashioned.
instructions: Stir the applejack, rye whiskey, brown sugar syrup and orange bitters with ice.
Strain into an old fashioned glass over fresh ice, ideally one large cube.
Express a long orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
Richard Boccato and Michael McIlroy created the American Trilogy in 2006 at Milk & Honey in New York City. Within a year the drink had moved onto the menu at Little Branch, the team's second bar, and it is still ordered today at Attaboy, which took over the old Milk & Honey address.

The name refers to its three American ingredients: rye whiskey, applejack and Regans' Orange Bitters. The original was built in the glass by muddling a sugar cube with the bitters, but Difford's Guide switches to brown sugar syrup so the sweetness can be adjusted and repeated consistently.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A Rye Old Fashioned with an orchard-fruit twist. Spicy, robust rye is softened by applejack's baked-apple and cider notes, while brown sugar syrup adds a little molasses richness. Orange bitters and a long orange twist bring bright citrus aromatics that lift the spirits. Strong, smooth and warming, it is best sipped slowly in the evening, especially in autumn.

cocktails.name: Americano
cocktails.shortDescription: Campari and sweet vermouth lengthened with soda: a low-strength Italian aperitivo and the forerunner of the Negroni.
cocktails.garnish: Half an orange slice and a lemon zest
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice cubes.
Pour in the Campari and sweet vermouth.
Add a splash of soda water and stir gently.
Garnish with half an orange slice and a lemon zest.
cocktails.history:
The name is Italian for "American-style". Difford's Guide links it to an American fashion for vermouth mixed with bitters, which led Italian producers to sell pre-bittered "vermouth Americano" and bars to improvise their own bittersweet blends, some lengthened with soda. As the Milano-Torino (Campari with vermouth) caught on, Campari became the preferred bitter element.

Wikipedia places the first serves at Gaspare Campari's café in Milan in the 1860s, though that date is not documented in print. The earliest recipes Difford's cites appear in Ferruccio Mazzon's 1920 Il Barista, and Elveio Grassi's 1936 Mille Misture lists around a dozen versions.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A low-strength, bittersweet aperitivo. Campari brings bitter orange peel and gentian, and the red vermouth softens it with herbal sweetness and a hint of spice. Soda lightens the body and adds a gentle fizz, so the drink is long and refreshing rather than heavy. The orange and lemon garnish adds a fresh citrus aroma that suits it to warm afternoons before a meal.

cocktails.name: Añejo Highball
cocktails.shortDescription: Aged rum, orange curaçao, lime and bitters topped with ginger beer: a long, spicy highball by Dale DeGroff.
instructions: Shake the rum, orange curaçao, lime juice and bitters with ice.
Half fill an ice-filled highball glass with half of the ginger beer.
Strain the shaken mix into the glass and top with the rest of the ginger beer.
Garnish with orange and lime wheels.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Añejo Highball to Dale DeGroff, who created it in the late 1990s at the Rainbow Room in New York City. It applies the highball format to aged rum, pairing it with orange curaçao, a little lime and aromatic bitters before lengthening the mix with spicy ginger beer. The drink has since earned a place on Difford's lists of modern classics and its cocktail hall of fame.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Long, spicy and thirst-quenching. Aged rum gives a base of molasses, caramel and gentle oak, orange curaçao adds sweet orange-peel fruitiness, and a small squeeze of lime keeps it fresh. Ginger beer brings fizz and a warming ginger bite, with aromatic bitters adding a hint of spice. Easy to drink and not too strong, it is a good choice for a warm afternoon or a casual gathering.

cocktails.name: Anejo Manhattan
cocktails.shortDescription: Añejo tequila stirred with sweet vermouth and bitters: an agave-based twist on the Manhattan from Seattle's Ryan Magarian.
cocktails.garnish: Maraschino cherry wrapped in salami on a skewer
instructions: Chill a martini glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a skewered cherry wrapped in salami.
cocktails.history: The Añejo Manhattan is a much-adapted version of a recipe created by Ryan Magarian, a bartender and drinks consultant based in Seattle. Difford's Guide notes that Magarian's original also included Licor 43, a Spanish vanilla-and-citrus liqueur, which later versions dropped in favour of a simpler Manhattan template. It swaps the classic Manhattan's whiskey for barrel-aged añejo tequila while keeping sweet vermouth and bitters, and it is now listed among Difford's Modern Classics.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smooth, rich and agave-forward. Añejo tequila brings cooked agave, vanilla, caramel and oak, which sit naturally alongside the dark fruit and spice of sweet vermouth. Angostura and orange bitters add depth and a citrus lift. The texture is silky and the strength considerable, so it is best sipped slowly in the evening. The salami-wrapped cherry adds a playful savoury-sweet bite.

cocktails.name: Angel Face
cocktails.shortDescription: An equal-parts, all-spirit Savoy-era cocktail of gin, apricot brandy and calvados, shaken and served straight up.
instructions: Add the gin, apricot brandy and calvados to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Angel Face is documented in Harry Craddock's 1930 The Savoy Cocktail Book as equal thirds of dry gin, apricot brandy and calvados, shaken and strained into a cocktail glass. The IBA keeps that formula unchanged in its Unforgettables category.

Difford's Guide points out that modern bartenders would normally stir an all-spirit drink like this, but that Craddock's original calls for shaking. Its own version is stirred with a splash of chilled water added, to recreate the extra dilution that shaking would have provided and to soften the drink's strength.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity and strong. Apricot brandy brings ripe stone-fruit sweetness, calvados adds baked-apple richness, and gin provides a dry, botanical backbone that stops the fruit from becoming jammy. The result is balanced rather than sweet or dry, with a warming finish. Because it is all spirit, it is best sipped slowly as a pre-dinner drink or a nightcap, ideally well chilled.

cocktails.name: Appletini
cocktails.shortDescription: A bright green vodka "Martini" with sour apple liqueur and a little citrus, created in West Hollywood in 1996.
cocktails.garnish: Maraschino cherry and/or an apple wedge or slice
instructions: Pre-chill a martini glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry and/or an apple slice.
cocktails.history:
Unusually, the Appletini's origin is well recorded. On the Fourth of July 1996, Loren "Lola" Dunsworth, owner of Lola's in West Hollywood, was encouraged by a Ketel One representative to add a signature vodka Martini to her menu. Spotting sour apple liqueur on the back bar, she asked bartender Adam Karston to make a drink with it.

His mix of equal parts vodka and apple liqueur with a splash of house sweet-and-sour, first called Adam's Apple Martini, was an instant hit. As the Appletini it swept North America in the 2000s and earned a place in Difford's Cocktail Hall of Fame.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, sour and unashamedly fun. Sour apple liqueur provides a bright green colour and a candy-like Granny Smith flavour, vodka gives a clean, neutral base, and touches of lime cordial, fresh lime and lemon add tang. A little syrup balances the acidity. Light, fruity and easy-drinking, it is a party drink rather than a serious sipper.

cocktails.name: Army and Navy
cocktails.shortDescription: A gin sour sweetened with orgeat, with lemon and Angostura bitters, first printed by David Embury in 1948.

ingredients.note: saline solution or a pinch of salt

instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: The Army and Navy first appears in David A. Embury's 1948 The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, which sets a latest date for its creation. Little else is known, though its name has led people to suggest it originated at the Army and Navy Club in Washington, D.C., whose lounge is also said to be where the Daiquiri was introduced to the United States. Embury gave the original formula as two parts gin to one each of lemon and orgeat, called it horrible and preferred his own drier 8:2:1 ratio. Difford's Guide settles on 8:3:2.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Nutty, citrusy and fairly dry. Gin provides crisp juniper, lemon juice adds bright acidity, and orgeat brings a soft almond sweetness with a hint of orange flower. Angostura bitters add spice and depth, and a few optional drops of saline sharpen the flavours. Smooth and well balanced, it is an elegant sour for any time of the evening.

cocktails.name: Aviation
cocktails.shortDescription: A pre-Prohibition gin sour tinted pale violet by crème de violette, with maraschino adding a floral, cherry-stone edge.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker.
Shake with cracked ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry if you like.
cocktails.history:
The Aviation first appears in print in Hugo R. Ensslin's 1916 book Recipes for Mixed Drinks. Ensslin was head bartender at the Hotel Wallick in New York and is widely credited with creating it. His version was two parts gin to one part lemon juice, sharpened with small dashes of maraschino and crème de violette.

Difford's Guide ties the name to the pale sky-blue tint the violette gives the drink and to the early days of flying, when air travel was a glamorous luxury. A 1930 version by Harry Craddock left out the violette, and Difford's lists it as a separate recipe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A crisp gin sour with a floral edge. Fresh lemon gives a bright, tart backbone, and maraschino adds a dry, nutty cherry sweetness rather than sugariness. A small amount of crème de violette brings a soft perfumed note and a pale lilac-blue colour. The botanicals of the gin come through clearly, and the finish is clean and lightly sour.

cocktails.name: B & B
cocktails.shortDescription: Cognac stirred with Bénédictine over ice: a honeyed, spiced after-dinner pairing so popular that it was later sold ready-bottled.
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice, ideally one large cube.
Stir the cognac and Bénédictine with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
Bénédictine and brandy have long been mixed, and the pairing first appears in cocktail books in the early 1900s as a layered pousse-café, with brandy floated over the liqueur, as in Raymond Sullivan's 1910 Barkeeper's Manual. Popular culture holds that the B & B was created in the 1930s, specifically in 1937 by a bartender at New York's 21 Club, though when and where it was first mixed is uncertain.

Its popularity is not in doubt. Around 1937 or 1938 Bénédictine began producing a bottled blend of 60% Bénédictine and 40% French brandy for the US market, and in America sales of the bottled B&B still exceed those of the original liqueur.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Honeyed, spiced brandy in its simplest form. Cognac brings dried fruit, vanilla and gentle oak, while Bénédictine adds honey, warm baking spices and a subtle herbal complexity. Stirred and served over a large cube, it gradually softens as the ice melts. Smooth, rich and warming, slightly drier than the traditional equal-parts mix, it is a classic after-dinner digestif for a cold evening.

cocktails.name: Bacardi Cocktail
cocktails.shortDescription: Light Cuban-style rum shaken with lime and grenadine: a pink, Daiquiri-like sour that dates from 1917 Cuba.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the rum, lime juice, grenadine and sugar syrup with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide traces the Bacardi Cocktail to Cuba in 1917. It spread with the American cocktail scene after Prohibition and became so familiar that people ordered it simply as "a Bacardi". Whether grenadine was part of the first recipe is disputed: some say the drink began as a Daiquiri made with Bacardi rum, and many vintage books list it without grenadine, which suggests the pink version came later.

The drink's fame led to a well-known trademark case. In 1936 the Bacardi company took two New York establishments to court for serving other rums under the name, and Justice John L. Walsh of the New York Supreme Court ruled that a Bacardi Cocktail had to be made with Bacardi rum.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A bright, softly sweet sour with the clean profile of a Daiquiri. Light rum gives a gentle sugar-cane base, lime brings a sharp citrus edge, and grenadine adds a pale pink colour along with a red-fruit sweetness that rounds out the acidity. It is light-bodied, crisp and very easy to drink, best served ice cold as an aperitif or a summer sipper.

cocktails.name: Bahama Mama
cocktails.shortDescription: Rums, coconut rum, a touch of coffee liqueur, lemon and pineapple: a fruity Bahamian tiki-style drink attributed to Oswald Greenslade in 1963.

ingredients.note: half 35-40% coconut rum liqueur, half Malibu
espresso coffee liqueur, e.g. Galliano Espresso

cocktails.garnish: Pineapple wedge, maraschino cherry and a bouquet of mint sprigs
instructions: Chill a tiki mug or Collins glass and fill it with ice.
Shake the rums, coconut rum, coffee liqueur, lemon juice and pineapple juice with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge, a cherry and mint sprigs.
cocktails.history:
The bartender most associated with the Bahama Mama is Oswald 'Slade' Greenslade, a Bahamian who worked at the Pink Elephant nightclub. He says he created it there in 1963 for three tourists who asked for something fruity and new, and named it after a calypso singer whose stage name was Bahama Mama when she walked into the bar shortly afterwards.

Greenslade sent his original recipe to Difford's Guide in 2024: dark rum, coconut rum, grenadine, pineapple and orange juice. He adds that the Bahamas Ministry of Tourism went on to promote the drink. Some dispute his claim, saying it appeared on menus in the 1940s or 1950s, though Difford's has seen no such evidence.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A tropical tiki-style drink built on rum, coconut and pineapple, kept in balance so the sweetness never takes over. Jamaican and overproof rums bring funky molasses and ripe tropical fruit, coconut rum adds creamy sweetness, and a little coffee liqueur gives a subtle roasted depth. Pineapple juice makes it long and juicy, while lemon keeps it bright. Fruity and easy-drinking, it suits beach days, pool parties and summer evenings.

cocktails.name: Bamboo (Difford's 'Perfect' recipe)
cocktails.shortDescription: Fino sherry stirred with dry, bianco and sweet vermouth and orange bitters: Difford's low-strength "perfect" take on the Bamboo.
instructions: Stir the fino sherry, dry, bianco and sweet vermouths and orange bitters with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: This version of the classic sherry-and-vermouth Bamboo was put together by Simon Difford on 2 August 2014, drawing on numerous earlier Bamboo recipes, and was further "perfected" in January 2023. Classic Bamboo recipes balance fino sherry against two vermouths; Difford's twist is to use three, adding sweet red vermouth to the dry and bianco styles. The result sits in Difford's Guide's cocktail hall of fame with a top five-star rating.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, dry and elegantly aromatic. Fino sherry gives crisp, saline and nutty mineral notes, while the trio of vermouths adds layered herbal sweetness: dry for bite, bianco for floral richness and red for a touch of spice and depth. A dash of orange bitters and an orange twist brighten the finish. Low in alcohol and very appetising, it is an ideal aperitif before a meal.

cocktails.name: Banana Calling
cocktails.shortDescription: London dry gin shaken with banana liqueur, fino sherry and lemon: a 2018 Dandelyan riff on the London Calling sour.
cocktails.garnish: Dried banana chip pegged to the rim, or a fresh banana slice
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the gin, banana liqueur, fino sherry, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a banana chip or banana slice on the rim.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide adapts the Banana Calling from a recipe created in August 2018 by Cameron Attfield at the Dandelyan bar in London, England. It is a riff on the London Calling, the gin and fino sherry sour created by Chris Jepson in 2002, with a measure of banana liqueur joining the sherry. Difford's describes the result as a banana and fino sherry gin sour.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A short, sharp gin sour with quiet layers of flavour. Juniper and citrus lead, fresh lemon gives a bright tartness and a little rich syrup keeps it balanced. Banana liqueur adds a soft ripe-fruit roundness, and fino sherry contributes a dry, nutty, saline edge. The banana is subtle rather than sweet or tropical, so the drink stays crisp and elegant, a good aperitif for gin lovers.

cocktails.name: Batanga
cocktails.shortDescription: A Mexican highball of tequila, lime and cola in a salt-rimmed glass, created in Tequila in 1961.

ingredients.note: sea salt, plus more for the rim

instructions: Pre-chill a collins glass.
Rim the glass with salt by moistening the edge with lime juice and dipping it in salt.
Stir a pinch of salt with the lime juice in the base of the glass to dissolve.
Add ice and the other ingredients and stir briefly.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Batanga to Don Javier Delgado Corona, the legendary owner and bartender of La Capilla (The Chapel) in the town of Tequila, Mexico, who created it in 1961. He famously stirred each drink with the knife he used to cut the limes, a ritual he kept up into his eighties. The Batanga became popular across Mexico, helped by an advertising campaign for El Tequileño, a tequila made close to his bar.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Simple, salty and refreshing. Cola gives sweetness, caramel and spice, blanco tequila adds peppery, vegetal agave, and a squeeze of lime cuts through the sugar. The salt is the secret: it softens the cola's sweetness and makes every flavour pop, both dissolved in the drink and on the rim. Think of a tequila Cuba Libre, perfect on a hot afternoon.

cocktails.name: Bee's Knees
cocktails.shortDescription: A 1920s gin sour sweetened with honey, bright with lemon and a splash of orange juice.
instructions: Stir the honey syrup with the lemon and orange juices until dissolved.
Add the gin and shake with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Optionally garnish with a lemon or orange zest.
cocktails.history:
For decades the Bee's Knees was described as a Prohibition-era American drink whose honey and lemon hid bad gin, an idea Difford's Guide traces to David Embury. Newer research points to Paris instead. Its first appearance in a cocktail book is the 1929 French title Cocktails de Paris, which credits Frank Meier, head bartender at the Hôtel Ritz.

A Brooklyn newspaper article from April 1929 instead credited the socialite Margaret "Molly" Brown. Difford's suggests Meier may have made it for her or at her suggestion. Meier claimed the recipe again in his 1936 book. Embury's 1948 book suggested adding a little orange juice.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright and gently floral. Honey gives the drink a rounder, more aromatic sweetness than sugar would, and fresh lemon balances it with clean acidity. The orange juice in this spec softens the sourness and adds a juicy, slightly fruity body. Dry gin keeps a juniper backbone underneath, so the finish is fresh and only lightly sweet.

cocktails.name: Bellini
cocktails.shortDescription: Venice's famous brunch sparkler from Harry's Bar: white peach purée topped with chilled prosecco.
instructions: Pour the white peach purée into a mixing glass with ice.
Add the Prosecco.
Stir gently and pour into a chilled flute.
cocktails.history:
Giuseppe Cipriani created the Bellini at Harry's Bar in Venice in 1945, according to Difford's Guide, drawing on the Italian habit of steeping fresh peaches in wine. He named it after the 15th-century Venetian painter Giovanni Bellini, because the drink's pink colour reminded him of the painter's rosy tones.

In his own later account, Cipriani said he mixed fresh peach juice with Prosecco one summer, found that guests loved it, and named it during an exhibition of the painter's work. Because white peaches are seasonal, Venetian bars that refuse to use frozen purée serve it only from late spring to autumn.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Soft, fruity and lightly sparkling. Ripe white peach gives a fragrant, velvety sweetness and a pale blush colour, while Prosecco adds crisp bubbles, green-apple freshness and gentle acidity. The texture is fuller than plain sparkling wine thanks to the purée, but the drink stays low in alcohol and easy-going, a natural fit for brunch or an early aperitivo.

cocktails.name: Bensonhurst
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye, dry vermouth, maraschino and a dash of Cynar stirred: Chad Solomon's 2006 Brooklyn-variation from Milk & Honey.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history: Chad Solomon created the Bensonhurst in 2006 while working at Milk & Honey in Manhattan. Solomon named his drink after Bensonhurst, a neighbourhood close to his home in Brooklyn, New York. Like the Brooklyn, it pairs rye whiskey with dry vermouth and maraschino, but it replaces the Brooklyn's bittersweet Picon with a small dose of Cynar, the Italian artichoke amaro.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry, spirit-forward and subtly complex. Rye whiskey brings pepper and grain, dry vermouth gives a crisp, herbal and slightly floral lift, and maraschino adds a delicate cherry-pit sweetness. A small dose of Cynar contributes a bittersweet, earthy depth on the finish. The overall effect is lighter and drier than a Manhattan, with a smooth texture. Enjoy it as a refined evening drink.

cocktails.name: Bernice
cocktails.shortDescription: Vodka shaken with lime, sugar, Galliano and a dash of absinthe: a herbal vodka daiquiri that won a 1950 bartenders' competition.
cocktails.garnish: Mint leaf pegged to the rim, or a floating mint tip
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the vodka, Galliano, lime juice, syrup and absinthe with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a mint leaf on the rim or a floating mint tip.
cocktails.history:
The Bernice is credited to a bartender named C. S. Berner, whose recipe won a 1950 cocktail competition held by the West Coast branch of the United Kingdom Bartenders' Guild in the USA. It was printed in the first edition of The U.K.B.G. Guide to Drinks in 1953, made with Smirnoff vodka, Galliano, a few drops of Pernod Fils absinthe and the juice of half a lime.

The drink has often been attributed to Ted Saucier's 1951 book Bottoms Up, but Difford's Guide checked that book and could not find it there, placing its first appearance in the U.K.B.G. guide instead. Difford's modern recipe keeps the original combination but adds a little rich sugar syrup and trims the Galliano.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Best thought of as a vodka daiquiri with a herbal twist. Clean vodka lets fresh lime and sugar set a crisp, sweet-and-sour balance, while a small measure of Galliano brings vanilla, anise and a cool, peppermint-like herbal note. A dash of absinthe deepens the aniseed aroma. Light, bright and refreshing, it is an easy aperitif or a summery drink for those who like their sours with a little intrigue.

cocktails.name: Between the Sheets
cocktails.shortDescription: A strong, cheekily named Sidecar cousin that splits the base between cognac and white rum.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker.
Shake with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The origins of this risqué-sounding drink are murky. Difford's Guide thinks it probably began in Prohibition-era America as a gin and rum drink, then took on brandy in Europe to become more like a Sidecar. Other claims point to a bartender at London's Berkeley Hotel in 1921, a New Rochelle speakeasy bartender, and Harry MacElhone in Paris.

The first printed recipe, in Frank Shay's 1929 Drawn From The Wood, used gin, rum and Cointreau. Several versions with different base spirits existed for years. The brandy, rum and triple sec version used today owes much to Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A strong, spirit-forward sour in the Sidecar family. Cognac brings warm notes of dried fruit and oak, and white rum lightens the body with a clean cane sweetness. Triple sec adds plenty of orange, and a modest measure of lemon keeps it bright without making it sharp. The result is rich, citrusy and noticeably boozy, with a smooth, slightly sweet finish.

cocktails.name: Bijou
cocktails.shortDescription: A rich stirred classic of gin, green Chartreuse and sweet vermouth with orange bitters, named after jewel colours.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist (discarded) and a skewered maraschino cherry
instructions: Pre-chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a skewered cherry.
cocktails.history:
A drink called Bijou first appeared in C. F. Lawlor's 1895 book The Mixicologist, but as equal parts gin, Grand Marnier and sweet vermouth. The Chartreuse version known today comes from Harry Johnson's 1900 Bartender's Manual, which mixed equal measures of green Chartreuse, Italian vermouth and Plymouth gin with a dash of orange bitters, stirred over shaved ice.

Bijou is French for jewel, and the name is said to reflect the colours of its ingredients: diamond for gin, ruby for vermouth and emerald for Chartreuse. Difford's Guide reduces the Chartreuse, finding the equal-parts version too strong and dominated by it.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, herbal and warming. Green Chartreuse brings an intense blast of alpine herbs, mint and spice, sweet vermouth adds dark fruit, vanilla and a gentle bitterness, and gin provides a juniper backbone. A dash of orange bitters and the lemon twist brighten everything. Even with less Chartreuse it remains bold and fairly sweet, best sipped slowly before or after dinner.

cocktails.name: Bitter Giuseppe
cocktails.shortDescription: A bittersweet stirred aperitivo built on Cynar with sweet vermouth, a little lemon and orange bitters.

ingredients.note: one swath of peel, oils squeezed into the mixing glass
preferably a large cube or block ice

instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass.
Squeeze the oils from a lemon zest into a mixing glass and drop the zest in.
Add the other ingredients and stir with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass, ideally over a large cube.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Bitter Giuseppe to Stephen Cole, who created it in 2007 at The Violet Hour in Chicago, Illinois; Difford's recipe is adapted from his. Unusually, the drink uses Cynar, an Italian carciofo (artichoke) amaro, as its base rather than a spirit, supported by a smaller measure of Carpano Antica Formula vermouth and just a touch of lemon juice. Difford's recommends enjoying it as an aperitivo and includes it among its modern classics.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet, herbal and low in alcohol for a stirred drink. Cynar brings earthy, vegetal bitterness with caramel sweetness, and the rich vanilla-spiced vermouth deepens it. Lemon oils and a splash of juice brighten the whole, while orange bitters add a zesty lift. Served over a large ice cube, it is smooth and contemplative, ideal before dinner.

cocktails.name: Black Manhattan
cocktails.shortDescription: A darker Manhattan made with Averna amaro in place of sweet vermouth, plus Angostura and orange bitters.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the Black Manhattan is adapted from a recipe created by Todd Smith at Bourbon & Branch in San Francisco, dating it to 2015. The idea is simple: take a classic Manhattan and replace the sweet vermouth with an amaro such as Averna, keeping both Angostura and orange bitters. The swap gives the drink its darker colour and name. Difford's includes it in its Cocktail Hall of Fame and World's Top 100 lists.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, bittersweet and spicy. Spicy, high-proof rye provides structure and warmth, while Averna adds dark caramel, bitter chocolate, liquorice and citrus peel. The two bitters lift the aroma with clove and orange. It is heavier and more bitter than a standard Manhattan, with a long, warming finish, and makes an excellent after-dinner or cold-weather sipper.

cocktails.name: Black Russian
cocktails.shortDescription: Vodka and coffee liqueur over ice, created in 1949 in Brussels: short, dark and dead simple.
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice cubes.
Pour in the vodka and coffee liqueur.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide credits Gustave Tops, a bartender at the Metropolitan Hotel in Brussels, with creating the Black Russian in 1949. He made it for Perle Mesta, the wealthy American socialite who served as US ambassador to Luxembourg from 1949 to 1953 and who appeared on the cover of TIME that year.

Mesta was famous for her lavish parties and was known as the "hostess with the mostest". She also inspired Irving Berlin's musical Call Me Madam. A float of cream turns the drink into a White Russian, and topping it with cream and cola makes a Colorado Bulldog.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Short, dark and simple. The coffee liqueur gives roasted coffee, light vanilla and a syrupy sweetness, while the vodka adds strength without much flavour of its own, so the result tastes like a strong, sweetened iced coffee. Served over ice, it gradually dilutes and softens. It is smooth and dessert-like but noticeably more alcoholic than it tastes.

cocktails.name: Blinker
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey shaken with pink grapefruit juice and grenadine: a fruity Prohibition-era sour first printed in 1934.

ingredients.note: Saline solution or a pinch of salt

instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a grapefruit zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The Blinker was first published in Patrick Gavin Duffy's 1934 Official Mixer's Manual, which appeared just after the repeal of Prohibition. Duffy's recipe is short and simple: one jigger of rye whiskey, one and a half jiggers of grapefruit juice and half a jigger of grenadine, shaken well with ice and strained. Difford's Guide follows the same structure, using pink grapefruit and adding a few drops of grapefruit bitters and saline to sharpen the flavours.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, tart and gently spicy. Pink grapefruit juice gives a juicy, slightly bitter citrus character, grenadine adds red-fruit sweetness and a rosy colour, and rye whiskey provides a peppery backbone that keeps the drink from becoming too sweet. Grapefruit bitters and a touch of salt brighten the finish. Light-bodied and refreshing, it suits brunch or a sunny afternoon.

cocktails.name: Blood and Sand
cocktails.shortDescription: A shaken Scotch whisky classic with cherry liqueur, sweet vermouth and orange juice, named after a 1922 Valentino film.
cocktails.garnish: Orange zest twist (discarded) and a skewered maraschino cherry
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a skewered maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
Perhaps the best-known Scotch whisky cocktail, the Blood and Sand takes its name from Blood and Sand, the 1922 bullfighting film starring Rudolph Valentino. The silent film, based on a 1909 Spanish novel by Vicente Blasco Ibáñez, was a box-office hit about a village boy who becomes a famous matador.

Who created the drink is unknown, but it first appears in print in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book as equal parts Scotch, cherry brandy, sweet vermouth and orange juice. The red cherry liqueur is said to represent blood and the orange juice the sand of the arena.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, rounded and gently smoky. Blended Scotch provides malt and honey, with a splash of peated whisky adding a hint of smoke. Cherry liqueur brings rich red-fruit sweetness, sweet vermouth adds spice and depth, and fresh orange juice gives body and a soft citrus tang. Difford's slightly drier proportions keep it from being cloying. A good introduction to whisky cocktails at any time of evening.

cocktails.name: Bloody Mary
cocktails.shortDescription: The classic savoury brunch cocktail: vodka and tomato juice seasoned with lemon, Worcestershire, hot sauce and spice.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir gently.
Pour into a rocks glass (or a highball over ice if requested).
Garnish with celery and, optionally, a lemon wedge.
cocktails.history:
The Bloody Mary is often credited to Fernand "Pete" Petiot, said to have created it in the early 1920s at Harry's New York Bar in Paris. Research by Jack McGarry, published by Difford's Guide, suggests Petiot instead spiced up an existing vodka and tomato mix while working at the St. Regis Hotel in New York.

That research names the Hollywood entertainer George Jessel as the more likely originator of the basic pairing, and possibly of the name. A 1939 drink credited to Jessel resembles today's recipe. Several stories explain the name, and the St. Regis has its own version of the drink's origin.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Savoury, spicy and full-bodied. Tomato juice provides a thick, umami-rich base, lemon lifts it with acidity, and Worcestershire sauce adds deep, salty and tangy notes. Hot sauce, celery salt and pepper can be adjusted from mild to fiery. The vodka sits quietly underneath, adding strength rather than flavour, which makes this the classic brunch and hair-of-the-dog drink.

sources.title: The history of the Bloody Mary

cocktails.name: Blue Hawaii
cocktails.shortDescription: Rum and vodka shaken with blue curaçao, pineapple and citrus: Harry Yee's vivid 1957 Waikiki tiki drink created to sell blue curaçao.
cocktails.garnish: Pineapple wedge and cherry skewered with a paper parasol; serve with a straw
instructions: Chill a hurricane glass and fill it with crushed ice.
Shake the rum, vodka, blue curaçao, pineapple juice, lime juice, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Fine strain into the glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and cherry on a parasol and serve with a straw.
cocktails.history:
The Blue Hawaii was created in 1957 by Harry K. Yee at Henry Kaiser's Hawaiian Village Hotel, later the Hilton, in Waikiki on Oahu. Bols reportedly asked for a drink to help sell its blue curaçao, and Yee obliged with this vivid tropical mix.

It takes its name from the hit song in the 1937 Bing Crosby film Waikiki Wedding rather than from the 1961 Elvis Presley film Blue Hawaii, though Difford's Guide suggests the Elvis musical probably helped the cocktail's popularity. Some bartenders serve it layered over the blue curaçao or add a rum float.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright blue, fruity and unashamedly tropical. Light rum and vodka make a clean, neutral base, letting pineapple juice dominate with its juicy sweetness, while blue curaçao adds a gentle bitter-orange note along with the famous colour. Fresh lime and lemon sharpen the finish and keep it refreshing. Served over crushed ice with a parasol, it is a fun, easy-drinking holiday drink for poolside afternoons and beach parties.

cocktails.name: Blue Lagoon
cocktails.shortDescription: Vodka, blue curaçao and lime topped with lemon-lime soda: a vivid, easy-drinking highball also called the Swimming Pool.
instructions: Pour the vodka, blue curaçao and lime juice into a collins glass and stir briefly.
Fill the glass with ice.
Top with lemon-lime soda (or lemonade) and stir briefly.
Garnish with an orange wheel and a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide describes two versions of this bright blue drink, both better regarded than the critically panned 1980 film of the same name. A blended version is credited to Andy MacElhone, son of Harry MacElhone, at Harry's New York Bar in Paris, created either at some point in the 1960s or, more specifically, in 1972.

Nobody is known to have claimed the simpler version built in the glass, which may have come later. Thanks to that simplicity, it is now the more popular way to make a Blue Lagoon. The drink is also sometimes called the Swimming Pool.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Lurid blue, zesty and easy-drinking. Clean vodka provides the base, blue curaçao adds sweet orange-peel flavour along with its vivid colour, and fresh lime keeps the drink tangy and bright. Lemon-lime soda lengthens it with sweetness and sparkle. Simple, cheerful and refreshing rather than complex, it is a fun choice for poolside lounging and summer parties.

cocktails.name: Blue Moon
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin shaken with crème de violette, lemon, sugar and egg white: a silky floral sour attributed to Oscar of the Waldorf around 1940.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice, then strain the liquid back into the shaker.
Dry shake without ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with raspberries.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide reports that the Blue Moon is said to have been created around 1940 by Oscar Tschirky at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel in Manhattan. Better known as Oscar of the Waldorf, Tschirky was the hotel's celebrated maître d'hôtel and is also credited with inventing the Waldorf salad and Eggs Benedict. Although he never worked as a chef, he traded on his reputation at the hotel to publish a cocktail book of his own.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Floral, delicate and smooth. Gin provides a crisp juniper base, crème de violette adds a perfumed violet sweetness and a soft lilac-grey colour, and a little lemon and sugar keep it balanced and fresh. Egg white gives a silky texture and a fine foam. Elegant and fairly strong, it is a pretty aperitif for anyone who enjoys the Aviation.

cocktails.name: Bobby Burns
cocktails.shortDescription: A stirred Scotch whisky classic with sweet vermouth and Bénédictine, here with Peychaud's bitters and a dash of absinthe.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist (discarded) and a slice of shortbread across the rim
instructions: Pre-chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Rest a slice of shortbread across the rim.
cocktails.history:
The earliest Bobby Burns recipe on Difford's Guide comes from Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book: equal parts Italian vermouth and Scotch whisky with three dashes of Bénédictine and a squeeze of lemon peel. Craddock called it one of the very best whisky cocktails and noted that it sold fast on Saint Andrew's Day.

This version was put together by Simon Difford in January 2017. It keeps Craddock's base with a little more whisky, adds Peychaud's Bitters as introduced by David Embury in his 1953 Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, and includes a dash of absinthe inspired by Albert Stevens Crockett's 1931 Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Days.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, rounded and gently spiced. Blended Scotch gives malt, honey and a light smokiness, sweet vermouth adds dark fruit and herbal depth, and Bénédictine contributes honeyed, saffron-tinged sweetness. Peychaud's brings anise and cherry notes that a dash of absinthe echoes. Think of a smoother, more aromatic Rob Roy. It suits cold evenings by the fire, ideally with a piece of shortbread.

cocktails.name: Boulevardier
cocktails.shortDescription: The whiskey-based cousin of the Negroni, swapping gin for bourbon for a richer, warmer bittersweet drink.
instructions: Pour all ingredients into a mixing glass with ice cubes.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with an orange zest, or optionally a lemon zest.
cocktails.history:
The Boulevardier first appears in Harry MacElhone's 1927 book Barflies and Cocktails. It is not in the main recipe list but in a chapter by Arthur Moss, a Paris newspaper columnist. Moss belonged to a group of wealthy American expatriates who called themselves boulevardiers because they roamed between Harry's New York Bar and other Paris nightspots.

Moss credited the drink to Erskine Gwynne, a nephew of the railroad tycoon Alfred Vanderbilt. Gwynne co-founded the Paris magazine Boulevardier, modelled on The New Yorker, which launched the same year as the book, hence the drink's name. The original recipe was equal parts Campari, Italian vermouth and bourbon.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A richer, warmer cousin of the Negroni. Bourbon or rye replaces gin, bringing vanilla, caramel and baking spice, or a drier peppery edge with rye. Campari adds bitter orange and a firm bitterness, and sweet vermouth ties everything together with dark fruit and herbal sweetness. Served cold and stirred, it is silky, bittersweet and warming, with an expressive orange-oil aroma.

cocktails.name: Bramble
cocktails.shortDescription: Dick Bradsell's 1980s London modern classic: a gin sour over crushed ice, drizzled with blackberry liqueur.
instructions: Shake the gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a chilled old fashioned glass filled with crushed ice.
Drizzle the crème de mûre over the top in a circular motion.
Optionally garnish with a lemon slice and blackberries.
cocktails.history:
Dick Bradsell, one of the most influential London bartenders of his generation, created the Bramble in the mid-1980s at Fred's Club in Soho. In accounts he wrote in 2001 and 2015, republished by Difford's Guide, he described the drink as essentially a gin sour with blackberry added.

The drink is served over crushed ice, with blackberry liqueur poured over the top so it bleeds down through the glass. Difford's ranks it among the best and most popular drinks to come out of the 1980s, and it is now a modern classic in British bars.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tart, juicy and refreshing. The base is a well-balanced gin sour with bright lemon and a clean juniper backbone, and crushed ice keeps it very cold. Crème de mûre bleeds down through the ice, adding dark berry sweetness and a purple streak. The first sips are fruitier, and the drink becomes more evenly blended and sour as the ice melts.

cocktails.name: Brandy Alexander
cocktails.shortDescription: A rich, creamy after-dinner classic of cognac, crème de cacao and cream, dusted with nutmeg.

ingredients.note: 15 ml brown (vanilla) plus 10 ml white crème de cacao

cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist (discarded) and freshly grated nutmeg
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Dust with freshly grated nutmeg.
cocktails.history: The original Alexander was made with gin. In the early 1920s Harry MacElhone, then a bartender at Ciro's in London, is credited with starting the trend of using brandy instead, and the Brandy Alexander soon displaced the gin version. Difford's Guide supports this with the first brandy-based recipe, published in MacElhone's 1923 Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails as equal parts crème de cacao, brandy and fresh cream. In his 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, Harry Craddock listed both: the gin Alexander as No. 1 and the brandy version as No. 2.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, creamy and subtly chocolatey. Cognac provides warmth with notes of dried fruit and oak, crème de cacao adds milk-chocolate and vanilla sweetness, and cream gives a velvety, dessert-like texture. Nutmeg on top lends a warm, spicy aroma, and the expressed lemon oil keeps it from feeling heavy. A classic after-dinner drink, ideal in place of dessert.

cocktails.name: Brandy Crusta
cocktails.shortDescription: A mid-1800s New Orleans brandy sour with maraschino, curaçao and lemon, served in a sugar-crusted glass lined with citrus peel.
cocktails.garnish: Sugar-crusted rim and a long curl of orange or lemon peel inside the glass
instructions: Rub a slice of orange or lemon around the rim of a slim cocktail glass and dip it in fine white sugar.
Line the inside of the glass with a long curl of orange or lemon peel.
Mix all the ingredients with ice in a mixing glass.
Strain into the prepared glass.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide credits the Brandy Crusta to Joseph Santini, an Italian from Trieste working in New Orleans in the 1850s, either at the City Exchange or at his own Jewel of the South saloon, opened in 1855. The name refers to the thick crust of sugar on the rim of the glass.

The drink appears in Jerry Thomas's 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide, the first cocktail book, which describes the sugared rim and the whole-lemon peel lining the glass. Many historians regard the Crusta as an ancestor of the Sidecar and, through it, of the Margarita.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright and elegant. Brandy provides a rounded, fruity base, while lemon juice gives a fresh sourness that is tempered by the cherry-almond notes of maraschino and a touch of orange curaçao. Aromatic bitters add a faint spice. Each sip passes over the sugar crust, so sweetness builds as you drink. It is lighter than its strength suggests and makes an excellent aperitif or a celebratory sipper.

cocktails.name: Brandy Daisy
cocktails.shortDescription: Cognac, Yellow Chartreuse, lemon and sugar over crushed ice with a splash of soda: an 1870s–80s daisy-style sour.

ingredients.note: For stirring, plus crushed ice in the glass

instructions: Fill a wine glass with crushed ice.
Stir the cognac, Yellow Chartreuse, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into the glass over the crushed ice.
Top with a splash of soda and stir briefly.
cocktails.history:
The Brandy Daisy is one of the earliest daisies on record. Difford's Guide finds it in a later edition of Jerry Thomas's Bar-Tender's Guide and in the 1888 second edition of Harry Johnson's Bartender's Manual, noting that both men left daisies out of their first editions. Thomas's version shakes brandy with gum syrup, orange cordial and lemon juice and fills the glass with seltzer.

Johnson's recipe, which Difford's prefers, instead stirs brandy with sugar, a little lemon, a squirt of seltzer and half a glass of Yellow Chartreuse, then strains it over fruit in a fancy glass. Difford's modern version follows Johnson's lead, keeping the Chartreuse and serving the drink over crushed ice with a short splash of soda on top.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, honeyed and herbal. Cognac gives a round, fruity warmth, Yellow Chartreuse adds honey, saffron and gentle herbs, and lemon juice keeps the drink fresh and tangy. Crushed ice chills it quickly and a splash of soda lightens the body. The result is a sweet-sour sipper that feels both old-fashioned and lively, best enjoyed slowly on a warm evening.

cocktails.name: Brandy Milk Punch
cocktails.shortDescription: Cognac shaken with whole milk and vanilla syrup, dusted with nutmeg: a creamy old American punch and New Orleans brunch favourite.
instructions: Chill a highball glass and fill it with ice.
Shake the cognac, milk and vanilla syrup with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Dust with freshly grated nutmeg.
cocktails.history:
Milk punch has a long history. Wikipedia notes that it was first recorded in 1688 and that the earliest known recipe appears in a 1711 cookbook; early versions were often clarified by curdling the milk and straining out the solids, which made them stable enough to bottle. Benjamin Franklin recorded a recipe in 1763.

Difford's Guide calls the brandy version a classic that dates back to colonial times and was popular during America's Prohibition era. It remains closely associated with New Orleans, where it is still widely served, especially with Sunday brunch, and it is traditional at Christmastime across the Deep South.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smooth, creamy and gently sweet. Whole milk gives a soft, rich body, vanilla syrup adds a dessert-like sweetness, and cognac provides warmth with notes of dried fruit and oak. Freshly grated nutmeg on top brings an aromatic spice that pulls the flavours together. It is mellow rather than boozy, and suits a lazy brunch, a festive gathering or a comforting nightcap.

cocktails.name: Brass Rail
cocktails.shortDescription: Aged rum and Bénédictine shaken with lemon and egg white: Tony Abou-Ganim's silky, spiced modern sour.
cocktails.garnish: Flamed orange zest twist (discarded) and a dusting of ground cinnamon
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice, then strain the liquid back into the shaker.
Dry shake without ice to build the foam.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Flame an orange zest twist over the drink and discard it, then dust with cinnamon.
cocktails.history: The Brass Rail is a modern classic adapted from a recipe by the Las Vegas bartender Tony Abou-Ganim. Difford's Guide explains that he was inspired by his late cousin, Helen David, who liked a glass of Bénédictine as a nightcap after special occasions. He named the drink after her bar, the Brass Rail in Port Huron, Michigan. Her memory is also honoured by the Helen David Spirit Award for lifetime achievement, presented each year at the Tales of the Cocktail festival.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich and comforting for a sour. Aged rum gives toffee, vanilla and oak, while Bénédictine layers in honey, herbs and baking spice. Lemon keeps it balanced and lively, and the egg white produces a soft, velvety foam. The flamed orange oil and cinnamon dusting add a warm, aromatic lift on the nose. It is medium-bodied and well suited to an evening or after-dinner drink.

cocktails.name: Breakfast Martini
cocktails.shortDescription: Salvatore Calabrese's 1996 gin sour sweetened with orange marmalade and triple sec, garnished with a slice of toast.
cocktails.garnish: Orange zest twist (discarded) and a slice of toast on the rim
instructions: Pre-chill a martini glass.
Stir the marmalade with the gin in the base of a shaker until it dissolves.
Add the other ingredients and shake with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and discard it, then garnish with a slice of toast on the rim.
cocktails.history: The Breakfast Martini was created in 1996 by Salvatore Calabrese, long-time president of the UK Bartenders' Guild. Difford's Guide tells how his English wife, Sue, insisted he sit down to a breakfast of toast and marmalade one morning; inspired, he took the jar to work and perfected the drink that day at the Library Bar in London's Lanesborough Hotel. Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book has a very similar Marmalade Cocktail, but Calabrese says his inspiration was the English breakfast, not the classic bar book.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tangy, bittersweet and zesty. Orange marmalade gives jammy sweetness with a pleasant bitter-peel edge, while triple sec reinforces the orange flavour. Lemon juice keeps it bright and sour, and London dry gin supplies juniper backbone. The texture is slightly richer than a standard sour thanks to the preserve. Despite the name, it suits brunch or an early-evening aperitif equally well.

cocktails.name: Bronx
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin shaken with sweet and dry vermouth, orange juice and orange bitters: a fruity turn-of-the-century New York classic.
instructions: Shake the gin, sweet and dry vermouths, orange juice and orange bitters with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
One of the cocktails named after New York's boroughs, the Bronx was probably named more directly after the Bronx Zoo, which opened in November 1899. The first known mention, in a February 1901 newspaper, credits John "Curly" O'Connor of the Waldorf-Astoria as its inventor, while a 1921 report notes rival claims from two Bronx cafés. A 1935 Waldorf-Astoria bar book names another of its bartenders, Johnny Solon.

The Bronx reached recipe books in 1908, appearing in three, but only William Boothby's version, credited to Billy Malloy of Pittsburgh, matches the drink we know: equal thirds of Plymouth gin, French and Italian vermouth with orange bitters and a little orange juice. Difford's Guide concludes that several bartenders may well have devised similar zoo-inspired drinks at around the same time.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fairly dry and complex, with a fruity orange heart. Gin provides a crisp juniper backbone, generous sweet vermouth adds herbal richness, and dry vermouth keeps the finish lean. Fresh orange juice softens and brightens the mix, while orange bitters and an orange zest twist give extra zing. Less bitter and fruitier than many drinks of its era, it makes a pleasant aperitif or brunch drink.

cocktails.name: Brooklyn
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey and dry vermouth stirred with Amer Picon and maraschino: a dry, bittersweet 1908 cousin of the Manhattan.
instructions: Stir the rye whiskey, dry vermouth, Amer Picon, maraschino liqueur and chilled water with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a skewered maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Brooklyn belongs to a family of borough-named drinks that followed the success of the Manhattan and the Bronx. It first appears in print in Jacob A. Grohusko's 1908 Jack's Manual, made with equal parts rye and Italian vermouth plus dashes of Amer Picon and maraschino. Grohusko lived in Hoboken and tended bar in lower Manhattan; his only link to Brooklyn was his boss.

Jacques Straub's 1913 manual switched to French (dry) vermouth, and that drier style was followed by The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930, using Canadian whisky, and by Patrick Gavin Duffy's 1934 Official Mixer's Manual, both of which used two parts whisky to one part vermouth. Difford's Guide also prefers the dry style, relying on the maraschino and the bitter, herbal Amer Picon to keep it from feeling austere.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry, complex and spirit-forward. Spicy rye and dry vermouth form a crisp, herbal base, Amer Picon adds a bittersweet orange and gentian note, and maraschino contributes a faint floral cherry sweetness that makes the drink approachable. A splash of water softens the alcohol. Elegant and layered rather than sweet, it is a sophisticated aperitif or an evening sipper for Manhattan fans.

cocktails.name: Brown Derby
cocktails.shortDescription: A 1930s Hollywood sour of bourbon, pink grapefruit juice and maple syrup, named after a famous restaurant.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a grapefruit zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: The Brown Derby is said to have been created in the 1930s by a bartender at the Vendôme Café on Sunset Boulevard in Hollywood, which opened in May 1933. It is named after another fashionable Hollywood restaurant, the Brown Derby on Vine Street. Difford's Guide notes that George Buzza Jr.'s 1933 Hollywood Cocktails gives a honey-sweetened recipe, a drink earlier books call the De Rigueur. Difford's also questions the base spirit: Esquire mentioned the drink in 1935 and printed a 1939 recipe using dark rum, maple sugar and lime.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tart, rich and refreshing. Bourbon provides vanilla, caramel and oak, pink grapefruit juice adds a juicy, slightly bitter citrus tang, and maple syrup brings a woody, autumnal sweetness that pairs naturally with the whiskey. Simple and well balanced, it is lighter than a Whiskey Sour and works as a brunch drink or an early-evening aperitif.

cocktails.name: Cable Car
cocktails.shortDescription: Spiced rum, orange curaçao and lemon shaken with egg white in a cinnamon-sugar-rimmed coupe: Tony Abou-Ganim's 1996 San Francisco sour.
cocktails.garnish: Cinnamon-sugar rim and an orange zest twist
instructions: Rim a chilled coupe with a mix of sugar and ground cinnamon.
Shake the spiced rum, orange curaçao, lemon juice, sugar syrup and egg white with ice.
Strain back into the shaker and dry shake without ice.
Fine strain into the prepared glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
Tony Abou-Ganim created the Cable Car in 1996 at the Starlight Room, the cocktail lounge on top of San Francisco's Sir Francis Drake Hotel. The bar's slogan, "between the stars and the cable cars", referred to the Nob Hill cable cars passing outside, and gave the drink its name.

Some have credited Cory Reistad, who also worked at the Starlight Room, but Abou-Ganim has said the drink and the menus were his own. His original 1996 recipe was Captain Morgan spiced rum, Marie Brizard orange curaçao and a fresh lemon sour mix of two parts lemon juice to one part syrup.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A spiced-rum take on the Sidecar. Vanilla and baking spice from the rum mingle with sweet orange curaçao, and generous lemon juice keeps it bright and tart. Egg white gives a light, silky foam, while the cinnamon-sugar rim adds a sweet, warmly spiced first impression with every sip. Lively and easy to like, it suits a night out or cooler autumn evenings.

cocktails.name: Caipirinha
cocktails.shortDescription: Brazil's national cocktail: cachaça muddled with fresh lime and sugar, rustic, zesty and powerful.
instructions: Place the lime wedges and sugar in a double old fashioned glass and muddle gently.
Fill the glass with cracked ice.
Add the cachaça and stir gently to combine.
cocktails.history:
The Caipirinha has no single known inventor. PUNCH describes it emerging in the mid-19th century among the caipiras, rural people of the countryside near Brazil's Atlantic rainforest, who drank this cheap mix of lime, sugar and cane spirit. Difford's Guide translates the name as "country little girl" and links it to rural São Paulo state.

One story ties it to a cachaça, lime, honey and garlic remedy drunk during the Spanish flu. Citing historian David Wondrich, PUNCH notes it was once called the Batida Paulista, appeared in travel accounts in the 1940s, and became popular abroad in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rustic, zesty and powerful. Muddled lime releases both juice and aromatic peel oils, giving sharp acidity and a slightly bitter citrus edge, while the sugar rounds it out. Cachaça adds a grassy, vegetal sugarcane character that sets it apart from rum-based sours. Served over plenty of ice, it starts bold and becomes more mellow and refreshing as it dilutes.

sources.title: The Caipirinha Has Been Here All Along

cocktails.name: Cameron's Kick
cocktails.shortDescription: Scotch and Irish whiskey shaken with lemon and orgeat: a nutty 1922 whisky sour from Harry MacElhone.

ingredients.note: Optional; pasteurised or a vegan foamer
Saline solution (20 g sea salt to 80 g water) or a pinch of salt

instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The Cameron's Kick first appears in Harry MacElhone's 1922 ABC of Mixing Cocktails. It was repeated in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book as one-third Scotch whisky, one-third Irish whiskey and one-sixth each of lemon juice and orgeat syrup, shaken and strained into a cocktail glass. Difford's Guide follows that structure, adding optional egg white and a few drops of saline.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A rounded, nutty whisky sour. Blended Scotch brings honey and a hint of smoke, Irish whiskey adds smooth, light fruitiness, and orgeat gives a creamy almond sweetness that softens the lemon's sharpness. A little salt brightens the flavours, and the optional egg white adds a silky foam. Balanced and approachable, it suits an early evening drink for whisky lovers.

cocktails.name: Canchánchara
cocktails.shortDescription: A rustic Cuban mix of cane spirit, lime and raw honey over cracked ice, often called the forerunner of the Daiquiri.

ingredients.note: Cuban aguardiente de caña in the IBA recipe; rum is the usual substitute
raw honey, mixed with the water

instructions: Mix the honey with the water and lime juice.
Spread the mixture over the bottom and sides of the glass.
Add cracked ice, then pour in the aguardiente or rum.
Stir energetically from bottom to top.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide describes the Canchánchara as a forerunner of the Daiquiri, drunk by Cuban independence fighters in the late nineteenth century. It was originally made with aguardiente de caña, a raw sugar-cane spirit, rather than rum, mixed with honey and citrus.

Its exact origin is debated. Most historians favour the Ten Years' War of 1868 to 1878, and Anistatia Miller and Jared Brown write in Cuban Cocktails that it was certainly being drunk by 1898. The IBA now lists it in its New Era category, built in the glass with honey, lime, water and cracked ice.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Simple, rustic and refreshing. Honey gives a floral, rounded sweetness that pairs naturally with sharp lime, while the cane spirit adds grassy, slightly funky depth. The added water and cracked ice keep it light and easy to drink despite the generous pour of spirit. Less polished than a Daiquiri but more characterful, it suits hot afternoons and outdoor drinking.

cocktails.name: Cantaritos
cocktails.shortDescription: Tequila with orange, grapefruit and lime juices, salt and grapefruit soda: a Jalisco street drink served in clay pots.
instructions: If using a clay cantarito pot, soak it in cold water first to clean the inside and wet the outside.
Pour the tequila, orange, grapefruit and lime juices, salt and grapefruit soda into the ice-filled pot or a collins glass.
Stir briefly.
Garnish with a lime wedge and serve with a straw.
cocktails.history: The Cantarito is commonly served in bars, cafés and even roadside stalls across Jalisco, Mexico, the heartland of tequila. It takes its name from the small, rustic clay pots it is traditionally served in, which are made locally and often used as disposable takeaway cups. Wikipedia describes it as a tequila highball similar to the Paloma but with extra citrus juices, noting that the clay vessel helps keep the drink cold.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Juicy, salty-sour and invigorating. Fresh orange, pink grapefruit and lime juices create a bright, fruity base, reposado tequila adds earthy agave with a touch of oak, and a pinch of salt sharpens every flavour. Grapefruit soda lifts it with fizz and a pleasant bitterness. Served ice-cold in a wet clay pot, it is a perfect thirst-quencher for hot days and outdoor feasts.

cocktails.name: Carajillo (Shakeado)
cocktails.shortDescription: Licor 43 shaken hard with hot espresso until foamy: the Mexican shaken take on Spain's coffee-and-liquor Carajillo.

ingredients.note: Saline solution or a pinch of salt

cocktails.garnish: Three coffee beans floated in a petal formation
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients hard with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Float three coffee beans on the foamy head.
cocktails.history: The original layered Carajillo is thought to have been created by Spanish troops in Cuba, when the island was a Spanish province, who mixed coffee with rum for courage; coraje means courage in Spanish. The Carajillo remains popular in Spain, where it varies by region, from brandy poured into an espresso to brandy heated with lemon, sugar and cinnamon before coffee is added. In Catalan it is called a cigaló. This shaken, or shakeado, version made with Licor 43 emerged in Mexico, and Difford's Guide notes that it has exploded in popularity since around 2015.
