cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, rich and invigorating. Hot espresso gives roasted, bitter coffee flavours, and Licor 43 adds vanilla, citrus and warm spice sweetness that balances the bitterness. Shaking hard with ice cools the drink and creates a thick, creamy foam like an iced coffee crema, while a touch of salt rounds the flavours. It is a perfect after-dinner pick-me-up.

cocktails.name: Cardinale
cocktails.shortDescription: A dry, Negroni-like Roman aperitivo of gin, dry vermouth and Campari, stirred and served straight up.
instructions: Pour the gin, dry vermouth and Campari into a mixing glass with ice.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with a lemon zest.
cocktails.history:
Some sources attribute the Cardinale to Harry's Bar in Venice, but evidence gathered by Luca Di Francia of the Orum Bar at Rome's Westin Excelsior points to the hotel's bar in 1950, during Pope Pius XII's Holy Jubilee year. Difford's Guide reports that it was created by Giovanni Raimondo and named in honour of New York's Cardinal Spellman, a fitting name for a cardinal-red drink.

The original recipe used three parts gin, two parts Riesling wine and one part Campari, and the drink is still served at the Excelsior's bar today. When the IBA adopted the Cardinale as an official cocktail in 2024, it updated the recipe to gin, dry vermouth and Campari, stirred with ice and strained into a chilled glass.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, dry and gently bitter. Gin leads with juniper and citrus, dry vermouth adds a lean herbal, wine-like note, and a small measure of Campari brings colour and a bittersweet orange edge without the richness of a Negroni. The lemon zest lifts the aroma. Clean and appetising, it is an aperitif for those who find a Negroni too sweet.

cocktails.name: Casino
cocktails.shortDescription: An early-1900s sour of Old Tom gin, maraschino and lemon with orange bitters, like an Aviation without the violette.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest and a maraschino cherry
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled rocks glass filled with ice.
Garnish with a lemon zest and a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
For years the Casino was credited to Hugo Ensslin's 1916 Recipes for Mixed Drinks, but Difford's Guide reports that it first appeared in Jacob A. Didier's 1909 The Reminder: Bartender's Vest Pocket Guide. The two recipes are almost identical, suggesting Ensslin copied Didier: Old Tom gin with dashes of maraschino, orange bitters and lemon, stirred and served with a cherry.

Ensslin's book is better known as the first printed source for the Aviation, and the Casino is essentially a stirred Aviation without crème de violette. Harry Craddock repeated the recipe almost word for word in his 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, and in 1948 David Embury published a version with orange juice instead of orange bitters.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Clean and tart with a delicate sweetness. Old Tom gin is softer and slightly sweeter than London dry, and maraschino adds its distinctive cherry-almond, floral note. Lemon gives freshness, while orange bitters add a bitter peel aroma that ties everything together. Served on the rocks it opens up as it dilutes. A good pre-dinner drink for fans of the Aviation.

cocktails.name: Champagne Cocktail
cocktails.shortDescription: One of the oldest cocktails: a bitters-soaked sugar cube and a splash of cognac topped with chilled Champagne.

ingredients.note: a few drops of Grand Marnier

cocktails.garnish: Orange zest and a maraschino cherry
instructions: Place the sugar cube in a large Champagne glass and soak it with the bitters.
Add the cognac and, if using, a few drops of Grand Marnier.
Gently top up with chilled Champagne.
Garnish with an orange zest and a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide calls the Champagne Cocktail one of the oldest cocktails, dating to at least the mid-1800s. Its first known written mention is in Robert Tomes's 1855 account of Panama, which describes one made with bitters, sugar and Champagne poured over crushed ice in a tumbler, with no brandy at all.

Jerry Thomas also left out brandy in his 1862 book and served the drink over broken ice. By his 1887 edition it had moved to a goblet with a single lump of ice. The splash of cognac common today is a later addition.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry, elegant and gently evolving. The Champagne gives crisp acidity and fine bubbles, while the sugar cube slowly dissolves, so the drink becomes slightly sweeter as you go. Bitters add a warm spice note and a hint of colour, and the small measure of cognac brings depth and a little extra warmth. Ideal for celebrations, brunch or as an aperitif.

cocktails.name: Champagne Snowball
cocktails.shortDescription: Advocaat, fino sherry and lime cordial shaken and poured over sparkling wine: Difford's fizz-lifted take on the Snowball.

ingredients.note: Brut champagne or other sparkling wine

cocktails.garnish: Lime zest twist (discarded) and a dusting of cacao powder
instructions: Chill a flute and pour in the sparkling wine.
Shake the fino sherry, lime cordial and advocaat with ice.
Fine strain over the sparkling wine in the glass.
Express a lime zest twist over the drink and discard it, then dust with cacao powder.
cocktails.history: The original Snowball mixes the egg liqueur advocaat with carbonated lemonade in roughly equal parts, usually with a squeeze of lime shaken in. Difford's Guide describes it as hugely popular in the 1970s and says it is now enjoying a well-deserved revival. This Champagne Snowball is Simon Difford's own update: instead of lemonade, the advocaat is shaken with dry fino sherry and lime cordial and then poured over sparkling wine for a lighter, drier finish.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Creamy yet lively. The advocaat provides a rich custard-like body with vanilla and egg-nog notes, while fino sherry adds a dry, nutty, slightly salty edge that stops it from cloying. Lime cordial gives a tangy sweetness and the sparkling wine lifts everything with fine bubbles and toasty acidity. The cacao dusting adds a hint of chocolate. It makes a festive aperitif or a light dessert drink.

cocktails.name: Champs-Élysées
cocktails.shortDescription: A brandy sour and Sidecar riff with green Chartreuse, lemon, sugar and Angostura, first recorded in 1925.

ingredients.note: saline solution or a pinch of salt

instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Named for the grand boulevard in Paris, the Champs-Élysées is a variation on the Sidecar. Difford's Guide finds the first known recipe in Nina Toye and Arthur H. Adair's 1925 book Drinks Long and Short, which called for three glasses of brandy, one of Chartreuse and one and a half of sweetened lemon juice, shaken with a dash of Angostura Bitters. Difford's modern version keeps those ingredients and adds a little water and saline to fine-tune dilution and balance.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, herbal and warming. Cognac gives rich grape, dried fruit and oak, while green Chartreuse adds a lift of alpine herbs and spice. Lemon juice and sugar balance the drink as a classic sour, and Angostura deepens it with a hint of clove. Achieving the right dilution matters to keep it smooth. It rewards anyone who enjoys both cognac and Chartreuse, ideally after dinner.

cocktails.name: Charlie Chaplin
cocktails.shortDescription: Equal parts apricot liqueur, sloe gin and lime juice, shaken: a tart, fruity sour from the old Waldorf-Astoria bar.

ingredients.note: Chilled water for dilution; omit if using wet ice

cocktails.garnish: Apricot wedge or dried apricot half on the rim
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the apricot liqueur, sloe gin, lime juice and water with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with an apricot wedge or a dried apricot half on the rim.
cocktails.history: The drink takes its name from Charlie Chaplin, the English star of silent slapstick comedy, and according to Difford's Guide it was created at New York's original Waldorf-Astoria hotel bar some time before 1920, when Chaplin was at the peak of his fame. The recipe survives because Albert Stevens Crockett recorded it in his 1935 Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book, which gives it as equal thirds of lime juice, sloe gin and apricot brandy.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet-tart and fruit-led rather than boozy. Sloe gin brings dark plum and berry flavours with a gentle almond bitterness, the apricot liqueur adds rich stone-fruit sweetness, and an equal measure of lime cuts through both so the finish is bright and sharp. Light in alcohol and silky in texture, it works as an easy pre-dinner sour or a fruity introduction for guests who usually avoid strong drinks.

cocktails.name: Chartreuse Swizzle
cocktails.shortDescription: A modern San Francisco swizzle of green Chartreuse, pineapple, lime and falernum over crushed ice.
instructions: Pour all the ingredients into a tall glass and add pebble ice.
Swizzle vigorously with a swizzle stick or bar spoon.
Top with more pebble ice.
Garnish with mint leaves and grated nutmeg.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Chartreuse Swizzle to Marco Dionysos, who created it in 2002 at Tres Agaves in San Francisco. PUNCH describes it as a twenty-first-century reworking of the traditional Caribbean Rum Swizzle, with green Chartreuse taking the place of rum, and Imbibe calls it a San Francisco classic and one of the most iconic modern cocktails.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Herbal, tropical and refreshing. Green Chartreuse dominates with intense alpine herbs, mint and a little heat, but pineapple softens it with fruity sweetness and lime keeps it bright. Falernum adds lime-zest, clove and almond spice. Lots of crushed ice dilutes the high-strength liqueur and makes it very drinkable. A great summer drink for herbal-liqueur fans, with a pale green colour.

cocktails.name: Chicago Fizz
cocktails.shortDescription: Jamaican-style dark rum and tawny port shaken with lemon, sugar and egg white, topped with soda: a pre-Prohibition Windy City fizz.

ingredients.note: For shaking only; served without ice

cocktails.garnish: Quarter lemon wheel on the rim
instructions: Chill a highball glass (no ice).
Shake the rum, port, lemon juice, sugar syrup and egg white with ice, then strain back into the shaker.
Dry shake without ice to emulsify.
Pour two-thirds of the mix from a height into the glass while pouring the soda in the same stream.
Let it settle for a minute, then top with the rest of the shaker so the head rises.
Garnish with a quarter lemon wheel on the rim.
cocktails.history:
The Chicago Fizz first appears in Jacques Straub's book Drinks, which Difford's Guide dates to 1914: lemon juice, sugar, half a jigger each of Jamaica rum and port wine and an egg white, shaken, strained and filled from a soda siphon.

In his 1931 Old Waldorf Bar Days, Albert Stevens Crockett recalled the drink at New York's pre-Prohibition Waldorf-Astoria bar as an importation from the Windy City, hence its name, adding that it arrived long before gangland violence disturbed Chicago's peace. Difford's notes that since Prohibition the drink has been somewhat forgotten.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, fruity and frothy. Dark rum brings molasses and spice, tawny port adds nutty dried fruit and a gentle sweetness, and lemon juice gives the drink a lively sour edge. Egg white creates a silky, souffle-like head, while soda lightens the body and adds sparkle. Fuller than most fizzes yet still refreshing, it suits a late afternoon or brunch.

cocktails.name: Chrysanthemum
cocktails.shortDescription: Dry vermouth and Bénédictine stirred with a touch of absinthe: a light, herbal aperitif first printed by Hugo Ensslin in 1917.
instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Stir the dry vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
The Chrysanthemum is first recorded in Hugo R. Ensslin's Recipes for Mixed Drinks of 1917, and Difford's Guide suggests it may already have featured in the book's 1916 first edition. Ensslin's version was half Bénédictine and half French vermouth with a few dashes of absinthe and an orange twist.

Harry Craddock reprinted it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930, shifting the balance to two parts vermouth to one of Bénédictine and noting it was a favourite at the American Bar of the liner S.S. Europa. Difford's adds that the name may honour The Chrysanthemum, a 1904 ragtime piece by Scott Joplin.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A light, aromatic and low-strength stirred drink. Dry vermouth forms a crisp, winey base, Bénédictine adds honeyed sweetness and a herbal, spiced depth, and the small amount of absinthe threads anise through the finish. Orange oils brighten the aroma. Long stirring gives it a silky, delicate texture, making it a good aperitif for anyone who wants complexity without a heavy spirit backbone.

cocktails.name: Clover Club
cocktails.shortDescription: A silky, pink Philadelphia classic of gin, raspberry, lemon and egg white, named after a journalists' club.
instructions: Pour all ingredients into a cocktail shaker.
Shake well with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with fresh raspberries.
cocktails.history:
The drink takes its name from the Clover Club, a club founded in January 1882 by a group of prominent Philadelphia journalists. From 1883 until 1897 its members met every Thursday at the city's Hotel Bellevue, and over time the membership grew to include lawyers, bankers and leading businessmen.

The earliest known reference, found by historian David Wondrich, is a 1901 New York Press article. In it, a wine steward at the Waldorf-Astoria gave a recipe of egg white, lemon, raspberry syrup and Plymouth gin. Recipes appeared in cocktail books from 1909. In 1911 a newspaper described it as fashionable in New York, especially with women, and said it came from Philadelphia.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Silky, pink and gently tart. Raspberry syrup gives bright red-berry sweetness, and lemon adds acidity that keeps the fruit from becoming cloying. Egg white makes a soft, foamy head and a smooth, rounded texture, while gin keeps a dry juniper backbone. It is elegant and fruity but balanced, finishing clean rather than sugary.

cocktails.name: Coffee Cocktail
cocktails.shortDescription: Tawny port and cognac shaken with a whole egg and sugar under nutmeg: an 1887 Jerry Thomas flip that only looks like coffee.
instructions: Shake the port, cognac, syrup and egg very thoroughly with ice.
Strain back into the shaker and dry shake without ice.
Strain into a small goblet or wine glass.
Grate a little nutmeg on top.
cocktails.history:
The Coffee Cocktail is adapted from a recipe in the 1887 edition of Jerry Thomas's Bar-Tenders Guide, published after the Professor's death in December 1885. It called for powdered sugar, a fresh egg, a large glass of port and a pony of brandy, shaken thoroughly with ice, strained into a bar goblet and finished with grated nutmeg.

The book itself admits the name is a misnomer, as the drink contains neither coffee nor bitters. It was probably so called because, properly mixed, it looks like a cup of coffee, with a creamy brown colour and a frothy head.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, velvety and gently sweet, like a fortified wine flip. Tawny port brings nutty, raisined and caramel notes, cognac adds warmth and dried-fruit depth, and the whole egg gives a thick, custard-like texture with a creamy foam. A little sugar rounds it out and grated nutmeg adds warm spice. Low in harshness and big on comfort, it is an ideal after-dinner or winter-evening drink.

cocktails.name: Combustible Edison
cocktails.shortDescription: Campari, lemon and sugar with a flaming stream of cognac poured in: a theatrical 1990s drink from the lounge band of the same name.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir the Campari, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice and strain into the glass.
Warm the cognac in a metal ladle, ignite it and carefully pour it from a height as a flaming stream into the glass. Take great care.
Express a flamed lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The Combustible Edison takes its name from the 1990s lounge band Combustible Edison. Difford's Guide says it was created in that decade by the band's leader, Michael "The Millionaire" Cudahy, and the drink appeared on the back cover of the band's first CD, I, Swinger. Difford's recipe is adapted from one by another band member, Robert "Brother Cleve" Toomey, a respected bartender, DJ and musician, and it is now listed among Difford's Modern Classics.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet, citrusy and warming. Campari gives bitter orange and herbal notes, lemon juice and a little sugar turn it into a tart sour, and the flamed cognac adds rich dried fruit, a hint of caramelisation and plenty of warmth. The flaming pour is mostly theatre, but it slightly softens the brandy. A dramatic party drink for the evening.

cocktails.name: Comte de Sureau
cocktails.shortDescription: A stirred "Elderflower Negroni" of gin, elderflower liqueur and a little bitter red aperitivo, created in Hamburg.

ingredients.note: preferably a large cube or block ice

instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass, ideally over a large cube.
Express orange and lemon zest twists over the drink and use both as garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the Comte de Sureau is adapted from a recipe created in 2007 or 2008 by Gonçalo de Sousa Monteiro at Le Lion, a bar in Hamburg, Germany. The drink pairs gin with a generous measure of elderflower liqueur and just a splash of bitter red aperitivo, and its bittersweet balance has led many drinkers to call it the Elderflower Negroni. Difford's lists it among its modern classics and Cocktail Hall of Fame drinks.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Floral, bittersweet and smooth. Gin supplies juniper and citrus backbone, elderflower liqueur adds a lush, honeyed blossom sweetness, and a small dose of red bitter aperitivo brings a gentle orange-peel bitterness and blush colour. The oils from both orange and lemon zests are key to its fine balance. Lighter and more floral than a Negroni, it makes an elegant aperitivo.

cocktails.name: Corn 'n' Oil
cocktails.shortDescription: Aged rum and falernum stirred with bitters over crushed ice, sometimes with a dark rum float: a Barbadian planters' drink.
instructions: Stir the aged rum, falernum and bitters with ice.
Strain into an old fashioned glass filled with crushed ice.
Optionally float the dark rum on the surface.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
cocktails.history:
The Corn 'n' Oil began as a traditional Barbadian planters' drink and evolved into today's cocktail over the course of the twentieth century. Its name is said to come from the Book of Deuteronomy, in a verse in which Moses promises rain so that the people may gather in their corn, wine and oil.

The drink became better known thanks to a recipe printed on the back label of John D. Taylor's Velvet Falernum, the best-selling falernum brand, which called for Barbados rum stirred with falernum over ice. Difford's Guide notes that the dark rum float is not traditional in Barbados, though it improves the look.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, spiced and spirit-forward. Aged rum provides caramel, vanilla and dried fruit, while falernum adds gentle sweetness and its signature lime-zest, clove and almond flavours. Aromatic bitters deepen the spice, and crushed ice brings chill and dilution. An optional float of dark blackstrap rum adds a molasses-heavy first sip and the oil-slick look of the name. A fine evening sipper.

cocktails.name: Coronation
cocktails.shortDescription: Dry sherry and dry vermouth stirred with maraschino and orange bitters: a light 1900s aperitif named for Edward VII's coronation.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon (or orange) zest twist, discarded, and a skewered green olive
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon or orange zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a skewered green olive.
cocktails.history:
The Coronation was created for, or soon after, the coronation of Edward VII, who became king on Queen Victoria's death in January 1901. His crowning, set for June 1902, was postponed to 9 August 1902 after emergency surgery for appendicitis.

The drink first appears in Charles S. Mahoney's 1905 Hoffman House Bartender's Guide, which credits it to Joseph Rose of Murray Bros.' Café in Newark, New Jersey, and notes that it won second prize in the 1903 Police Gazette Bartenders' Contest. Mahoney's version was sherry-heavy; Difford's adapts Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy recipe of equal sherry and French vermouth.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry, delicate and savoury. Fino sherry brings a crisp, nutty and slightly saline character, and dry vermouth adds herbal and floral notes. A small amount of maraschino gives a hint of cherry-pit sweetness and orange bitters add aroma and depth. Low in alcohol and very appetising, especially with its olive garnish, it is an ideal pre-dinner aperitif.

cocktails.name: Corpse Reviver #2
cocktails.shortDescription: A bright, equal-parts sour of gin, orange liqueur, Lillet Blanc and lemon with an absinthe dash, from the Savoy era.
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with an orange zest.
cocktails.history:
Corpse Revivers belong to the family of 'pick-me-up' drinks that nineteenth-century bartenders served to customers suffering from the night before. Difford's Guide finds the name in an 1861 issue of Punch magazine, and the first known recipe, of brandy, maraschino and bitters, in the 1871 Gentleman's Table Guide.

The version drunk today comes from Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, which gave equal parts lemon, Kina Lillet, Cointreau and gin with a dash of absinthe, and warned that four taken in quick succession would 'unrevive' the corpse again.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sharp, zesty and refreshing. Lemon and orange liqueur give a lively citrus core, Lillet Blanc adds a soft, floral wine note and a hint of bitterness, and gin brings botanical structure. The tiny amount of absinthe lifts the aroma with anise without taking over. Balanced between sweet and sour, light on its feet and surprisingly strong, it makes an excellent brunch or aperitif drink.

cocktails.name: Corpse Reviver No.1
cocktails.shortDescription: Cognac, calvados and sweet vermouth stirred with orange bitters: the brandy-based Savoy 'reviver' meant for mornings.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The Corpse Reviver No.1 is generally credited to Frank Meier, who ran the bar at the Ritz in Paris in the 1920s and 1930s, although Meier makes no claim to it in his own 1936 book, The Artistry of Mixing Drinks. Its first known recipe is in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book: half brandy with a quarter each of Italian vermouth and apple brandy or calvados, to be taken before 11 a.m. or whenever steam and energy are needed. Difford's Guide follows the version of Frank Caiafa, author of The Waldorf Astoria Bar Book, who adds a dash of orange bitters and specifies the assertive Carpano Antica vermouth.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, fruity and warming. Cognac provides a smooth base of dried fruit, vanilla and oak, calvados adds a crisp baked-apple note, and sweet vermouth brings dark fruit, spice and a gentle bitterness. A dash of orange bitters and the orange twist brighten the aroma. Spirit-forward and rounded, it is better suited to a nightcap than its morning reputation suggests.

cocktails.name: Cosmonaut
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, lemon juice and raspberry jam shaken and served up: Sasha Petraske's tart, fruity Milk & Honey sour.

ingredients.note: raspberry jam or preserves, about 15-20 ml

instructions: Stir the gin, lemon juice and raspberry jam together in the base of a shaker until the jam dissolves.
Shake with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a skewered raspberry.
cocktails.history: The Cosmonaut was created by Sasha Petraske at his Milk & Honey bar in New York City. In Georgette Moger-Petraske's 2016 book Sasha Petraske: Regarding Cocktails, his former colleague Michael Madrusan explains that Petraske chose the name as a dig at the popularity of the Cosmopolitan, a drink the Cosmonaut emphatically does not resemble. The book's recipe is simply gin, fresh lemon juice and a heaped bar spoon of raspberry preserves, shaken and served in a coupe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, fruity and tart. Raspberry jam gives deep colour, a jammy berry sweetness and a slightly fuller texture than a syrup would, while plenty of lemon juice keeps it sharp and lively. Gin's juniper and botanicals hold the fruit in check so it never becomes sugary. Simple yet rich in flavour, it is a cheerful drink for a summer evening or a weekend brunch.

cocktails.name: Cosmopolitan
cocktails.shortDescription: The tart, pink vodka sour with cranberry, orange liqueur and lime that defined late-20th-century cocktail culture.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a large cocktail glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
cocktails.history:
Several bartenders have a claim to the Cosmopolitan. Drawing on research by Miss Charming, Difford's Guide reports that Neal Murray mixed a pink combination of a Cape Codder and a Kamikaze in Minnesota in 1975. He later spread it in San Francisco, where the drink circulated during the late 1970s and 1980s.

Separately, Cheryl Cook has a well-supported claim to a version made with the new Absolut Citron at The Strand in Miami in the late 1980s. In New York, Melissa Huffsmith and Toby Cecchini upgraded it with fresh lime and Cointreau at The Odeon. Dale DeGroff later helped popularise it.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tart, fruity and crisp. Citrus vodka and Cointreau give bright lemon and orange notes, fresh lime adds a sharp, refreshing acidity, and cranberry juice contributes a light, dry berry flavour and the signature pale pink colour. It is cleaner and less sweet than its reputation suggests, with a light body and a zesty finish lifted by the lemon twist.

cocktails.name: Cuba Libre
cocktails.shortDescription: Rum and cola brightened with lime, the easy-going highball tied to Havana around 1900.
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Build the rum, lime juice and cola in the glass.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
cocktails.history:
The most widely told story, which Difford's Guide notes follows Bacardi's account, places the Cuba Libre in Havana around 1900. American soldiers were stationed in Cuba after the war with Spain, and Coca-Cola had recently reached the island. A Captain Russell of the US Signal Corps is said to have ordered rum and cola with lime in a Havana bar. His toast to a free Cuba, "Por Cuba libre", gave the drink its name.

The story rests on a sworn statement made in 1964 by a witness, Fausto Rodriguez. The drink was hugely popular in America in the 1940s, helped by the Andrews Sisters' 1945 hit "Rum and Coca-Cola" and by wartime shortages of whiskey and gin, which pushed drinkers toward Caribbean rum.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Easy, refreshing and familiar. Cola provides sweetness, caramel and spice, and white rum adds a light, clean sugarcane warmth without dominating. The squeeze of lime is what turns a simple rum and cola into a Cuba Libre, cutting the sweetness with acidity and adding fresh citrus aroma. It is long, fizzy and very cold, ideal for casual drinking.

cocktails.name: Daiquiri
cocktails.shortDescription: Cuba's crisp three-ingredient classic of white rum, lime and sugar, and the benchmark for a balanced sour.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker and stir to dissolve the sugar.
Add ice and shake.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Daiquiri is credited to Jennings Stockton Cox, an American mining engineer working near the small town of Daiquirí in southeastern Cuba around 1898. Difford's Guide reports that he experimented with the local Bacardi rum, mixing it with limes and sugar. A fellow engineer, Francesco Pagliuchi, later wrote a letter in 1948 backing Cox's claim.

The drink is closely related to the older Cuban Canchanchara. US Admiral Lucius Johnson tasted it with Cox in 1909 and brought it to the Army & Navy Club in Washington. Its first appearance in a recipe book was Jacques Straub's 1914 Drinks.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, clean and perfectly simple. Light rum provides a gentle sugarcane sweetness and subtle vanilla, fresh lime brings vivid, mouth-watering sourness, and fine sugar rounds off the edges. Shaken hard and served very cold, it is bright and refreshing, with sweet and sour in close balance and no single flavour dominating. It is a benchmark for how good a three-ingredient sour can be.

cocktails.name: Daisy Buchanan
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey stirred with dry vermouth, Aperol-style aperitivo and Yellow Chartreuse: Joaquín Simó's 2009 Death & Co creation.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a skewered maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history: Joaquín Simó created the Daisy Buchanan in 2009 at Death & Company in Manhattan, New York City. He named it after Daisy Fay Buchanan, the wealthy socialite at the heart of F. Scott Fitzgerald's 1925 novel The Great Gatsby. The recipe pairs rye whiskey with dry vermouth, a bittersweet orange aperitivo and a touch of Yellow Chartreuse, and Difford's Guide lists it among its Modern Classics.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry, elegant and gently bittersweet. Rye whiskey provides spice and structure, dry vermouth adds a crisp herbal lift, and the Aperol-style aperitivo brings orange peel, rhubarb and a soft bitterness. A small measure of Yellow Chartreuse rounds it with honeyed herbal sweetness. It is lighter on its feet than a Manhattan but still spirit-forward, ideal as a sophisticated pre-dinner drink.

cocktails.name: Daisy de Santiago
cocktails.shortDescription: Cuban rum, lime and sugar over crushed ice with a float of Yellow Chartreuse: Charles H. Baker's 1939 favourite.

ingredients.note: Lightly aged Cuban rum (Havana Club Añejo 3 Años)
7.5 ml shaken + 5 ml drizzled on top
For shaking, plus crushed ice in the glass

cocktails.garnish: Seasonal berries and mint sprigs dusted with icing sugar, or a dehydrated lime wheel
instructions: Fill a wine glass or goblet with crushed ice.
Shake the rum, lime juice, 7.5 ml Yellow Chartreuse and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain over the crushed ice.
Drizzle the remaining Yellow Chartreuse over the drink.
Garnish with berries and a mint bouquet dusted with icing sugar, or a lime wheel.
cocktails.history:
The Daisy de Santiago comes from Charles H. Baker Jr.'s 1939 The Gentleman's Companion, volume II, An Exotic Drinking Book. Baker says the drink was introduced to him through the late Facundo Bacardi, and he recalls the company's generous factory tours for visiting yachtsmen and its free bar in a Havana skyscraper. He rated it, alongside the Daiquiri, the best Bacardi drink on record.

Baker's method was to stir rum, lime juice and optional syrup, pour it over a goblet of shaved ice, garnish with mint and fruit, and float Yellow Chartreuse on top, adding that a squirt of soda gives it sparkle. He also felt the Chartreuse supplied all the sweetening the drink needed.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A crisp, herbal Daiquiri on crushed ice. Light Cuban rum and fresh lime give a clean, zesty sourness, while Yellow Chartreuse adds honey, saffron and gentle alpine herbs, both mixed in and floated on top so the aroma is fragrant from the first sip. The crushed ice keeps it very cold and slowly dilutes it. Refreshing and elegant, it is a perfect summer afternoon drink.

cocktails.name: Dark 'n' Stormy
cocktails.shortDescription: Bermuda's national drink: dark rum floated over spicy ginger beer, bold and refreshing.
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the ginger beer.
Float the rum on top.
Garnish with a lime wedge or slice.
cocktails.history: The Dark 'n' Stormy is regarded as the national drink of Bermuda, which produces both ginger beer and Gosling's rum, the dark rum most associated with it. Difford's Guide says nobody knows who first mixed or named it. Legend has it that British sailors on shore leave in Bermuda after the First World War created it, or at least enjoyed it first. Difford's places it in the Mule family of spirit and ginger drinks, and the IBA recipe names Gosling's rum.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bold and spicy. Dark rum brings molasses, caramel and dried-fruit richness, floating in a dark layer at first before it mixes in. Ginger beer adds sweetness, plenty of fizz and a peppery ginger heat that builds with each sip. A squeeze of the lime garnish adds welcome acidity. The drink is long and refreshing yet full-flavoured, with a warming finish.

cocktails.name: Dawa
cocktails.shortDescription: Muddled lime, vodka, honey and brown sugar over crushed ice: a Caipirinha-inspired 1980s favourite from Nairobi, Kenya.

ingredients.note: neat honey, on a honey dipper or spoon

cocktails.garnish: Honey dipper stick left in the glass as a stirrer
instructions: Core half a lime, cut it into six chunks and drop them into a double old fashioned glass.
Muddle the lime chunks in the base of the glass.
Add the vodka and a honey-coated dipper stick (or a bar spoon of honey) and stir until the honey dissolves.
Add the brown sugar syrup, fill with crushed ice and leave the dipper in the glass for further stirring.
cocktails.history: The Dawa was inspired by Brazil's Caipirinha and first made and named during the 1980s at the Carnivore Restaurant in Nairobi, Kenya. It has become especially popular in upmarket Kenyan hotel bars frequented by visitors on safari. The name means "medicine" in Kiswahili. Difford's Guide notes that in Kenya a similar name, Dowa, is also used for a hot, non-alcoholic drink of honey, ginger and lime juice made with hot water.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Zesty, sweet and refreshing. Muddled lime releases sharp juice and fragrant oils from the peel, honey adds a floral, rounded sweetness, and brown sugar syrup gives a hint of caramel depth. Clean vodka lets these flavours lead, and crushed ice keeps the drink cold while slowly diluting it. Like a honeyed Caipiroska, it is a great choice for hot afternoons and outdoor drinking.

cocktails.name: Diamondback
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey stirred with calvados and Yellow Chartreuse: a potent, herbal Baltimore hotel cocktail first printed in 1951.

ingredients.note: chilled; omit if using wet ice

instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Stir the rye, calvados, Yellow Chartreuse and water with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a skewered cherry.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide adapts the Diamondback from Ted Saucier's 1951 book Bottoms Up, where it appears as the Diamondback Lounge, courtesy of the Lord Baltimore Hotel in Baltimore, Maryland. Saucier's recipe used two parts rye to one each of applejack and yellow Chartreuse, shaken and served over cracked ice with mint. The hotel opened in 1928 and still stands, though the lounge itself is long gone.

Both the bar and the drink take their name from the diamondback terrapin, a turtle of the tidal marshes of America's east coast with a diamond-patterned shell. It has been the University of Maryland's mascot since 1932 and is Maryland's state reptile.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A potent, rich and herbal sipper. High-proof rye provides spice and a firm backbone, calvados adds baked apple and orchard fruit, and Yellow Chartreuse brings honeyed sweetness with saffron, citrus and alpine herbs. Stirring with a little water smooths the strength without hiding the layered flavours. Warming and complex, it is best saved for after dinner or as a nightcap.

cocktails.name: Dirty Banana
cocktails.shortDescription: A Jamaican frozen drink blending rum, coffee liqueur, banana liqueur, cream and a whole ripe banana.
instructions: Cut a banana chunk for garnish from the centre of the banana.
Blend the rest of the banana with all other ingredients and a 12 oz scoop of crushed ice.
Pour into a chilled poco grande or hurricane glass.
Garnish with the banana chunk on the rim.
cocktails.history: The Dirty Banana is a popular drink in Jamaica, where Difford's Guide discovered it in the 1990s. The recipe is essentially a blended, rum-laced banana milkshake made "dirty" with coffee liqueur. Difford's notes that it is filling enough to be a dessert and suggests sharing it between two glasses or making a half-sized version with lighter rum, less liqueur and half a banana. It sits in Difford's Cocktail Hall of Fame and modern classics lists.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Creamy, fruity and indulgent. Ripe banana and banana liqueur give a deep, sweet tropical flavour, coffee liqueur adds roasted bitterness and caramel, and rum provides warmth beneath. Blended with cream and crushed ice, it is thick and frosty like a milkshake. The riper the banana, the better it tastes. A beach-bar dessert drink best shared on a hot afternoon.

cocktails.name: Dirty Martini
cocktails.shortDescription: A savoury gin Martini made cloudy and salty with green olive brine, garnished with skewered olives.
instructions: Pre-chill a martini glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with skewered olives.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide cites cocktail historian David Wondrich, who traced the Dirty Martini back to 1901 and a bartender named John E. O'Connor, who served a Dry Martini with muddled olives at New York's Waldorf Astoria. The first written reference to adding brine to a Martini-style drink appears in G. H. Steele's 1930 My New Cocktail Book. President Franklin D. Roosevelt is often linked to the drink, hence the nickname F.D.R. Martini, but Difford's finds no evidence that he used olive brine, and his Martinis were reportedly horrendous.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Salty, savoury and bracingly cold. Ice-cold gin delivers juniper and citrus, dry vermouth adds a subtle herbal note, and olive brine gives a briny, umami-rich depth and a slightly cloudy look. The amount of brine is a matter of taste; Difford's settles on a middle-of-the-road measure. Served very cold with olives, it is a classic aperitif for lovers of savoury flavours.

cocktails.name: Division Bell
cocktails.shortDescription: Phil Ward's smoky 2009 Last Word variation of mezcal, Aperol-style aperitivo, maraschino and lime.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express a grapefruit zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Division Bell to Phil Ward, who created it in 2009 at Mayahuel in Manhattan, New York City. Ward had already made his name with the Final Ward, and here he again works from the template of the Last Word, using mezcal as the base, a bittersweet orange aperitivo in place of Chartreuse, maraschino liqueur and lime juice. Difford's files it among more than 50 Last Word variations and lists it as a modern classic.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smoky, bittersweet and refreshing. Mezcal brings earthy agave and gentle smoke, while the Aperol-style aperitivo adds bright orange and rhubarb with a light bitter edge. Maraschino lends a funky cherry-almond sweetness, and lime juice keeps the drink tangy and clean. The grapefruit twist adds a fresh citrus aroma. It works as an aperitif or alongside a barbecue on a warm evening.

cocktails.name: Doctor Funk
cocktails.shortDescription: Dark rum, absinthe, grenadine, lemon and lime over crushed ice: Don Beach's 1950s tiki take on a Samoan doctor's tonic.
instructions: Shake the dark rum, absinthe, grenadine, sugar syrup and lemon and lime juices with ice.
Strain into a double old fashioned glass filled with crushed ice.
Garnish with a lime wedge and serve with a straw.
cocktails.history:
Don Beach created the Doctor Funk in the early 1950s at his Don the Beachcomber restaurant in Palm Springs. He adapted a medicinal absinthe limeade devised decades earlier by Dr Bernard Funk, a German physician in Samoa who arrived there in 1880.

Funk was the personal doctor of Robert Louis Stevenson, author of Treasure Island, who settled in Samoa in 1890 and suffered from lifelong bronchial trouble. The doctor reportedly prescribed him a tonic of absinthe, lemon and lime juices, grenadine and soda, a potion described by Frederick O'Brien in his 1921 book Mystic Isles of the South Seas.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, fruity and potent with a hint of anise. A generous measure of dark rum brings molasses and caramel depth, lemon and lime juices add sharp citrus, and grenadine contributes pomegranate-red sweetness and colour. A small splash of absinthe threads a faint liquorice note through the whole drink. Served over crushed ice, it is a bold tiki sipper for warm evenings.

cocktails.name: Don's Special Daiquiri
cocktails.shortDescription: Donn Beach's blended Daiquiri twist with gold Jamaican and Cuban rums, passion fruit syrup, honey and lime.
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a blender with crushed ice.
Blend for a few seconds.
Pour into a footed glass.
Top with more crushed ice and garnish with half a passion fruit.
cocktails.history:
PUNCH describes Don's Special Daiquiri as a Daiquiri twice removed. It descends from the Mona Daiquiri, which Donn Beach created in 1934 around a 30-year-old Myers's 'Mona' rum, the spirit that gave the drink its name, adding passion fruit and honey syrups to the classic rum, lime and sugar formula.

When Mona rum was discontinued in 1946, Beach, who believed that several rums could do what one could not, reworked the drink with a blend of gold Jamaican and light rums, and the result became known as Don's Special Daiquiri. Wikipedia credits Beach with founding tiki culture at his Hollywood bar, opened in 1933.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tropical, rounded and lightly tart. The gold Jamaican rum brings rich, funky molasses notes while the lighter rum keeps it lively. Passion fruit syrup gives a perfumed, tangy fruitiness and honey adds a soft floral sweetness, both kept in check by fresh lime. Flash-blending with crushed ice makes it frosty and smooth. A sunny, easy-drinking tiki sour for hot days.

cocktails.name: Downhill Daring
cocktails.shortDescription: A modern stirred bourbon drink with Punt e Mes, Cocchi Americano and Bénédictine, created in Washington, D.C. in 2019.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Stir all the ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: Downhill Daring is named after a work by the American painter and illustrator Norman Rockwell (1894–1978). Difford's Guide adapts its recipe from one created in 2019 by Brian Nixon at the Truxton Inn in Washington, D.C. Difford's describes it as a rich and characterful riff on a sweet Manhattan, built on a large measure of Punt e Mes with bourbon, Cocchi Americano and Bénédictine, and lists it among its modern classics.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, layered and bittersweet. Punt e Mes leads with dark, bitter-edged vermouth notes, bourbon adds vanilla and caramel warmth, Cocchi Americano brings a lighter, citrusy quinine bitterness, and Bénédictine contributes honey and herbs. Two kinds of bitters add spice and orange peel. Smooth and spirit-forward but not overly strong, it is an excellent nightcap or sipping drink for Manhattan fans.

cocktails.name: Dry Daiquiri
cocktails.shortDescription: Light rum, lime and a little Campari with a touch of passion fruit syrup: Kevin Armstrong's bittersweet mid-2000s London Daiquiri.

ingredients.note: Lightly aged Cuban rum (Havana Club Añejo 3 Años)
Saline solution or a pinch of salt

instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Flame an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The Dry Daiquiri was created around 2005 by Kevin Armstrong at Match Bar in London. Difford's Guide says its journey to becoming a contemporary classic began in 2006 or 2007, when it was added to the menu at Trailer Happiness in London's Notting Hill. The recipe keeps the Daiquiri's rum and lime but swaps much of the sugar for Campari and a little passion fruit syrup, giving a drier, more bittersweet result.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, tart and subtly bitter. Light rum provides a clean sugar-cane base and lime juice a bright, sharp acidity, as in a classic Daiquiri. Campari adds bitter orange and a pale blush, a touch of passion fruit syrup brings a tropical fragrance, and a little salt sharpens the flavours. Drier than most Daiquiris, it is a refreshing aperitif.

cocktails.name: Dry Martini
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin and dry vermouth stirred ice-cold: the bracing, elegant cocktail of uncertain origin that became an icon.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon peel oils expressed over the drink, or green olives on request
instructions: Pour the gin and dry vermouth into a mixing glass with ice cubes.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled martini glass.
Express lemon peel oils over the drink, or garnish with green olives if requested.
cocktails.history:
Nobody knows exactly where the Martini began. Difford's Guide reports the widely accepted theory that it evolved from the Martinez, itself a descendant of the Manhattan, during a period full of similar gin and vermouth drinks. Harry Johnson printed the first known "Martini" recipe in 1888, and it was sweet.

Over time the drink became drier. The first known recipe actually titled "Dry Martini Cocktail" appeared in a 1904 French book by Frank P. Newman, a bartender at the Ritz in Paris. It called for equal parts gin and dry vermouth with bitters. Ratios kept shifting toward less vermouth through the 20th century.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bracing, cold and elegant. Gin dominates, so juniper, citrus peel and other botanicals lead the palate, while the small measure of dry vermouth adds a subtle herbal, wine-like dryness and a silky texture. Stirring keeps it crystal clear and very cold. A twist of lemon adds a bright aromatic lift, while olives instead give a faintly briny, savoury edge.

cocktails.name: Eastern Standard (Soho House Tonic)
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin shaken with muddled cucumber, mint, lime and sugar: a Soho House take on the Eastside, itself a Southside cousin.
instructions: Muddle the cucumber slices in the base of a shaker, ideally peeled first.
Add the mint, gin, lime juice and sugar syrup.
Shake with ice and fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Float a thin cucumber slice on top as garnish.
cocktails.history: The Eastern Standard belongs to the Soho House group's range of "House Tonic" cocktails. Difford's Guide describes it as being based on the Eastside, a drink that was itself inspired by the older Southside. The recipe Difford's publishes calls for muddled cucumber and fresh mint shaken with gin, lime and sugar, and is served straight up in a coupe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fresh, green and thoroughly refreshing. Muddled cucumber gives a cool, watery crispness, mint adds a bright herbal lift, and gin supplies juniper and botanical depth. Lime and sugar are in close balance, so the drink is gently sour rather than sharp. Light and clean on the palate, it is perfect for warm afternoons, garden parties and anyone who likes a Mojito or Southside.

cocktails.name: Eastside Gimlet
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin shaken with muddled cucumber, mint, lime and sugar, served up: a cool 2004 New York riff on the Southside and Gimlet.
cocktails.garnish: Mint leaf pegged to the rim and a cucumber slice floated on top
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Muddle the cucumber in the base of a shaker, then add the mint and press lightly just to bruise it.
Add the gin, lime juice and syrup and shake with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass and top with the soda water.
Garnish with a mint leaf on the rim and a floating cucumber slice.
cocktails.history: The Eastside was created in 2004 by George Delgado at Libation in Manhattan, New York City, originally served as a long drink. Christy Pope later took it to Milk & Honey, where this popular straight-up version was developed. It is a riff on both the Southside and the Gimlet, and Difford's Guide suggests the cucumber was inspired by the then-recent launch of Hendrick's Gin, which is known for its cucumber notes.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Cool, green and refreshing. Fresh cucumber gives a clean, garden-fresh character and lightly bruised mint adds a gentle, aromatic lift, while gin brings juniper and citrus botanicals. Fresh lime supplies a bright, tart edge and rich syrup balances it, with a splash of soda adding a faint sparkle. Light and crisp, it is an ideal warm-weather drink or a fresh aperitif before dinner.

cocktails.name: Eggnog
cocktails.shortDescription: Cognac and aged rum shaken with a whole egg, milk and sugar under grated nutmeg: a quick single-serve take on the Christmas classic.

ingredients.note: whole; use cream for a thicker drink

instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice.
Shake the cognac, rum, syrup, milk and egg with ice.
Strain back into the shaker and dry shake without ice.
Fine strain into the ice-filled glass.
Dust with freshly grated nutmeg.
cocktails.history:
Eggnog is a vintage Christmas drink; Difford's Guide notes that George Washington famously made his own. It is traditionally prepared in batches by whisking egg yolks with sugar, mixing milk, cream and spirits separately, then folding in beaten egg white. Difford's offers a quick single-serve shaken version instead.

According to Wikipedia, the drink's origins and the meaning of 'nog' are debated, and it may descend from posset, a medieval hot milk drink. The word eggnog is first recorded in a 1775 poem by Maryland clergyman Jonathan Boucher, and first appeared in print in a New Jersey newspaper in 1788.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, creamy and comforting, like a boozy thickened milkshake. Cognac brings dried fruit and gentle oak, aged rum adds molasses and vanilla, and the whole egg and milk give a velvety, custard-like body once shaken. Sugar syrup sweetens it and freshly grated nutmeg adds the classic warm, festive spice. Indulgent but not heavy in single-serve form, it is a natural choice for Christmas and cold winter evenings.

cocktails.name: El Diablo
cocktails.shortDescription: Tequila, crème de cassis and lime topped with ginger beer: a fruity, spicy highball popularised by Trader Vic in 1946.
instructions: Shake the tequila, crème de cassis and lime juice with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled collins glass.
Top with ginger beer and stir briefly.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
cocktails.history:
The drink began as the "Diablo" in the tropical specialties section of Hyman Gale and Gerald F. Marco's 1940 book The How and When, made with white rum, lime, crème de cassis and ginger ale. Trader Vic Bergeron's 1946 Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink is the first to swap in tequila, calling it the "Mexican El Diablo" and marking it as a house original.

By his 1968 Pacific Island Cookbook the name had shrunk to "El Diablo". Difford's Guide concludes that Bergeron adapted rather than invented the drink, and doubts claims it was created for his Señor Pico restaurants, which only opened in 1964.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bold, fruity and refreshing. Reposado tequila provides an earthy, peppery agave base, crème de cassis adds deep blackcurrant sweetness and a vivid purple-red colour, and lime keeps the balance sour and bright. Ginger beer lengthens the drink with fizz and a spicy kick. Not subtle, but easy to love, it is a great choice for hot days, barbecues and parties.

cocktails.name: El Presidente
cocktails.shortDescription: A Cuban stirred classic of lightly aged rum, dry and bianco vermouth, orange curaçao and a touch of grenadine.

ingredients.note: saline solution or a pinch of salt

instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: El Presidente is thought to date from the mid-1910s in Havana. The earliest known recipe was found in Cuba's Biblioteca Nacional by historian Fernando Castellon, in John B. Escalante's Manual del Cantinero, published in Havana in 1915. David Wondrich credits the drink to Constantino Ribalaigua, based on a 1937 interview, and calls it a Cuban answer to the Manhattan. By 1919 a New York newspaper called it a favourite of the Cubans, and in 1928 Basil Woon named it the aristocrat of cocktails. Vintage recipes balance rich grenadine with vermouth rather than lime juice.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Delicate, smooth and subtly fruity. Lightly aged rum gives soft vanilla and sugar-cane notes, dry vermouth adds herbal crispness while bianco vermouth brings floral sweetness, and orange curaçao contributes bright citrus. A small measure of grenadine adds a pink blush and gentle berry sweetness. Elegant and easy to sip, it suits drinkers who like a Manhattan but want something lighter.

cocktails.name: Enzoni
cocktails.shortDescription: A Negroni-inspired sour of muddled green grapes, gin, Campari, lemon and sugar, created by Vincenzo Errico in 2001.
cocktails.garnish: Skewered orange slice and/or green grape
instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass.
Muddle the grapes in the base of a shaker.
Add the other ingredients and shake with ice.
Fine strain into the ice-filled glass.
Garnish with a skewered orange slice and/or a grape.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide attributes the Enzoni to Vincenzo Errico, who created it in 2001 at Match Bar in London. His original recipe muddled six green grapes with a larger measure of London dry gin, a smaller dose of Campari, lemon juice and simple syrup. Difford's current version evens out the gin and the bitter red aperitivo and uses rich sugar syrup. The drink sits on Difford's Cocktail Hall of Fame and modern classics lists and has spawned seasonal riffs such as the Fall Enzoni.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Think of a Negroni crossed with a fruity sour. Muddled green grapes give fresh, juicy sweetness and a soft body, while Campari brings bittersweet orange and gentian. Gin adds juniper backbone and lemon keeps the finish clean and zesty. Served over ice, it is lighter and more refreshing than a Negroni, ideal as an aperitif on a warm evening.

cocktails.name: Espresso Martini
cocktails.shortDescription: Dick Bradsell's 1980s pick-me-up of vodka, coffee liqueur and fresh espresso, shaken to a creamy foam.
instructions: Pour all ingredients into a cocktail shaker.
Shake well with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with three coffee beans.
cocktails.history:
London bartender Dick Bradsell created the drink around 1983 at the Soho Brasserie on Old Compton Street, according to Difford's Guide. It was then called the Vodka Espresso and served on the rocks. A customer, said to be a model, asked for something that would wake her up and get her drunk. The coffee machine sat right beside Bradsell's station, and vodka was the fashionable spirit.

In 1997, while Bradsell was working at Match bar in Clerkenwell, a colleague served it straight up in a martini glass, during the 1990s craze for vodka "martinis". Bradsell adjusted the recipe, and in 1998 he renamed it the Pharmaceutical Stimulant for Damien Hirst's Pharmacy restaurant in Notting Hill.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, bittersweet and energising. Fresh espresso gives roasted, slightly bitter coffee flavour and, when shaken hot and hard, a creamy tan foam on top. Coffee liqueur adds sweetness and hints of vanilla and caramel, and a touch of sugar syrup balances the coffee's bitterness. Vodka provides clean strength. It is silky and dessert-like, but the finish is dry and coffee-forward.

cocktails.name: Fancy Free
cocktails.shortDescription: Bourbon stirred with maraschino liqueur and aromatic and orange bitters: a 1940 recipe now served as an improved Old Fashioned.
instructions: Stir the bourbon, maraschino liqueur and both bitters with ice.
Strain into an old fashioned glass over fresh ice, ideally one large cube.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
The earliest known printed recipe for the Fancy Free is in Crosby Gaige's Cocktail Guide and Ladies' Companion of 1940. There it was a shaken whiskey drink with maraschino and both aromatic and orange bitters, served straight up in a cocktail glass with a lemon-and-sugar frosted rim.

Difford's Guide notes that modern bartenders have reinterpreted it as an "improved" Old Fashioned, using maraschino liqueur in place of sugar syrup. The sugared rim and stemmed glass have been dropped in favour of a stirred drink served over ice in an old fashioned glass.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A spirit-forward bourbon drink in the Old Fashioned mould. Maraschino brings a subtle floral, cherry-stone sweetness in place of plain sugar, while generous dashes of aromatic and orange bitters add spice and zest. The result is drier than you might expect, with the bourbon's vanilla and oak in the lead and a long, warming finish. A slow sipper for the evening or after dinner.

cocktails.name: Fernandito
cocktails.shortDescription: Argentina's favourite highball: bittersweet Fernet-Branca topped with cola over ice, closely tied to the province of Córdoba.
instructions: Pour the Fernet-Branca into a double old fashioned glass filled with ice.
Fill the glass with cola.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide describes fernet and cola as being as much of a staple in Argentina as the gin and tonic is in England. The drink is most closely identified with the province of Córdoba, where legend credits a bartender called Oscar 'el Negro' Becerra with serving it in the 1970s, although others date it to the 1950s.

Its popularity grew further in the 1990s, when Fratelli Branca and the Coca-Cola Company ran a joint national advertising campaign in Argentina. The drink goes by many nicknames, including Fernet con coca, Fernuco, Fercola and Fernando, and Difford's cross-references it with its near-identical Fernet con Coca recipe. The IBA lists it in its New Era category.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet, herbal and fizzy. Fernet-Branca brings an intense blend of mint, menthol, myrrh and bitter roots, and cola softens it with caramel sweetness and vanilla, so the result tastes like a grown-up, herbal cola. The bitterness still dominates, encouraging slow sipping. It is long, refreshing and low on fuss, perfect for parties, barbecues or watching football.

cocktails.name: Final Ward
cocktails.shortDescription: Phil Ward's 2007 equal-parts riff on the Last Word, using rye whiskey and lemon instead of gin and lime.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist (discarded) and skewered maraschino cherries
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with skewered maraschino cherries.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide calls the Final Ward perhaps the best-known riff on the classic Last Word. It was created in 2007 by Phil Ward at Death & Co in New York City. Ward kept the Last Word's equal-parts structure with green Chartreuse and maraschino liqueur, but swapped the gin for rye whiskey and the lime juice for lemon. Difford's lists it among more than 50 Last Word variations and includes it in its Cocktail Hall of Fame and modern classics lists.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bold, herbal and tangy. Green Chartreuse fills the glass with alpine herbs, mint and pepper, maraschino adds a funky cherry-almond sweetness, and spicy, high-proof rye gives more grip and warmth than the gin in a Last Word. Lemon keeps the drink sharp and balanced. Pale and strong, it suits drinkers who like intense, complex sours before or after dinner.

cocktails.name: Fitzgerald
cocktails.shortDescription: Dale DeGroff's gin sour with lemon, sugar and a generous dose of Angostura bitters, served over ice.

ingredients.note: saline solution or a pinch of salt

instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the Fitzgerald was created in the early 1990s by Dale DeGroff at the Rainbow Room in Manhattan, New York City. In his 2020 book The New Craft of the Cocktail, DeGroff recalls inventing it on the fly during a busy shift at the Rainbow Room Promenade Bar, when a customer tired of his usual summer Gin and Tonic asked for a new gin drink. DeGroff credits the internet with spreading it onto craft cocktail menus around the world.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tangy, fresh and aromatic. London dry gin brings juniper and citrus, lemon juice gives a sharp sour edge, and rich sugar syrup balances it. The three dashes of Angostura are the signature, adding clove, cinnamon and a hint of bitterness plus a blush of colour. With no egg white, it is lighter and crisper than many sours, an ideal summer refresher.

cocktails.name: Fluffy Duck
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, advocaat, triple sec and orange juice topped with soda: a creamy, retro long drink from 1970s Sydney.
instructions: Shake the gin, advocaat, triple sec and orange juice with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled collins glass.
Top with soda water.
Garnish with an orange slice.
cocktails.history:
A newspaper advertisement from 15 December 1971 in Potts Point, New South Wales, suggests the Fluffy Duck was created at the Cauldron Bubbles restaurant in Darlinghurst, Sydney. The owners announced a newly perfected cocktail of gin, rum, vodka, a big dash of advocaat and fresh orange, shaken and served in a cocktail glass.

The drink rarely appears in cocktail books, but Difford's Guide found a recipe in Helen Spence's 1985 Cocktails For Two: two parts gin and advocaat, one part Cointreau and orange juice, served over ice and topped with soda. That long version is the basis of the modern recipe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, creamy and easy-drinking. Advocaat brings a soft, custardy egg-and-vanilla richness, orange juice and triple sec add sweet citrus, and gin's juniper keeps the drink from becoming too sweet or cloying. Soda water lightens the body with gentle fizz. A playful, retro long drink that suits brunch, parties or anyone who likes creamy cocktails without heaviness.

cocktails.name: Flying Grasshopper
cocktails.shortDescription: Vodka, white crème de cacao, crème de menthe and cream shaken: a stronger 1970s take on the Grasshopper.
cocktails.garnish: Cocoa powder and sugar rim; a mint sprig tip floated in the centre
instructions: Rim a chilled coupe with a mix of cocoa powder and sugar.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Float a mint sprig tip in the centre.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide describes the Flying Grasshopper as a 1970s or earlier riff on the Grasshopper that adds vodka to make the drink more alcoholic. Not every recipe includes cream. Stanley M. Jones's 1977 Complete Barguide leaves it out, mixing one part vodka with three-quarters each of green crème de menthe and white crème de cacao to produce a clear, emerald-green cocktail, while Difford's version keeps the cream of the original Grasshopper for a richer, dessert-style drink.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Minty, chocolatey and creamy, like an after-dinner mint in a glass. Crème de menthe gives a cool peppermint freshness and a pale green colour, white crème de cacao adds sweet chocolate and vanilla, and the cream brings a soft, velvety body. Vodka adds a stronger kick than the classic Grasshopper without changing the flavour much. It is a sweet dessert drink for after dinner.

cocktails.name: Fog Cutter
cocktails.shortDescription: Rum, gin, cognac and pisco shaken with orange, lemon and orgeat under a sherry float: Trader Vic's potent 1946 tiki classic.
instructions: Fill a chilled Collins glass with crushed ice.
Shake the rum, gin, cognac, pisco, orange juice, orgeat and lemon juice with ice.
Strain into the glass.
Float the oloroso sherry on top.
Garnish with a bouquet of mint sprigs.
cocktails.history:
The Fog Cutter is a tiki classic credited to Victor 'Trader Vic' Bergeron. It first appears in his 1946 Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink, marked with his TV logo as a house signature, where he warns that it is delicious but a triple threat. His recipe combined Puerto Rican rum, brandy and gin with orange and lemon juice and orgeat, finished with a sherry float.

Bergeron included it again in his revised 1972 Bartender's Guide, this time calling for light rum and a sweet sherry float and joking that after two of them you would not see any fog at all. Difford's Guide adds a little pisco to the spirit mix.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Long, fruity and deceptively strong. A blend of light rum, gin, cognac and pisco gives a complex spirituous base, while orange and lemon juice make it juicy and tart. Orgeat brings a sweet almond richness that masks the alcohol, and the floated oloroso sherry adds a nutty, raisined depth to the first sips. Served over crushed ice, it is a classic tiki party drink to treat with respect.

cocktails.name: Ford Cocktail
cocktails.shortDescription: Old Tom gin and dry vermouth stirred with Bénédictine and orange bitters: an herbal, Martini-like aperitif from 1895.
instructions: Stir the Old Tom gin, dry vermouth, Bénédictine, orange bitters and saline solution with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
The Ford Cocktail is adapted from George J. Kappeler's 1895 book Modern American Drinks. Kappeler's recipe called for half a jigger each of Old Tom gin and French vermouth with three dashes each of Bénédictine and orange bitters, stirred over fine ice and finished with an orange twist.

Difford's Guide once preferred two parts gin to one of vermouth, but has returned to the original equal parts out of respect for the source and readers' comments. It does, however, use a full 10 ml of Bénédictine D.O.M., finding the original few dashes too timid.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Elegant, aromatic and spirit-forward. Lightly sweetened Old Tom gin and dry vermouth form a smooth, herbal, Martini-like base, while Bénédictine adds honeyed sweetness and warm herbal spice. Orange bitters and an orange twist bring zesty brightness, and a touch of saline sharpens the flavours. Softer and rounder than a Dry Martini, it is a superb pre-dinner aperitif.

cocktails.name: French 125
cocktails.shortDescription: Cognac shaken with lemon and sugar, topped with sparkling wine: the brandy version of the French 75, named in 1977.

ingredients.note: Powdered; or 5 ml rich sugar syrup per spoon
Brut champagne or other sparkling wine

instructions: Chill a flute glass.
Stir the powdered sugar into the lemon juice in the base of a shaker until dissolved.
Add the cognac and shake with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Top with sparkling wine and stir briefly.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history:
The French 75 is named after the French army's 75 mm field gun of the First World War. Its cognac-based relative takes the joke further: Difford's Guide says it is named after a Soviet 125 mm tank cannon. The first recipe for a French 75 made with cognac instead of gin appears under the name French 125 in Stanley M. Jones's Complete Barguide of 1977, where it is served long over ice in a Collins glass.

The flute serve is more recent but is now the usual presentation. Some bars still call the cognac version a French 75: Arnaud's French 75 Bar in New Orleans makes its signature drink with cognac in honour of the cocktail's French roots.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Elegant and celebratory. Cognac gives a rounder, fruitier and more warming base than gin, with notes of dried fruit, vanilla and oak. Lemon juice and sugar balance it into a crisp sour, and the sparkling wine adds lively bubbles, a toasty character and extra acidity. It is drier and lighter than it looks, making it a fine aperitif or a drink for toasts and brunch.

cocktails.name: French 75
cocktails.shortDescription: A celebratory First World War-era classic of gin, lemon and sugar topped with sparkling wine.
instructions: Shake the gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a Champagne flute.
Top up with Champagne.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The French 75 is named after the French 75mm field gun, a symbol of hope during the First World War. Difford's Guide suggests a Paris bartender, probably Henry Tépé of Henry's Bar, named a "Soixante-Quinze" after it around 1914 or 1915. That first version mixed gin, apple brandy, grenadine and lemon and was served in a cocktail glass.

The gin, lemon, sugar and champagne version first appears in Judge Jr.'s 1927 book Here's How, served in a tall glass. Serving it in a champagne flute only became standard in the 1980s. Cognac versions arrived later, sometimes under the name French 125.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, elegant and celebratory. The gin sour base gives zesty lemon, a touch of sweetness and a clean juniper lift. Champagne adds fine bubbles, toasty, biscuity notes and crisp acidity that lengthen the drink. Despite its light, sparkling feel, it is stronger than it seems, a playful nod to the artillery piece it is named after.

cocktails.name: French Connection
cocktails.shortDescription: A simple two-ingredient sipper of cognac and amaretto over ice, named after the 1971 crime film.
instructions: Pour the cognac and amaretto into an old fashioned glass filled with ice.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The French Connection is named after the 1971 American crime thriller of the same name. Difford's Guide calls it a sibling of the Scotch-based Godfather, and notes that both drinks, together with the vodka-based Godmother, appear in Brian F. Rea's 1976 Brian's Booze Guide, which gives brandy or cognac with amaretto built over ice.

The drink was repeated in Stanley M. Jones's 1977 bar guide and in Mark Torre's 1987 The Bartenders Cherry, which distinguished it from the similar Godchild: the French Connection specifically called for cognac and could be served in a snifter.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smooth, sweet and warming. Cognac provides rich grape, oak and dried-fruit notes, while amaretto adds marzipan, almond and a soft, syrupy sweetness. Served over ice, it gradually dilutes and becomes rounder. With equal parts it leans sweet, so it suits those who like dessert-style drinks. Best enjoyed slowly after dinner, by a fire or with coffee.

cocktails.name: French Maid
cocktails.shortDescription: Cognac shaken with muddled cucumber, mint, falernum and lime, topped with ginger beer: Jim Meehan's 2007 PDT highball.
cocktails.garnish: Cucumber slice speared with a mint sprig bouquet
instructions: Chill a collins glass and fill it with ice.
Muddle the cucumber in the base of a shaker.
Add the mint, cognac, falernum, lime juice and sugar syrup and shake with ice.
Fine strain into the ice-filled glass.
Top with ginger beer.
Garnish with a cucumber slice speared with mint sprigs.
cocktails.history: Jim Meehan created the French Maid in the autumn of 2007 at PDT, his speakeasy-style bar in New York City. According to Difford's Guide, he devised it for an art gallery opening hosted by John Pellaton of Hine Cognac, which explains the French brandy at its heart. The recipe combines cognac with cucumber and mint in the manner of a mojito or mule, sharpened with lime and spiced with falernum and ginger beer.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Cool, fresh and gently spiced. Muddled cucumber and mint give a garden-fresh aroma, while cognac adds a rounded, fruity warmth that sets it apart from rum or vodka highballs. Falernum contributes lime zest, clove and almond, lime juice keeps it zesty, and a top of ginger beer adds fizz and a peppery bite. Long and refreshing, it is perfect for summer.

cocktails.name: French Martini
cocktails.shortDescription: A fruity late-1980s New York vodka cocktail with raspberry liqueur and pineapple juice, served in a martini glass.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon peel oils squeezed over the drink
instructions: Add the vodka, raspberry liqueur and pineapple juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Squeeze the oil from a lemon peel over the drink.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide places the French Martini in late-1980s New York, when almost any drink served in a V-shaped glass was called a Martini. The name comes from the French black raspberry liqueur it uses, though Difford's says it was not invented as a marketing campaign by the liqueur brand.

In 1996 Dale DeGroff put it on the menu at Keith McNally's vodka bar Pravda, and it took off later that year at McNally's Balthazar restaurant in SoHo. By 1997 and 1998 it had reached fashionable London bars such as the Met Bar, helped by Dick Bradsell and a magazine campaign.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, soft and easy to like. Vodka provides a clean base, raspberry liqueur adds sweet berry and vanilla notes, and pineapple juice gives tropical fruitiness and, once shaken, a frothy, silky head. The lemon oil on top adds a fresh aroma that balances the sweetness. It is light and approachable, a good party or early-evening drink for those who prefer fruit to bitterness.

cocktails.name: Garibaldi
cocktails.shortDescription: An Italian two-ingredient aperitivo of Campari and fresh orange juice over ice, named after Giuseppe Garibaldi.
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the Campari and the orange juice.
Garnish with an orange wedge.
cocktails.history:
The Garibaldi is named after Giuseppe Garibaldi, the general who helped unify Italy. Wikipedia notes the symbolism of its two ingredients: Campari from Milan in the north, and oranges from Sicily in the south, where Garibaldi's Redshirts landed in 1860. It says the drink was popularised around 1960 and was listed as an IBA cocktail in 1986 and 1993, then re-added in 2024.

Difford's Guide calls it a little-known classic found on cocktail lists across Italy, and credits Naren Young with reviving it at Dante for the October 2015 relaunch of Dante in New York City, a bar that has since featured among the World's 50 Best Bars.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet, juicy and refreshing. Campari brings bitter orange peel, gentian and a gentle herbal spice, while plenty of fresh orange juice softens the bitterness with natural sweetness and acidity. Freshly pressed juice gives a lighter, almost fluffy texture. Low in alcohol and easy to make, it is a classic Italian aperitivo that also works well at brunch.

cocktails.name: Gibson
cocktails.shortDescription: A bitters-free 1890s Martini of London dry gin and dry vermouth, finished with pickled cocktail onions for a savoury twist.
instructions: Chill a coupe or martini glass.
Stir the gin and dry vermouth with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with two skewered cocktail onions.
cocktails.history:
The first written mention of a Gibson cocktail is in an 1898 piece by Edward W. Townsend in New York's The World, describing gin mixed with an equal part of dry vermouth. Townsend had been a vice president of San Francisco's Bohemian Club, the drink's reputed birthplace. Two Gibsons are put forward as its namesake, the businessman Walter D. K. Gibson and the illustrator Charles Dana Gibson, and most historians favour Walter.

At first the Gibson was set apart from the Martini by its lack of orange bitters, not its garnish. William Boothby printed a full recipe in 1908, and the pickled onion, credited to Charles Gibson, arrived about a decade later. By 1948 David Embury defined the drink by the onion.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A crisp, bone-dry Martini with a savoury edge. London dry gin dominates with juniper, citrus peel and botanicals, while a small measure of dry vermouth adds a soft, winey, herbal note. With no bitters, the drink is clean and austere, and the pickled cocktail onions add a subtle umami, briny sharpness to the finish. Ice-cold and elegant, it is a classic aperitif for Martini lovers.

cocktails.name: Gimlet
cocktails.shortDescription: A British naval classic of gin and lime cordial, here sharpened with fresh lime and lemon and a touch of genever.
cocktails.garnish: Lime zest twist (discarded) and a lime wedge
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lime zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
cocktails.history: The Gimlet grew out of the Royal Navy's fight against scurvy. Lime juice became a standard ration, and in 1867 Lauchlin Rose of Leith patented a way to preserve it with sugar rather than alcohol, selling it as Rose's Lime Cordial. Legend says officers mixed it with their gin. The name may come from the gimlet tool used to tap barrels, or from naval surgeon Sir Thomas Gimlette, though Difford's Guide finds no proof of the latter. The earliest recipe Difford's cites is in Harry MacElhone's 1923 ABC of Mixing Cocktails: equal parts Plymouth gin and Rose's, described as very popular in the Navy.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sharp, zesty and refreshing. Gin brings juniper and botanicals, a touch of malty genever adds depth, and lime cordial gives a distinctive candied-lime sweetness. Fresh lime and lemon juices cut the sugar and add a bright acidity, so the drink is balanced rather than cloying. Shaken ice-cold, it is crisp and clean, ideal before dinner on a warm evening.

cocktails.name: Gin & It
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin stirred with sweet Italian vermouth and orange bitters: a simple, aromatic classic once known as the Sweet Martini.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist (or an orange wheel if served on the rocks)
instructions: Stir the gin, sweet vermouth and orange bitters with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe, or into an ice-filled old fashioned glass to serve on the rocks.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink, or garnish with an orange wheel if serving on the rocks.
cocktails.history:
The "It" stands for Italian, a reminder that sweet red vermouth was traditionally Italian while dry vermouth was French. Dale DeGroff wrote in 2002 that the drink was first known as the Sweet Martini, popular in the 1880s and 1890s at the Hoffman House and other Manhattan bars, then as Gin & Italian, before being shortened to Gin & It during Prohibition.

The first printed use of the "Gin & It" name is in Frank Meier's 1936 The Artistry of Mixing Drinks. The drink crossed to London during Prohibition and became a pub staple, faded in the late 1980s, and is now enjoying a revival. Difford's recipe follows Stanley M. Jones's 1977 proportions.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Simple, aromatic and spirit-forward. Gin and sweet vermouth share many botanicals, so they blend seamlessly: juniper and citrus from the gin meet the vermouth's wine, vanilla, dried fruit and gentle bitter herbs.
