A dash of orange bitters brightens the finish. Richer and sweeter than a dry Martini but still bracing, it makes an elegant aperitif or a relaxed early-evening sipper.

cocktails.name: Gin and Tonic
cocktails.shortDescription: The classic British highball of gin and quinine tonic water over ice, born in nineteenth-century colonial India.
instructions: Pour the gin and tonic water into a chilled collins glass.
Fill the glass with ice.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
cocktails.history: The precise origin of the G&T is unknown. Juniper spirits had been drunk for medicinal reasons since the 1600s, and quinine, the bitter bark extract that flavours tonic, had been used against malaria for even longer. The first quinine-based tonics were sold in the 1850s, and in 1870 Schweppes launched a carbonated version branded Indian Tonic Water. The British in India drank large quantities of both gin and tonic, so Difford's Guide concludes that the drink emerged there in the second half of the nineteenth century, taken partly to ward off malaria.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, bitter and refreshing. Gin brings juniper, citrus and botanical spice, while tonic water adds quinine bitterness, gentle sweetness and lively bubbles. Plenty of ice keeps it cold and the squeeze of lime adds a fresh, zesty lift. Clean and dry, it is one of the simplest mixed drinks and a perfect long refresher for warm afternoons and early evenings.

cocktails.name: Gin Basil Smash
cocktails.shortDescription: A vivid green modern gin sour shaken with fresh basil, lemon and sugar, created in Hamburg in 2008.
instructions: Add all the ingredients, including the basil leaves, to a shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously.
Pour into a chilled glass.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide credits the Gin Basil Smash to Jörg Meyer, who created it in the summer of 2008 at Le Lion • Bar de Paris in Hamburg, Germany. He originally called it the Gin Pesto, a nod to the basil that dominates the drink.

Meyer wrote about his new creation on his blog on 10 July 2008, and from there it spread quickly among bartenders and drinkers, becoming internationally known under the name Gin Basil Smash. It is now listed by the IBA in its New Era category.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fresh, herbaceous and zesty. Hard-shaken basil releases peppery, slightly aniseed green flavours and a bright green colour, which sit beautifully alongside the juniper of the gin. Lemon gives a clean sourness and sugar syrup rounds it off, so the drink is balanced rather than sweet. Light and aromatic, it is a perfect summer or garden-party cocktail.

cocktails.name: Gin Blossom Martini
cocktails.shortDescription: Julie Reiner's 2008 house Martini at Clover Club: gin and blanc vermouth with apricot eau-de-vie and orange bitters.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Stir all the ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide adapts the Gin Blossom from a recipe created by Julie Reiner in 2008 as the house Martini for the first menu of her bar, Clover Club, which opened in June of that year. The recipe pairs equal measures of gin and blanc vermouth with a smaller dose of apricot eau-de-vie and two dashes of orange bitters, stirred and served straight up. Difford's rates it five stars and includes it in its list of modern classics.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fragrant, delicate and lightly fruity. Apricot eau-de-vie gives an aromatic stone-fruit perfume without much sweetness, while gin brings piney juniper and botanicals. Blanc vermouth adds a soft, floral and gently sweet herbal body, and orange bitters lift the finish. Silky and elegant, it is a perfect aperitif for those who find a dry Martini too austere.

cocktails.name: Gin Cocktail
cocktails.shortDescription: Genever stirred with dry curaçao, sugar and Boker's-style bitters: one of the oldest recorded cocktails, printed in 1862.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history:
The Gin Cocktail is one of the oldest cocktail recipes on record and a close relation of the Martinez, and so of the Martini. Some claim it dates back to 1824, the year Dr Siegert created Angostura bitters, but the first known recipe is in Jerry Thomas's 1862 Bartender's Guide: gum syrup, two dashes of Bogart's (generally read as Boker's) bitters, a wine glass of gin and a dash or two of curaçao, shaken with ice.

Thomas also gives a Fancy Gin Cocktail, strained into a fancy wine glass with a moistened rim and lemon peel. Writers still disagree on what separates a plain, Fancy or Improved Gin Cocktail: some point to the glass, others to the lemon peel or the curaçao. Some versions even swap the curaçao for absinthe, and without either it becomes a Gin Old Fashioned.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Malty, aromatic and gently sweet. Oude genever has a rich, bread-like grain character quite different from London dry gin, and dry curaçao adds bitter orange sweetness. A little sugar smooths the edges while aromatic bitters bring spice and depth, and the lemon twist lifts the nose. Spirit-forward but rounded, it is a historic sipper for the early evening.

cocktails.name: Gin Fizz
cocktails.shortDescription: A 19th-century gin sour shaken hard and lengthened with soda for a clean, tart sparkle.

ingredients.note: For shaking only; served without ice

instructions: Shake the gin, lemon juice and simple syrup with ice.
Strain into a thin tall tumbler with no ice.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Garnish with a lemon slice and, optionally, a lemon zest.
cocktails.history:
The Gin Fizz is a mid-19th-century classic. Difford's Guide points to its appearance in the 1876 edition of Jerry Thomas's Bar-tenders Guide. There it is listed as a variation of the Whiskey Fizz: spirit, lemon and gum syrup shaken with ice, strained, and topped up with soda water from a siphon.

Difford's notes that a fizz is traditionally served in a smaller glass than a Collins, with no ice in the glass. Adding egg white makes a Silver Fizz, egg yolk a Golden Fizz, a whole egg a Royal Fizz, and sparkling wine a Diamond Fizz.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Clean, tart and effervescent. Fresh lemon leads with lively acidity, a little syrup takes off the sharp edge, and gin adds crisp juniper and botanical notes. The soda lengthens the drink and adds a light sparkle. Served without ice, it is meant to be drunk quickly while it is cold and fizzy. It is a simple, thirst-quenching sour.

cocktails.name: Gin Gin Mule
cocktails.shortDescription: Audrey Saunders' 2000 cross between a Mojito and a Moscow Mule: gin, mint, lime and ginger, topped with ginger beer.
cocktails.garnish: Lime wedge and a bouquet of mint sprigs
instructions: Shake all ingredients except the ginger beer with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled highball glass.
Top with ginger beer.
Fill the glass with ice.
Garnish with a lime wedge and mint sprigs.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the Gin Gin Mule is adapted from a recipe created in 2000 by Audrey Saunders at Beacon in New York City. Her original, which was also Difford's previous recipe, used two thumbnail-sized slices of fresh ginger muddled with sugar syrup instead of ginger liqueur, along with gin, lime juice, a dozen mint leaves and a ginger beer top. Difford's current version swaps the muddled root for a small measure of ginger liqueur and lists the drink among its modern classics.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Zingy, minty and refreshing. Gin's juniper and botanicals sit on a base of lime and fresh mint, while ginger liqueur and ginger beer add a warm, peppery spice and lively fizz. A touch of syrup balances the citrus. It is more aromatic and complex than a Moscow Mule, served long over plenty of ice: ideal for a hot summer afternoon.

cocktails.name: Gin Rickey
cocktails.shortDescription: A sharp, dry highball of gin, lime and soda from the 1880s Rickey family, barely sweetened.
instructions: Pre-chill the glass.
Shake the gin, lime juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled glass.
Top with soda water.
cocktails.history:
The Rickey family of drinks is believed to have been created around 1880 by bartender George A. Williamson at Shoemaker's bar in Washington, D.C. It is named after Colonel Joseph Kyle Rickey, a Democratic lobbyist who reportedly liked to squeeze fresh lime into his whiskey and lengthen it with soda. Rickey later bought Shoemaker's in 1883 and also became a major importer of limes into the United States.

The gin version appears in print in Harry Johnson's bartender's manual of 1900, which called for Old Tom or Holland gin. The Rickey differs from the Collins mainly in using lime instead of lemon, and it is traditionally served in a smaller glass. One reader note on Difford's Guide recalls that the Colonel preferred his Rickeys without sugar.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sharp, dry and fizzy. London dry gin gives a crisp juniper and citrus-peel backbone, while fresh lime adds a bright, tart bite that dominates the drink. Only a touch of sugar softens the edges, so it stays much drier than a Collins or Gimlet. Lengthened with soda over ice, it feels light, clean and bracing, a simple, thirst-quenching highball with a zesty lime aroma.

cocktails.name: Gin Sour
cocktails.shortDescription: Old tom gin, lemon juice and rich sugar syrup, optionally foamed with egg white: the classic pre-Prohibition gin sour.

ingredients.note: saline solution, or a pinch of salt

cocktails.garnish: Lemon wheel and maraschino cherry on a skewer
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice.
Shake the gin, lemon juice, syrup, egg white, bitters and saline with ice.
Strain back into the shaker and dry shake without ice.
Fine strain into the ice-filled glass.
Garnish with a skewered lemon wheel and cherry.
cocktails.history:
Sours are one of the oldest families of mixed drinks, already described by Jerry Thomas in his 1862 bartender's guide: a base spirit, lemon or lime juice and sweetener, sometimes with egg white. Wikipedia describes the Gin Sour as a simple pre-Prohibition mix of gin, lemon and sugar, and notes that adding soda water turns it into a Gin Fizz.

The drink stayed popular into the 1940s, and historian Kevin Starr lists it among the period cocktails of that era. Difford's Guide recommends old tom gin and an 8:4:2 ratio of gin, lemon and rich syrup, slightly sourer than the classic sour formula.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A crisp, tangy sour with a gentle sweetness. Old tom gin gives a softly sweetened juniper and botanical base, fresh lemon brings a bright, mouth-watering acidity, and rich syrup rounds it out. When egg white is used, the dry shake builds a silky foam that softens the edges and carries a few drops of aromatic bitters. Clean and refreshing, it works as an aperitif or an easy-drinking classic at any time.

cocktails.name: Godfather
cocktails.shortDescription: A 1970s two-ingredient sipper of Scotch whisky sweetened with amaretto, served over ice.

ingredients.note: preferably a large cube or block ice

instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass.
Stir both ingredients with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass, ideally over a large cube.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: The Godfather is one of the enduring classics of the 1970s and is named after the Mafia novel and film trilogy: Mario Puzo's book appeared in 1969 and Francis Ford Coppola's first film followed in 1972. Difford's Guide finds its earliest recipe-book mention, alongside the Godmother and French Connection, in Brian F. Rea's 1976 Brian's Booze Guide, using one part amaretto to one and a half parts Scotch. Most books of the period, including Stanley M. Jones's 1977 Barguide, called for equal parts, giving a sweeter, dessert-style drink.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Simple, smooth and gently sweet. Blended Scotch provides malt, honey and a light smokiness, and amaretto softens it with marzipan, cherry-stone and vanilla notes. At three parts whisky to one of liqueur, the almond flavour takes the edge off without masking the whisky. An orange twist lifts the aroma. A relaxed after-dinner sipper over a big ice cube.

cocktails.name: Gold Rush
cocktails.shortDescription: Bourbon shaken with lemon juice and honey syrup: a Whiskey Sour variation created at Milk & Honey, New York, in 2001.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist (expressed and discarded) and a lemon wedge
instructions: Shake the bourbon, lemon juice, honey syrup and saline solution hard with ice, adding a swath of grapefruit zest to the shaker.
Fine strain into an ice-filled old fashioned glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a lemon wedge.
cocktails.history: The Gold Rush was dreamed up by T. J. Siegel one night in 2001 at Milk & Honey in New York City, and it was Sasha Petraske who first mixed it there. In essence it is a Whiskey Sour that uses honey syrup in place of sugar, a simple swap that turned it into one of the best-known drinks to come out of that influential bar. Difford's Guide lists it among its modern classics and adds grapefruit zest and saline to its adapted recipe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, rounded and gently sour. Bourbon supplies vanilla, caramel and oak, fresh lemon brings a bright acidity, and honey syrup adds a fuller, floral sweetness and a slightly silky body that ordinary sugar lacks. A twist of grapefruit zest shaken with the drink lifts the aroma, and a pinch of saline sharpens everything. Comforting yet refreshing over ice, it works at any time of year.

cocktails.name: Golden Cadillac
cocktails.shortDescription: White crème de cacao, Galliano, orange juice and cream shaken together: a golden, creamy dessert drink created at Poor Red's in 1952.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the white crème de cacao, Galliano, orange juice, cream and orange bitters with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Dust with freshly grated nutmeg.
cocktails.history:
According to Poor Red's, a bar famous for its barbecue, the drink was created there in 1952 when a newly engaged couple asked bartender Frank Klein to invent a cocktail to match their new gold-coloured Cadillac. He served hers in a champagne coupe and his in a sidecar glass, so each order still comes as two glasses. The bar calls itself the world's largest consumer of Galliano.

Galliano noticed rising sales in Northern California and advertised the drink from 1964 to 1967. Poor Red's and some books call it the Gold Cadillac, but books such as Stanley Jones's 1977 Barguide used Golden Cadillac, the name now better known.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A creamy, dessert-like drink with a gentle golden glow. White crème de cacao brings milk-chocolate sweetness and Galliano adds vanilla, anise and soft herbal notes. Difford's adds fresh orange juice, which lightens the cream and gives the drink its golden hue, while orange bitters sharpen the citrus and balance the sweetness. Smooth and indulgent, it is an ideal after-dinner treat.

cocktails.name: Grand Margarita
cocktails.shortDescription: A richer Margarita using Grand Marnier in place of triple sec, served on the rocks with a salt rim.
cocktails.garnish: Sea salt rim and a lime slice
instructions: Rim a rocks glass with good sea salt.
Pour the tequila, Grand Marnier and lime juice into a shaker.
Add ice to both the glass and the shaker.
Shake hard for 10 seconds and strain into the glass.
Garnish with a lime slice.
cocktails.history: Also known as the Cadillac Margarita, this variation replaces triple sec with Grand Marnier, the cognac-based orange liqueur. Difford's Guide says it became well known in the 1980s thanks to marketing by El Torito Grill, a Southern California restaurant chain. Wikipedia's Margarita article likewise lists Grand Marnier as one of the orange liqueurs that turn a Margarita into a 'Cadillac', alongside other variations such as the blue Margarita made with blue curaçao.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, citrusy and smooth. Agave tequila gives earthy, peppery freshness, while Grand Marnier brings a deeper, rounder orange flavour with cognac warmth and a touch of vanilla. A small measure of lime keeps it tangy, and the salt rim sharpens the flavours. Fuller and slightly sweeter than a classic Margarita, it is a treat for sipping slowly on the rocks.

cocktails.name: Grasshopper
cocktails.shortDescription: A sweet, mint-green after-dinner drink of crème de menthe, white crème de cacao and cream, linked to New Orleans.
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake briskly for a few seconds.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with a mint leaf if you like.
cocktails.history:
The Grasshopper is the signature drink of Tujague's in New Orleans, and legend says owner Philibert Guichet won a prize for it in a New York competition around 1918 or 1919, although Difford's Guide finds no evidence for this. A layered two-ingredient Grasshopper of crème de menthe over crème de cacao already appears in William Boothby's 1908 World's Drinks.

At some point cream was added to create the shaken drink known today. Several 1950 newspapers credit the modern version to Milwaukee in the late 1940s, and Wikipedia notes it became popular across the American South during the 1950s and 1960s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, creamy and minty, like a liquid after-dinner mint. Green crème de menthe gives cool peppermint and its famous colour, white crème de cacao adds gentle chocolate and vanilla, and the cream makes it smooth and velvety. Low in alcohol and very dessert-like, it is best served small and cold after a meal or as a holiday treat.

cocktails.name: Green Swizzle
cocktails.shortDescription: White rums swizzled with falernum, lime, absinthe and a touch of mint liqueur: a legendary green Caribbean hotel drink of 1890s-1930s.
cocktails.garnish: Three dashes of aromatic bitters on the ice cap, a lime wedge and mint sprigs; serve with a straw
instructions: Pour the rums, absinthe, falernum, crème de menthe and lime juice into a chilled Collins glass.
Fill the glass two-thirds with crushed ice and swizzle.
Top with more crushed ice.
Dash aromatic bitters over the ice cap and garnish with a lime wedge and mint sprigs.
cocktails.history:
The Green Swizzle had its heyday between roughly 1890 and 1930, the golden age of luxury Caribbean hotels like Trinidad's Queen's Park Hotel. Its legendary status owes much to P. G. Wodehouse, whose Bertie Wooster praises the drink after several at the West Indian stand of the 1924 British Empire Exhibition at Wembley.

David Wondrich has written that no definitive recipe is possible, as versions existed with rum, whiskey, old tom gin and genever. Its colour first came from a few dashes of absinthe bitters; green crème de menthe is a later shortcut used by some bartenders today. Difford's Guide uses absinthe and a little mint liqueur over a white rum base.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Long, bold and thoroughly cooling. Light and funky overproof white rums give a lively base, falernum adds lime, clove and almond spice, and a touch of absinthe and peppermint crème de menthe bring a cool, herbal anise-and-mint character. Fresh lime keeps it sharp, and the aromatic bitters on top add spice to the first sips. Packed with crushed ice, it is ideal for hot afternoons.

cocktails.name: Greenpoint
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey stirred with Yellow Chartreuse, sweet vermouth and bitters: a 2005 Manhattan riff from Milk & Honey.
cocktails.garnish: Orange zest twist (the original uses lemon)
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The Greenpoint was created in 2005 by Michael McIlroy at Milk & Honey in New York City. Its name refers to Greenpoint, a neighbourhood of Brooklyn, and the drink is listed by Difford's Guide among its Modern Classics. McIlroy's original specification called for two ounces of rye with half an ounce each of sweet vermouth and Yellow Chartreuse, Angostura and orange bitters, and a lemon twist.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A spirit-forward, Manhattan-style drink with a herbal accent. Spicy rye leads, and the sweet vermouth adds dark fruit and gentle bitterness. Yellow Chartreuse brings honey, saffron and alpine herbs, which soften the whiskey and give the drink a smooth, rounded texture. The bitters tie the flavours together and the citrus twist brightens the aroma. Strong and warming, it is a good choice for the evening.

cocktails.name: Grog
cocktails.shortDescription: Navy rum diluted with water and sharpened with lime and sugar: the British Navy's 18th-century ration turned cocktail.
instructions: Shake the navy rum, lime juice, sugar syrup, chilled water and bitters with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled double old fashioned glass.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
cocktails.history:
For more than 300 years the British Navy issued sailors a daily tot of rum, a tradition begun in Jamaica in 1665. In 1740, to curb drunkenness, Admiral Vernon ordered that the half-pint of neat rum be replaced by two quarter-pint servings diluted four to one with water. Vernon was nicknamed "Old Grogram" after his grogram cloak, so the mixture became known as grog.

Lime juice was often added to fight scurvy, earning British sailors the nickname "limeys". The tot tradition finally ended on 31 July 1970, a date remembered as Black Tot Day, by which time the ration had shrunk to a mere two ounces. Difford's Guide adds that historians now believe the word grog predates Vernon.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Strong, flavoursome and surprisingly refreshing. Navy rum brings rich molasses, dark fruit and a warming, robust alcohol, which chilled water tames to an easy-drinking strength. A splash of lime adds sharp citrus freshness and plain sugar syrup rounds it out without masking the rum, while aromatic bitters lend a hint of spice. A straightforward, historic sipper for rum lovers on any evening.

cocktails.name: Gypsy Queen
cocktails.shortDescription: Vodka stirred with Bénédictine and a dash of bitters: one of America's earliest vodka cocktails, recorded in 1938.
instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: Drinks historian David Wondrich found the earliest known reference to the Gypsy Queen in a 1938 booklet from New York's Russian Tea Room, which makes it one of the first vodka cocktails recorded in the United States. David Embury included it in his 1948 Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, observing that the original two-to-one proportion was rather sweet and recommending five or six parts vodka to one of Bénédictine, with orange bitters.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smooth, honeyed and herbal. Vodka provides a clean, neutral backbone that lets Bénédictine's honey, citrus peel and baking-spice character take the lead. A dash of aromatic bitters adds depth and keeps the sweetness in check, and the orange twist lifts the aroma. Silky in texture and fairly strong, it makes a simple, elegant nightcap.

cocktails.name: Hanky Panky
cocktails.shortDescription: A Savoy classic created by Ada Coleman: gin and sweet vermouth sharpened with a little Fernet-Branca.
instructions: Pour the gin, sweet vermouth and Fernet into a mixing glass with ice.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with an orange zest.
cocktails.history:
The Hanky Panky was created by Ada 'Coley' Coleman, who tended bar at the American Bar of the Savoy Hotel in London, for the actor Sir Charles Hawtrey. Newspaper pieces published around her retirement in 1925 and 1926 tell how Hawtrey asked for something to revive him and declared the result 'the real hanky panky'.

Difford's Guide suggests she made it around 1921, when Hawtrey was working at the Savoy Theatre next door. The recipe was printed in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book as equal parts gin and Italian vermouth with two dashes of Fernet-Branca.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, bittersweet and herbal. Sweet vermouth gives a velvety body with notes of dried fruit and spice, gin adds juniper and backbone, and a small measure of Fernet-Branca cuts through with menthol, bitter herbs and a long, dry finish. The orange zest brightens the aroma. Like a more herbal sweet Martini, it is a great before-dinner drink or nightcap.

cocktails.name: Harvard
cocktails.shortDescription: Cognac and sweet vermouth stirred with bitters and a splash of soda: an 1895 brandy Manhattan named after Harvard.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir the cognac, vermouth, gomme syrup and bitters with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Top with the soda water.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history:
The first known reference to the Harvard Cocktail is in George J. Kappeler's 1895 Modern American Drinks, which mixes gum syrup, Angostura bitters and equal half-jiggers of Italian vermouth and brandy, then fills the glass up with seltzer. Difford's Guide keeps its recipe faithful to that original.

In his 1931 book Old Waldorf Bar Days, Albert Stevens Crockett explained that the drink was named after the school for young men beside the Charles River in a suburb of Boston, and joked that alumni who drank it sometimes lost their Harvard accent.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Essentially a brandy Manhattan with a light sparkle. Cognac gives a soft, fruity warmth, sweet vermouth adds dark fruit, herbs and a gentle bitterness, and Angostura brings spice. The small splash of soda lifts the aroma and lightens the body without diluting the flavour much. Smooth and medium-strong, it suits an early evening drink.

cocktails.name: Harvey Wallbanger
cocktails.shortDescription: Vodka and orange juice with a Galliano float: the Screwdriver variation that became one of the 1970s' biggest drinks.
instructions: Chill a highball glass and fill it with ice.
Briefly stir the vodka, orange juice, sugar syrup and bitters with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Float the Galliano on top.
Garnish with an orange slice.
cocktails.history:
The best-known legend says Harvey was a Californian surfer who, after celebrating a contest win with Screwdrivers topped with Galliano, staggered from bar to bar banging his board against the walls. Another story credits a mid-1960s house party in Newport Beach. Historian Robert Simonson found a 1977 Hartford Courant article naming bartender Donato "Duke" Antone as the drink's creator.

Simonson suspects Antone devised it in the late 1960s as a marketing consultant for Galliano's US importer. George Bednar, the importer's marketing director, commissioned a cartoon poster whose sandal-wearing Harvey character became a pop phenomenon, and by 1973 even a canned version was on sale.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, juicy and easy-going. Fresh orange juice dominates, vodka adds a clean kick, and the float of Galliano brings vanilla and anise aromatics that give the familiar Screwdriver a more interesting finish. Orange bitters and a touch of sugar round out the citrus. Light, bright and refreshing, it works well for brunch or relaxed daytime drinking, especially made with freshly squeezed juice.

cocktails.name: Hemingway Special
cocktails.shortDescription: El Floridita's Daiquiri variation with grapefruit and maraschino: sharp, dry and citrus-driven.

ingredients.note: IBA specifies 'rum'; El Floridita uses light Cuban rum

instructions: Pour all ingredients into a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a large cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
This Daiquiri variation comes from El Floridita in Havana. Difford's Guide credits its legendary head bartender, Constantino "Constante" Ribalaigua Vert, who made it for Ernest Hemingway. After trying the bar's standard frozen Daiquiri, Hemingway is said to have asked for it without sugar and with double the rum. Difford's links his dislike of sugar to a hereditary illness.

The drink was first called "Daiquiri like Papa" and then the Papa Doble. Later, head bartender Antonio Meilan added maraschino and grapefruit juice, and the drink took the name Hemingway Special. Hemingway kept a room in Havana in the 1930s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sharp, dry and citrus-driven. Without added sugar, it relies on maraschino for a subtle, nutty cherry sweetness, while grapefruit juice adds a bittersweet, slightly floral tartness alongside fresh lime. A generous pour of rum gives body and a clean cane note. It is noticeably more sour and spirit-forward than a standard Daiquiri, a drink for lovers of tart flavours.

cocktails.name: Honeysuckle Daiquiri
cocktails.shortDescription: Golden rum shaken with lemon, orange juice and honey syrup: a floral 1948 Daiquiri variation from David Embury.
cocktails.garnish: Mint leaf floated on the drink, or a honeysuckle flower when in season
instructions: Shake the rum, lemon juice, orange juice and honey syrup with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Float a mint leaf on the drink, or peg a honeysuckle flower to the rim.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide adapts its Honeysuckle Daiquiri from David A. Embury's influential 1948 book The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, one of several Embury recipes it features. The drink swaps the plain sugar of a classic Daiquiri for honey and adds a little orange juice to lemon. Difford's suggests it can be seen either as a honeyed Daiquiri or as a Bee's Knees made with rum in place of gin, and rates it among its cocktail hall of fame.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Soft, floral and gently sour. Light golden rum brings sugar-cane sweetness and a touch of vanilla, lemon adds sharp acidity, and a splash of orange juice rounds out the fruit. Honey syrup gives a fuller, more aromatic sweetness than sugar, with a silky texture and floral finish. Balanced and easy to like, it is a delightful aperitif for spring and summer evenings.

cocktails.name: Horse's Neck
cocktails.shortDescription: A long highball of cognac and ginger ale with a dash of bitters and a trademark spiral of lemon peel.
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the cognac and ginger ale.
Stir gently.
Add a dash or two of Angostura bitters if preferred.
Garnish with a long spiral of lemon rind draped over the rim.
cocktails.history:
The Horse's Neck began as a non-alcoholic drink. Wikipedia dates it to at least the 1900s as a mix of ginger ale, ice and lemon peel, Difford's Guide dates the alcoholic 'kick' to around 1910, and Wikipedia adds that by the 1910s a measure of brandy or bourbon was being added to make a 'Horse's Neck with a kick'.

The soft version lasted for decades: Wikipedia records that Franklin Roosevelt sometimes ordered one when he wanted to avoid alcohol at long drinking sessions. The drink also turns up in 1930s films such as Top Hat. The IBA lists the cognac version as a long drink.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, spicy and refreshing. Ginger ale gives gentle sweetness and a warm ginger bite, while cognac adds fruity depth and a smooth, warming finish. The long lemon spiral perfumes every sip with citrus oil, and a dash of bitters adds extra spice if wanted. Easy-going and not too strong, it suits afternoons, light aperitifs and anyone who likes a Highball.

cocktails.name: Hot Toddy
cocktails.shortDescription: Scotch, lemon, honey and cloves topped with boiling water: the classic warming toddy, a drink first recorded in England in 1741.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon wheel on the rim and a cinnamon stick
instructions: Warm a toddy glass.
Pour the Scotch, lemon juice, honey syrup and sugar syrup into the warm glass.
Add the cloves.
Top with boiling water and stir.
Garnish with a lemon wheel on the rim and a cinnamon stick.
cocktails.history:
The earliest known reference to a toddy was published in England in 1741, and Charles Dickens mentions a whisky toddy in The Pickwick Papers of 1836. Jerry Thomas included a Whiskey Toddy in his 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide, made simply with sugar, water, whiskey and a small lump of ice, showing that toddies were not always served hot.

Difford's Guide's version, also called Hot Scotch and Lemon, is a warming mix of blended Scotch, lemon, honey and sugar topped with boiling water and spiced with cloves, long recommended as a comfort when feeling under the weather with a cold.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Warm, soothing and gently spiced. Blended Scotch provides malt and a faint smoky spice, softened by honey and a little sugar, while a splash of lemon keeps it bright. Cloves infuse the hot water with aromatic warmth, and a cinnamon stick adds a sweet spice aroma. Mild in strength once lengthened, it is the classic winter nightcap and a comforting drink when you are feeling run down.

cocktails.name: Hotel Nacional Special
cocktails.shortDescription: Light rum shaken with apricot liqueur, pineapple and lime: the 1930s house cocktail of Havana's Hotel Nacional de Cuba.

ingredients.note: saline solution, or a pinch of salt

cocktails.garnish: Pineapple (or lime) wedge on the rim
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the rum, apricot liqueur, pineapple juice, lime juice, syrup and any optional agricole rum and saline with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a pineapple or lime wedge on the rim.
cocktails.history:
This was the signature drink of Havana's Hotel Nacional de Cuba, created around the hotel's 1930 opening, when Prohibition drew top American bartenders to Cuba. Will P. Taylor, Eddie Woelke and Fred Kaufman have all been credited with it. The first printed recipe, called simply the National, leads the Cuban section of Albert Stevens Crockett's 1935 Old Waldorf Astoria Bar Book, contributed by Taylor as the hotel's manager.

Charles H. Baker's 1939 Gentleman's Companion also credits Taylor, calling the drink one of the three finest Bacardi drinks known to science and recommending gold rum over white. Woelke, however, claimed to be the originator in his 1936 book The Barman's Mentor.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A fruity yet refined twist on the Daiquiri. Light Cuban rum provides a clean, gently sweet base, pineapple juice adds tropical body and a soft froth, and apricot liqueur brings a ripe stone-fruit richness. Fresh lime keeps it tart and lively. An optional splash of grassy agricole rum adds character. Bright, balanced and smooth, it is a perfect warm-weather drink before dinner or by the pool.

cocktails.name: Hugo Spritz
cocktails.shortDescription: A floral South Tyrolean spritz of elderflower liqueur, prosecco, soda and fresh mint, created in 2005.
cocktails.garnish: Lime wedge and a bouquet of mint sprigs
instructions: Add the mint leaves to a chilled wine glass.
Fill the glass with ice.
Add the elderflower liqueur, soda water and prosecco.
Stir briefly.
Garnish with a lime wedge and mint sprigs.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the Hugo was created in June 2005 by Roland "AK" Gruber at his Sanzeno wine and cocktail bar in Naturno, South Tyrol, in northern Italy. Gruber first called it "Otto" before renaming it, and the drink spread widely after he returned to bartending in Switzerland, where it became a well-known contemporary classic. The Hugo began as a riff on the Spritz Veneziano made with lemon balm syrup. Over time that was swapped for easier-to-find elderflower syrup, and later for elderflower liqueur.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, floral and refreshing. Elderflower liqueur gives a sweet, lychee-like perfume, prosecco adds crisp orchard fruit and bubbles, and soda stretches the drink into a gentle, low-strength sipper. Fresh mint brings a cool, green aroma, and the lime garnish adds a hint of citrus. It is a sunny afternoon spritz, sweeter and more aromatic than the classic Aperol version.

cocktails.name: Hunter
cocktails.shortDescription: Bourbon stirred with cherry liqueur, a touch of maraschino and orange bitters: a rich 1908 sipper revived by Tokyo's Hidetsugu Ueno.
cocktails.garnish: Orange zest twist (expressed and discarded) and a skewered maraschino cherry
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice, ideally one large cube.
Stir the bourbon, cherry liqueur, maraschino and orange bitters with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a skewered maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history: The Hunter first appears in Jack A. Grohusko's 1908 book Jack's Manual, where it is simply three parts rye whiskey stirred over ice with one part cherry brandy. The drink was later revived and reimagined by the celebrated Japanese bartender Hidetsugu Ueno at his High Five bar in Ginza, Tokyo. Traditionally it was served straight up in a coupe, but Difford's Guide prefers it on the rocks and switches to bourbon.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A rich, spirit-forward late-night sipper. Bourbon provides vanilla, caramel and oak, cherry liqueur adds deep, ripe red-fruit sweetness, and a small measure of maraschino brings a floral, slightly nutty cherry note. Orange bitters and an orange twist lift the aroma and keep the sweetness balanced. Served over a large cube, it is smooth and warming, a good choice as a nightcap.

cocktails.name: Hurricane
cocktails.shortDescription: Light and navy rums shaken with pineapple, orange, lime and passion fruit: a strong, fruity party drink made famous in New Orleans.
instructions: Chill a hurricane glass and fill it with crushed ice.
Shake both rums, the pineapple, orange and lime juices, lime cordial, sugar syrup and passion fruit syrup with ice.
Strain into the glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a cherry.
cocktails.history: The Hurricane is named after the shape of a hurricane lamp and is served in the tall, curvaceous glass of the same name. It is thought to have originated in 1939 at The Hurricane Bar in New York City, but it was Pat O'Brien's bar in New Orleans that made it famous. Difford's Guide also notes that some old cocktail books list a much earlier and entirely different Hurricane made with cognac, absinthe and vodka.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A strong, tangy and refreshing rum drink packed with fruit. Light Cuban rum and a punchy navy rum provide a rich, molasses-tinged backbone, while pineapple, orange and lime juices bring juicy sweetness and a bright sour edge. Lime cordial and passion fruit syrup add depth and a tropical perfume. Served long over crushed ice, it is a lively party drink for summer days and celebrations.

cocktails.name: Income Tax Cocktail
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin with dry and sweet vermouth, orange juice and bitters: a Bronx riff first printed in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book.

ingredients.note: Saline solution or a pinch of salt

instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The Income Tax Cocktail is a riff on the Bronx, the gin, orange juice and mixed-vermouth classic, and its first known appearance is in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book. Craddock's recipe is half dry gin, a quarter each of French and Italian vermouth, the juice of a quarter orange and a dash of Angostura bitters, shaken and strained into a cocktail glass. The bitters are the main difference from the Bronx, giving it a little more depth.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, aromatic and gently dry. Gin gives a juniper backbone, the two vermouths add herbal, floral and dark-fruit notes in balance, and fresh orange juice brings sweetness and a soft citrus tang. A dash of Angostura adds spice and depth, and a touch of salt brightens the flavours. Medium-bodied and easy-going, it works well as a brunch or pre-dinner drink.

cocktails.name: Industry Sour
cocktails.shortDescription: Fernet-Branca and Green Chartreuse shaken with lime and sugar: a bittersweet, herbal 2011 bartenders' sour from St. Louis.

ingredients.note: saline solution, or a pinch of salt

cocktails.garnish: Lime wheel (ideally dehydrated) floated on top
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the Fernet-Branca, Green Chartreuse, lime juice, syrup, egg white and saline with ice.
Strain back into the shaker and dry shake without ice to emulsify.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Float a lime wheel on the surface.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide adapts the Industry Sour from a recipe created in 2011 by Ted Kilgore at Taste by Niche in St. Louis, Missouri, made for a fellow bartender who was visiting the bar. Kilgore's original called for equal parts Fernet-Branca, Green Chartreuse, lime juice and simple syrup; Difford's version adds egg white and a few drops of saline to make it a fuller sour.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Intensely herbal, bittersweet and sour all at once. Fernet-Branca brings menthol, saffron and a bracing bitterness, while Green Chartreuse adds a sweet, alpine-herb intensity and plenty of warmth. Lime cuts through with sharp acidity and rich syrup softens the edges, and egg white gives a silky, foamy texture that tames the bitterness. A bold drink for amaro lovers, it works as a nightcap or a digestif.

cocktails.name: Irish Coffee
cocktails.shortDescription: Hot coffee, Irish whiskey and sugar under a layer of cream, first served at Foynes airport in the 1940s.

ingredients.note: At least one teaspoon; sugar syrup may be used instead

instructions: Pour warm black coffee into a preheated Irish coffee glass.
Add the whiskey and at least one teaspoon of sugar, and stir until dissolved.
Carefully pour the chilled cream over the back of a spoon held just above the coffee so it floats on top without mixing.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide credits Joe Sheridan, a chef turned bartender from County Tyrone, with creating the drink in late 1944 or early 1945 at the flying-boat port of Foynes in western Ireland. He added whiskey to hot coffee to warm American passengers arriving on a cold, wet evening. When they asked whether it was Brazilian coffee, he said it was Irish coffee.

The drink continued at nearby Shannon Airport, where travel writer Stanton Delaplane tried it. In 1952 he and Jack Koeppler of San Francisco's Buena Vista Café set out to recreate it. After much trial and error, including getting the cream to float, the Buena Vista made it famous in America.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Warming, comforting and layered. Hot black coffee and Irish whiskey make a robust, slightly sweet base with roasted, toasty and gently fruity notes. The cold cream floating on top gives a contrast in both temperature and texture: you sip the hot, boozy coffee through the cool, rich cream. Sugar balances the coffee's bitterness and helps the cream float.

cocktails.name: Italian Margarita
cocktails.shortDescription: Reposado tequila, amaretto, lime and triple sec shaken and served up: a Margarita with an almond, Italian accent.
instructions: Shake the tequila, amaretto, lime juice, triple sec, agave syrup and saline solution with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
cocktails.history: Simon Difford came across the Italian Margarita in 2005 at the Club Bar of The Peninsula Beverly Hills hotel in California, and the recipe published by Difford's Guide is adapted from the version he tasted there. As the name suggests, it is a Margarita given an Italian accent: a generous measure of amaretto joins the tequila, lime and orange liqueur, and the drink now appears on Difford's list of modern classics.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A Margarita with a soft, nutty twist. Reposado tequila brings agave and light oak, sharp lime keeps it tart, and amaretto adds marzipan and apricot-kernel sweetness that rounds the edges and lengthens the finish. A touch of agave syrup and a few drops of saline sharpen the flavours without making it salty. Balanced, approachable and smooth, it suits an early evening or a summer party.

cocktails.name: Jack Rose
cocktails.shortDescription: Applejack and calvados shaken with lemon, lime, raspberry syrup and grenadine: a rosy apple brandy sour first recorded around 1905.

ingredients.note: 30 ml bottled-in-bond applejack plus 20 ml calvados

instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Shake the applejack, calvados, lemon and lime juices, sugar syrup, raspberry syrup, grenadine and bitters with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a lemon zest twist.
cocktails.history:
The first known Jack Rose recipe appears in Jacob Grohusko's 1908 Jack's Manual, with cider brandy, raspberry syrup, lemon, orange and lime, lengthened with soda. By Jacques Straub's 1914 Drinks it had been pared down to applejack, lime and grenadine, close to modern versions.

Many origins are claimed for the name. Albert Crockett said its colour matched the Jacqueminot rose; others link it to a Laird family member named Jack, a claim the family disputes, or simply to applejack. The 1905 Police Gazette credited a Jersey City bartender, Frank J. May, known as Jack Rose, while some tie it to gangster 'Bald' Jack Rose of a 1912 murder case.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A bright, fruity apple brandy sour with a rosy pink hue. Applejack and calvados give a warm, spicy orchard-fruit backbone, while lemon and lime bring a sharp, mouth-watering tartness. Raspberry syrup and grenadine add red-fruit sweetness and colour, and a dash of orange bitters adds depth. Balanced and lively, far more than a simple grenadine sour, it suits an aperitif or early evening.

cocktails.name: Japanese Cocktail
cocktails.shortDescription: Cognac stirred with orgeat, aromatic bitters and lemon peel: Jerry Thomas's 1862 tribute to the first Japanese mission to the USA.

ingredients.note: swaths of lemon peel, stirred with the drink
chilled; omit if using wet ice

instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Stir the cognac, orgeat, water, bitters and lemon peel swaths with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
The Japanese Cocktail was first published in Jerry Thomas's 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide and is one of the few drinks in that book believed to be his own creation. His recipe stirred brandy with orgeat, Boker's bitters and lemon peel over ice.

Thomas is thought to have created it in 1860 to mark the first Japanese diplomatic mission to the United States, whose delegates stayed at New York's Metropolitan Hotel, a block from his bar at 622 Broadway. Historian David Wondrich has suggested the visitors could hardly have missed calling in on the Professor during their stay.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A lightly sweetened, gently diluted cognac drink. The brandy's dried fruit, vanilla and oak take centre stage, while orgeat adds a soft almond and floral sweetness that rounds the spirit. A few dashes of aromatic bitters bring a hint of spice, and the lemon peel stirred into the drink lends bright citrus oils. Smooth and elegant, it is a refined pre-dinner drink or a quiet evening sipper.

cocktails.name: Jasmine
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, lemon, a little Campari and orange liqueur shaken and served up: Paul Harrington's bittersweet 1990s riff on the Pegu Club.
instructions: Shake the gin, red bitter liqueur, triple sec, lemon juice and sugar syrup (if using) with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
Paul Harrington created the Jasmine in the mid-1990s at the Townhouse Bar & Grill in Emeryville, California. He named it after his college friend Matt Jasmin, who had challenged him to make something he had never made before, and the result took its cue from the classic Pegu Club.

The drink spread through its inclusion in Harrington's 1998 book Cocktail: The Drinks Bible for the 21st Century, which printed it as gin, Cointreau, Campari and lemon juice shaken and served in a cocktail glass. Difford's Guide adds an optional spoon of sugar syrup to soften its tartness.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Pale pink, tart and bittersweet. Dry gin provides a juniper backbone, lemon gives a sharp sourness, and small measures of Campari and orange liqueur add bitter orange peel and a hint of sweetness. Without the optional syrup it sits just on the sour side of balanced. A crisp, appetising drink for before dinner.

cocktails.name: Jet Pilot
cocktails.shortDescription: Overproof rums, falernum, cinnamon, grapefruit and lime with absinthe: a potent late-1950s tiki drink from Hollywood's Luau.

ingredients.note: 30 ml high-ester aged pot still + 22.5 ml light-bodied aged rum, both overproof
Havana Club Añejo 3 Años (lightly aged Cuban)

cocktails.garnish: Skewered maraschino cherry; serve with a straw
instructions: Chill a double old fashioned glass.
Blend all ingredients without ice on a slow setting (Difford's optionally adds a little xanthan gum at this stage).
Add a scoop of crushed ice and blend briefly again.
Pour into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a skewered cherry and serve with a straw.
cocktails.history: According to Difford's Guide, the Jet Pilot was created around 1958 by the socialite Steve Crane at the Luau, his Polynesian-themed restaurant in Hollywood. It is a riff on the Test Pilot, which Donn Beach created in 1941. The two recipes are very similar, but Crane's version adds grapefruit juice and cinnamon syrup, giving it a spicier, more citrus-driven profile that has kept it on tiki bar menus ever since.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Strong, spicy and intensely tropical. A blend of rich pot-still and lighter rums gives molasses, funk and plenty of heat. Falernum adds lime zest, clove and almond, cinnamon syrup brings warm sweetness, and grapefruit and lime keep it sharp. A touch of absinthe and bitters adds an aniseed and spice lift. Crushed ice tames the strength a little, but this is still a potent drink for sipping slowly.

cocktails.name: John Collins
cocktails.shortDescription: The tall, crisp gin collins of lemon, sugar and soda that grew out of 19th-century Gin Punch.
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour all ingredients directly into the glass.
Stir gently.
Garnish with a lemon slice and a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Collins appears to have developed from Gin Punch. Its creation and name are attributed to John (or possibly Jim) Collins, head waiter at Limmer's Hotel on Conduit Street in London during the 1800s. Limmer's coffee house was popular with sporting men and was already known for its Gin Punch in the early 1800s.

Difford's Guide suggests the drink may have become the Tom Collins when it was made with Old Tom gin. Harry Johnson's 1882 Bartenders' Manual lists a John Collins made with Dutch gin and a Tom Collins with Old Tom. The John Collins was first made with genever, then Old Tom, and finally London dry gin.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tall, crisp and thirst-quenching. Think of it as sparkling gin lemonade: fresh lemon gives bright acidity, sugar syrup softens it, and gin adds dry juniper and botanical notes. Soda water lengthens the drink and keeps it lively, so it is light-bodied and very refreshing over plenty of ice. The cherry garnish adds a small touch of sweetness at the end.

cocktails.name: Jungle Bird
cocktails.shortDescription: A bittersweet tiki drink of dark rum, Campari, pineapple and lime, created in 1973 at the Kuala Lumpur Hilton.
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a rocks glass filled with ice.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide reports that the Jungle Bird was created by beverage manager Jeffrey Ong as the welcome drink for the opening of the Kuala Lumpur Hilton on 6 July 1973. The hotel bar was called the Aviary, and guests could see birds kept near the pool, so the name fitted. It was first served in a ceramic bird-shaped vessel.

The recipe was printed in John J. Poister's 1989 New American Bartender's Guide, and the drink's revival owes much to Jeff 'Beachbum' Berry's 2003 book Intoxica!. When Ong died in 2019, a Malaysian newspaper called it Malaysia's only internationally recognised classic cocktail.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet and tropical. Dark blackstrap rum brings deep molasses, toffee and smoky notes, Campari adds bitter orange and a striking red colour, and pineapple juice provides juicy sweetness and a frothy texture. Lime and demerara syrup balance the sour and sweet sides. It is an unusual tiki drink, more bitter than most, and great for summer evenings.

cocktails.name: Kir
cocktails.shortDescription: A light French aperitif of dry white wine with a dash of blackcurrant liqueur.
instructions: Pour the crème de cassis into a chilled glass.
Top up with chilled dry white wine.
cocktails.history:
According to Difford's Guide, the drink is said to date to 1904. That year a waiter named Faivre at the Café George in Dijon is said to have first mixed white wine with crème de cassis, and the drink was first called "Cassis Blanc".

It took its current name from Canon Félix Kir, a Catholic priest and French Resistance hero who became mayor of Dijon in 1945. He served the local cassis and Bourgogne Aligoté wine at official receptions to promote regional products. In 1951 he gave a cassis producer the right to use his name, and "Kir" was registered as a brand the following year.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, fruity and refreshing. A crisp, acidic dry white wine forms the base, and a small measure of crème de cassis adds ripe blackcurrant sweetness and a pretty ruby-pink colour. When the proportions are right, the wine's acidity balances the rich liqueur, so the drink is gently sweet rather than syrupy. It is a low-alcohol, easy French aperitif to serve well chilled.

cocktails.name: Kir Royale
cocktails.shortDescription: Crème de cassis topped with chilled champagne: the sparkling version of Dijon's Kir aperitif.

ingredients.note: Brut, chilled; Difford's also allows other sparkling wine

cocktails.garnish: A seasonal berry such as a blackcurrant
instructions: Pour the crème de cassis into a chilled flute.
Top with the champagne.
Garnish with a berry.
cocktails.history: The Kir Royale is the sparkling version of the Kir, the blackcurrant-and-white-wine aperitif that Difford's Guide says was probably first mixed in 1904 at Café George in Dijon. Originally called blanc-cassis, the drink takes its name from Canon Félix Kir, who as mayor of Dijon after the Second World War served it at receptions for visiting delegations, promoting two Burgundy products at once. Making it with champagne in place of still white wine turns it into a Kir Royale.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Elegant, fruity and celebratory. The crème de cassis adds a deep ruby blush and a ripe blackcurrant sweetness that sinks to the bottom, while dry champagne brings fine bubbles, toasty notes and crisp acidity. The balance should lean dry, with the fruit as an accent rather than the main event. Light and refreshing, it is a classic aperitif for celebrations and special dinners.

cocktails.name: Knickerbocker
cocktails.shortDescription: Rum shaken with raspberry syrup, lime and a dash of curaçao over crushed ice: a fruity New York-named classic first printed in 1862.
cocktails.garnish: Spent lime shell and seasonal berries; serve with a straw
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass two-thirds full with cubed ice.
Shake the rum, dry curaçao, raspberry syrup and lime juice with ice.
Strain into the glass and top up with crushed ice.
Garnish with the spent lime shell and seasonal berries, and serve with a straw.
cocktails.history:
The Knickerbocker first appears in print in Jerry Thomas's 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide, made with Santa Cruz rum, lime or lemon, raspberry syrup and a little curaçao, shaken with shaved ice and dressed with berries. It was long assumed to come from New York's Knickerbocker Hotel, but that hotel was not built until 1906, so its creator remains unknown.

The name traces back to Washington Irving, who wrote his satirical 1809 History of New York as Diedrich Knickerbocker, after which the word came to mean an old Dutch-descended New Yorker and then anything from New York. Later versions by William Terrington (1869) and Harry Johnson (1882) varied the formula, Johnson adding pineapple and orange.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, refreshing and easy-drinking, with rum and raspberry to the fore. Light Cuban rum gives a clean, gently sweet base, raspberry syrup adds ripe berry sweetness and colour, and lime juice provides a bright, tart counterpoint. A dash of dry curaçao adds a subtle orange note. Served over a mix of cubed and crushed ice with fresh berries, it is a cheerful summer party drink.

cocktails.name: La Louisiane
cocktails.shortDescription: A New Orleans rye cocktail with sweet vermouth, Bénédictine, absinthe and Peychaud's bitters, recorded in 1937.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a skewered maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history: La Louisiane comes from Stanley Clisby Arthur's 1937 book Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em. Arthur named it as the house drink of the Restaurant de la Louisiane, a celebrated French Quarter dining room that had long drawn devotees of Creole food. His recipe used equal parts rye, Italian vermouth and Bénédictine with dashes of absinthe substitute and Peychaud's bitters, served over a cherry. Difford's Guide increases the whiskey and reduces the liqueur for balance, and has twice cut back the absinthe, most recently in December 2025.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, herbal and spicy. Rye provides peppery grain and warmth, sweet vermouth brings dark fruit and vanilla, and Bénédictine adds honeyed herbs and saffron. Peychaud's and a whisper of absinthe give anise and cherry aromatics that recall a Sazerac. A splash of water opens up the high-proof rye. Think of a richer, more aromatic Manhattan to sip after dinner.

cocktails.name: Last Word
cocktails.shortDescription: An equal-parts Prohibition-era gem of gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino and lime: intense, herbal and balanced.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker.
Shake with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The earliest known mention of the Last Word is in a souvenir menu sent to Detroit Athletic Club members with the club's July-August 1916 magazine. It lists only the name and the price, which was twice that of a Manhattan. Ted Saucier's 1951 book Bottoms Up! confirms the link to the club and gives an equal-parts recipe.

Saucier credits the vaudeville performer Frank Fogarty, known as the "Dublin Minstrel", with bringing the drink to New York. Fogarty usually ended his act with a recitation, which some think explains the name. The club put the drink back on its menu in 2009.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Intense, herbal and finely balanced. Green Chartreuse brings a powerful mix of alpine herbs, mint and spice, while maraschino adds a dry, funky cherry-almond sweetness. Fresh lime cuts through both with sharp acidity, and gin adds a juniper backbone. Equal parts produce a pale green drink that is sweet, sour and herbal at once, with a long, complex finish.

cocktails.name: Left Bank Martini
cocktails.shortDescription: A floral stirred Martini of gin, elderflower liqueur, dry white wine and dry vermouth, created by Simon Difford in 2006.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lime zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Simon Difford created this drink in 2006 at the Cabinet Room in London for the launch of St-Germain elderflower liqueur. The name points to Saint-Germain-des-Prés, the district on the left (south) bank of the Seine in Paris, rather than to the Left Bank wine region of Bordeaux, even though the recipe includes wine. It was first made with Sauvignon Blanc rather than Chardonnay. In 2013 Difford cut the elderflower liqueur and vermouth, and he notes he originally shook it before switching to stirring.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry, aromatic and floral. Gin forms the backbone with juniper and citrus, elderflower liqueur adds a soft, honeyed blossom note, and white wine contributes crisp, mineral acidity in place of a large dose of vermouth. A small measure of dry vermouth rounds out the finish, and a fine mist of lime oil lifts the aroma. An elegant pre-dinner Martini with a lighter, wine-like character.

cocktails.name: Left Hand
cocktails.shortDescription: Bourbon stirred with Campari, sweet vermouth and chocolate bitters: Sam Ross's 2006 Milk & Honey riff on the Boulevardier.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir the bourbon, red bitter, sweet vermouth and chocolate bitters with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a skewered cherry.
cocktails.history: The Left Hand was created in 2006 by Sam Ross at Milk & Honey in New York City, as a straight-up riff on the Boulevardier, the bourbon-based cousin of the Negroni. It was first made soon after the launch of Bittermens Xocolatl Mole Bitters and originally used those spiced chocolate bitters. Difford's Guide prefers ordinary chocolate bitters in its adapted recipe and describes the drink as the Negroni meeting a Manhattan.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, bittersweet and velvety. Bourbon provides vanilla, caramel and oak, red bitter liqueur adds bitter orange and gentian, and a full-bodied Italian vermouth brings vanilla, dried fruit and herbal spice. A few drops of chocolate bitters deepen everything with a cocoa note that ties the bourbon and bitter together. Smooth and stirred, it is ideal as an after-dinner drink or for Negroni fans seeking more depth.

cocktails.name: Lemon Drop Martini
cocktails.shortDescription: A sweet-and-sour vodka cocktail of triple sec and fresh lemon, a 1990s favourite descended from a San Francisco original.
instructions: Add the vodka, triple sec and lemon juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide says the Lemon Drop Martini emerged and became popular in the 1990s. Like the Lemon Drop shot, it is believed to have grown out of the Lemon Drop cocktail created in the 1970s by Norman Jay Hobday at Henry Africa's, his bar in San Francisco.

Wikipedia describes Henry Africa's as a fern bar in the Russian Hill neighbourhood that opened in 1969, and suggests the drink was named after lemon drop sweets. It notes the original was served in a cocktail glass, often with a sugared rim, and that despite the name it is closer to a daisy than a Martini.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, tangy and sweet, much like the sweet it is named after. Fresh lemon juice gives a sharp, zesty acidity, triple sec rounds it with orange sweetness, and vodka provides a clean, neutral base that lets the citrus shine. Served very cold, it is crisp and easy to drink. A sugared rim, if added, increases the sweetness. A fun party drink.

cocktails.name: Limoncello Spritz
cocktails.shortDescription: Limoncello with prosecco and soda over ice: a lemony modern member of the Italian Spritz family.
instructions: Fill a chilled wine glass with ice.
Pour in the prosecco, limoncello and soda water.
Stir briefly.
Garnish with an orange slice.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide describes the Limoncello Spritz as a modern addition to the long-established Spritz family. The Spritz itself grew out of the Habsburg period in the Veneto during the 1800s, when visitors diluted the strong local wines with water. Between the 1920s and 1930s it was combined with local bitter aperitifs in Venice and Padua, and by the 1970s prosecco had become standard. This version replaces the bitter liqueur with limoncello, the sweet lemon liqueur of southern Italy.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, zesty and sparkling. Limoncello brings an intense lemon-peel flavour with plenty of sweetness, while dry prosecco adds crisp acidity, fruity notes and fine bubbles. Soda water lengthens and lightens the mix, so it drinks like a grown-up lemonade. Without the bitterness of an Aperol Spritz, it is easy and refreshing, perfect for a summer aperitivo or a sunny afternoon.

cocktails.name: Little Italy
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey, sweet vermouth and Cynar stirred together: Audrey Saunders' bittersweet 2005 Manhattan variation from Pegu Club.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history: Audrey Saunders created the Little Italy in 2005 for the opening menu of the Pegu Club, her influential cocktail bar in New York City. The drink is a twist on the Manhattan, built on rye whiskey and sweet vermouth, that adds a measure of Cynar, the Italian artichoke-based amaro, for a bittersweet edge. It appears in Difford's Guide among its Modern Classics, alongside other Manhattan variations from the same period of New York bartending.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A darker, more bitter Manhattan. Rye whiskey gives spice and a firm backbone, sweet vermouth adds dried fruit and vanilla, and Cynar contributes a bittersweet, vegetal and slightly caramel note that lingers on the finish. The texture is smooth and weighty, and the cherry garnish adds a final touch of sweetness. It is strong and contemplative, suited to sipping before or after dinner.

cocktails.name: London Calling
cocktails.shortDescription: A gin sour with fino sherry, lemon and orange bitters, created by Chris Jepson in London in 2002.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a grapefruit zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the London Calling was created in 2002 by Chris Jepson at Milk & Honey in London, originally as an entry for a Drinks International magazine competition. It has since become a widely copied contemporary classic and has inspired riffs such as the Banana Calling. Difford's also records an unrelated stirred drink of the same name, found at London's Oxo Tower Bar & Brasserie in 2003, that combined dry gin, sloe gin, sweet vermouth and orange bitters.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, dry and delicate. London dry gin provides juniper and citrus, while fino sherry adds a nutty, slightly saline edge with hints of celery. Lemon and a measure of rich syrup keep the sour in balance, and orange bitters plus the grapefruit twist give a bright, zesty aroma. Light on its feet and savoury rather than sweet, it makes a fine aperitif.

cocktails.name: Long Island Iced Tea
cocktails.shortDescription: A deceptively easy, very strong 1970s highball of four white spirits, orange liqueur, lemon and cola.
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka, tequila, rum, gin, Cointreau, lemon juice and simple syrup.
Top with cola.
Stir gently and garnish with a lemon slice if desired.
cocktails.history:
Of the many origin stories, Difford's Guide considers this the most credible: Robert "Rosebud" Butt created the drink in the 1970s, perhaps in 1972, at the Oak Beach Inn in Babylon, on New York's Long Island. The name comes from that location and from the way the cola-topped drink looks like iced tea.

Because it disguises how much alcohol it contains, some people claim it dates back to Prohibition. Its popularity peaked in the early 1980s. In 1985 The New York Times reported that the drink was sweeping bars on Long Island and across the country.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Deceptively easy-drinking and very strong. Five spirits combine into a fairly neutral, boozy base, with the tequila and gin adding faint earthy and botanical notes. Lemon and sugar syrup create a sweet-and-sour, lemonade-like body, Cointreau adds orange, and a splash of cola gives the tea colour and a hint of caramel. It drinks like spiked iced tea but packs a punch.

cocktails.name: Lynchburg Lemonade
cocktails.shortDescription: Tennessee whiskey, triple sec and lemon topped with lemon-lime soda: a tangy, easy highball named after Jack Daniel's hometown.
instructions: Pour the Tennessee whiskey, triple sec, lemon juice and lemon-lime soda into a chilled collins glass.
Fill the glass with ice.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.
cocktails.history:
The Lynchburg Lemonade is named after Lynchburg, Tennessee, home of the Jack Daniel's distillery, and Difford's Guide says its recipe is adapted from one created for the distillery. Wikipedia, however, attributes the drink and its name to Tony Mason, an Alabama restaurant and lounge owner, in 1980.

Mason claimed that a Jack Daniel's sales representative learned his recipe, which he regarded as a trade secret, before the company launched a national campaign promoting the drink. The dispute went to court as Mason v. Jack Daniel Distillery in 1987; after an appeal and a retrial, the distillery eventually won.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tangy, light and very easy to drink, like a grown-up lemonade. Tennessee whiskey gives a mellow base of vanilla, caramel and gentle smoke, triple sec adds sweet orange, and fresh lemon brings a sharp, sour lift. Lemon-lime soda lengthens it with sweetness and sparkle. Built over plenty of ice, it is an uncomplicated, refreshing choice for summer afternoons and outdoor parties.

cocktails.name: M and M
cocktails.shortDescription: A two-ingredient stirred drink of equal parts Amaro Montenegro and mezcal, also known as Monte y Mezcal.

ingredients.note: preferably a large cube or block ice

instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass.
Stir both ingredients with ice.
Strain into the glass over a large ice cube.
Express an orange or lime zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Short for Monte y Mezcal, the M and M was created in 2015 by Marco Montefiori of Amaro Montenegro, according to Difford's Guide, and popularised by Robert Krueger at Employees Only in New York. The equal-parts mix of Montenegro and mezcal became so popular among bartenders, often served as a straight shot, that it picked up the nickname "Manager's Meeting". Difford's mentions versions with a few drops of chocolate bitters or served in clay mezcal copitas.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Simple, boozy and smoky-sweet. Mezcal gives earthy agave and wood smoke, while Amaro Montenegro adds orange peel, rose and gentle bitter herbs with a light sweetness. Together they taste a little like a smoky Negroni without the gin. The orange twist brightens the aroma. Sip it slowly over a big ice cube as a nightcap.

cocktails.name: Macunaíma
cocktails.shortDescription: Cachaça, citrus, sugar and a dash of Fernet-Branca: a bittersweet 2014 São Paulo sour named after a classic Brazilian novel.

ingredients.note: the bar recipe uses lime juice

instructions: Chill an old fashioned glass.
Shake the cachaça, lemon juice, syrup and Fernet-Branca with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass without ice.
Serve without garnish.
cocktails.history:
The Macunaíma was created in 2014 by Arnaldo Hirai at his Boca de Ouro bar in São Paulo, Brazil. Hirai almost named it Caxirola, after the rattle designed by Carlinhos Brown as the official instrument of that year's World Cup in Brazil, but the instrument flopped and was banned from stadiums. He chose instead to name it after Mário de Andrade's 1928 novel, a founding text of Brazilian modernism.

The drink quickly became the bar's best seller, with hundreds sold each month, and Hirai has gradually made it less sweet. The bar uses lime juice and a 1:1 syrup. Difford's Guide, after first mistranslating lime as lemon, tried both side by side and settled on lemon, switching to a smaller measure of richer sugar syrup as well.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A bright, grassy cachaça sour with a bittersweet herbal twist. Unaged cachaça gives a fresh, vegetal sugar-cane character, citrus adds a sharp, clean acidity, and rich syrup brings balance. A small measure of Fernet-Branca threads menthol, bitter herbs and spice through the finish, adding depth without overwhelming. Served chilled without ice, it is crisp and lively, a great choice for an aperitif or a hot evening.

cocktails.name: Mai Tai
cocktails.shortDescription: Trader Vic's 1944 tiki classic: aged rum with orange liqueur, orgeat and lime, rich yet tart.

ingredients.note: 30 ml amber Jamaican rum + 30 ml Martinique molasses rum (not rhum agricole)

cocktails.garnish: Pineapple spear, mint leaves and lime peel
instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a double rocks (old fashioned) or highball glass.
cocktails.history:
Victor Bergeron, better known as Trader Vic, said he came up with the Mai Tai in 1944 at his restaurant in Oakland, California, which he had opened a decade earlier. He served the new mix to two friends visiting from Tahiti, and one of them reportedly reacted with a Tahitian phrase meaning roughly 'out of this world', which gave the drink its name. His original build leaned on a 17-year-old Jamaican rum, lime, orange curaçao, rich sugar syrup and French orgeat.

The story is not uncontested. Ernest Raymond Beaumont-Gantt, owner of Don the Beachcomber's in Hollywood, also claimed the drink, and some accounts even place its birth in Tahiti; Bergeron firmly rejected both claims in his 1972 writing. The cocktail spread from California to Hawaii in the 1950s, when Bergeron set it up for Matson Line hotel bars, and it went on to become the emblem of the tiki movement.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A rich, rum-forward sour with real depth. Aged rums bring molasses, toffee and funky fruit notes, sharp lime cuts through, and orange curaçao adds bittersweet citrus peel. Orgeat gives a soft, nutty almond sweetness and a slightly creamy texture that rounds everything off. Served over plenty of ice with fragrant mint on top, it tastes tropical without being sugary, balancing boozy warmth against bright acidity.

cocktails.name: Mamie Taylor Highball
cocktails.shortDescription: Scotch whisky topped with ginger ale over ice: a simple 1899 highball from Rochester, New York, once wildly popular.
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the Scotch whisky and ginger ale.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.
cocktails.history:
The Mamie Taylor was invented in 1899 in Rochester, New York, and spread like wildfire. Its name is something of a mystery, though several versions of a story link it to the Broadway star of the same name. In the 1900s bartenders reportedly grew so tired of making it that they raised the price to discourage orders.

The drink appears in Albert Stevens Crockett's Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book of the mid-1930s as Scotch, ginger ale and the juice of half a lime, served in a collins glass. It never really recovered from Prohibition and has since faded from view.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Simple, mellow and refreshing. Malty Scotch whisky, with a faint wisp of smoke, pairs naturally with the gentle sweetness and soft spice of ginger ale, which lengthens the drink with lively bubbles. A lemon wheel adds a fresh citrus aroma. Light in alcohol and very easy to drink, it is an ideal relaxed highball for warm afternoons or casual evenings.

cocktails.name: Man O' War
cocktails.shortDescription: A bourbon sour with orange liqueur, sweet vermouth and lemon, named after the famous American racehorse.

ingredients.note: saline solution (20 g sea salt to 80 g water) or a pinch of salt

cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist (discarded) and a skewered maraschino cherry
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a skewered maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history: The drink is said to be named after Man o' War, the American thoroughbred that won 20 of 21 races in 1919 and 1920. Some say it originated in the mid-20th century, but Difford's Guide could not find it in the many cocktail books from the 1930s onward, so it treats the Man O' War as a modern drink. The earliest matching recipe Difford's cites is from The Indianapolis Star in April 2015, which listed it as a Kentucky Derby cocktail. An unrelated "man-o'-war cocktail" of 1915 was more like eggnog.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Zingy, fruity and bourbon-rich. Bourbon brings vanilla and caramel, orange liqueur adds bright citrus sweetness, and sweet vermouth gives depth with gentle herbal spice. Lemon juice keeps it sharp and lively, while an optional touch of syrup and saline can be adjusted to taste. It drinks like a cross between a Whiskey Sour and a Manhattan, ideal on Derby day or before dinner.

cocktails.name: Manhattan
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey, sweet vermouth and bitters stirred cold: the 19th-century New York template for modern cocktails.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice cubes.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Manhattan surfaced in New York in the 1860s or 1870s and is often called the first 'modern' cocktail, because it brought sweet vermouth into an Old Fashioned-style whiskey drink. A New York newspaper letter of 1882 described the whiskey, vermouth and bitters mix as newly fashionable, and full recipes appeared in several bar books in 1884.

A long-repeated legend places its invention at an 1874 Manhattan Club banquet for Samuel Tilden, sometimes linked to Lady Randolph Churchill, but historians have shown she was in England giving birth to Winston at the time. Difford's Guide considers the most plausible account the one given by Hoffman House bartender William Mulhall in 1923, which points to a bar owner named Black; research suggests George Black, who ran the Manhattan Inn on Broadway.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Spirit-forward, smooth and gently sweet. Rye whiskey gives a spicy, slightly dry backbone with notes of grain, pepper and oak, while sweet vermouth adds dark fruit, herbs and a soft wine richness. A dash of Angostura ties them together with warm baking spice and a faint bitter edge. Stirred and served very cold, it feels silky and weighty, finishing with a hint of cherry from the garnish.

cocktails.name: Margarita
cocktails.shortDescription: Tequila, orange liqueur and lime in a salt-rimmed glass: the world's favourite tequila sour.
instructions: Optionally rim half of a chilled cocktail glass with salt.
Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into the chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Margarita is widely seen as a tequila version of the Daisy, an old family of spirit, citrus and liqueur drinks; 'margarita' is Spanish for daisy. A Tequila Daisy was being promoted in a Tijuana-area saloon by 1936, the 1937 Café Royal Cocktail Book printed a near-identical 'Picador', and a 1939 Tequila Sour with Cointreau, lime and a salted rim came close to the modern drink.

The name 'Margarita' first appears in print in 1953. Many people have claimed to have invented or named it, including Danny Negrete, Francisco 'Pancho' Morales in Ciudad Juárez, Carlos 'Danny' Herrera at Rancho La Gloria and the socialite Margaret Sames in Acapulco. None of these claims has been proven. A José Cuervo promotional push by distributor Young's Market from 1955 helped make the drink famous across the United States.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, tart and refreshing with an agave core. Tequila brings earthy, vegetal and peppery notes, fresh lime supplies a sharp sour snap, and triple sec adds sweet orange that softens the edges. The optional salt rim lifts the citrus and tames any bitterness, making each sip pop. Served cold and straight up, it is clean, zesty and lively, with a slightly dry, lingering finish.

cocktails.name: Martinez
