cocktails.shortDescription: A nineteenth-century forerunner of the Martini: gin and sweet vermouth with maraschino and orange bitters, stirred.
instructions: Pour all the ingredients into a mixing glass with ice.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with a lemon zest.
cocktails.history:
Drinks historians broadly agree that the Martinez developed from the Manhattan and came before the Martini, emerging in the 1860s or early 1870s. Difford's Guide notes that the first known recipe, in O.H. Byron's 1884 The Modern Bartender's Guide, simply describes it as a Manhattan made with gin instead of whisky.

Which gin was used is debated. Difford's argues that Dutch genever, far more common in nineteenth-century America than English gin, is the likely original, as its malty style is closer to whiskey. Modern versions, including the IBA's, use London dry gin.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, aromatic and gently sweet. Equal parts gin and sweet vermouth make a rounder, softer drink than a dry Martini, with juniper and botanicals mingling with vermouth's dried fruit, vanilla and spice. A barspoon of maraschino adds a subtle cherry-almond note, and orange bitters lift the finish. Silky after stirring, it is ideal as an aperitif or an evening sipper.

cocktails.name: Mary Pickford
cocktails.shortDescription: A Prohibition-era Havana cocktail of white rum, pineapple, maraschino and grenadine, named after the silent film star.
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide credits the Mary Pickford to Fred Kaufman at the Hotel Nacional de Cuba in Havana during the 1920s, when Prohibition sent thirsty Americans to Cuba. It was named after the silent film star, who was visiting with her husband Douglas Fairbanks and his friend Charlie Chaplin.

Basil Woon's 1928 book When It's Cocktail Time in Cuba describes it as two-thirds fresh pineapple juice and one-third Bacardi with a dash of grenadine, well shaken. Because Woon makes no mention of it, Difford's concludes that the maraschino now seen as essential was a later addition.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, soft and gently sweet. Fresh pineapple juice dominates, giving tropical sweetness and a light, frothy texture when shaken, while white rum adds a clean, grassy base. Maraschino adds a subtle cherry-almond perfume and grenadine a pink blush with a little extra sweetness. Light and approachable, it is a pleasant brunch or poolside drink with an old-Hollywood story.

cocktails.name: Matador
cocktails.shortDescription: Reposado tequila, orange curaçao and dry vermouth stirred with a dash of mezcal: a 1937 Café Royal recipe, served up.
instructions: Stir the tequila, orange curaçao, dry vermouth and mezcal with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: This Matador is adapted from W. J. Tarling's 1937 Café Royal Cocktail Book, which gave it as equal thirds of orange curaçao, French vermouth and tequila, shaken. Difford's Guide stirs it instead and adds slightly more vermouth to mellow the drink, then a tiny splash of mezcal to give it back some kick. The adaptation was influenced by Jason E. Clapham, who suggested a spoon of overproof rum to give the equal-parts original "a bump".
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry, smooth and orange-scented, a tequila alternative to the Dry Martini. Reposado tequila offers agave with gentle oak, dry vermouth adds crisp herbal and wine notes, and orange curaçao brings rounded orange-peel sweetness. A few drops of mezcal leave a faint wisp of smoke on the finish, and a lemon twist lifts the aroma. Best savoured as a nightcap.

cocktails.name: Mexican Firing Squad Special
cocktails.shortDescription: Reposado tequila shaken with lime, grenadine and Angostura, served tall over ice: Charles H. Baker's 1937 Mexico City find.
cocktails.garnish: Orange slice, pineapple wedge and maraschino cherry
instructions: Chill a highball glass and fill it with ice.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Garnish with an orange slice, a pineapple wedge and a cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Mexican Firing Squad Special comes from Charles H. Baker Jr.'s 1939 The Gentleman's Companion. Baker writes that he nearly came to grief on it at La Cucaracha Bar in Mexico City in 1937, after slipping away from two well-connected young Mexican guides who kept steering him to dull places serving warm drinks.

His recipe calls for two jiggers of a good tequila, the juice of two small limes, one and a half to two teaspoons of grenadine or plain syrup and two dashes of Angostura, poured over finely cracked ice in a tall collins glass and garnished with orange, pineapple and a red cherry.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tart, fruity and gently spiced. Reposado tequila gives earthy agave with a touch of vanilla and oak, lime juice brings a sharp, refreshing acidity, and grenadine adds a red-fruit sweetness and a rosy colour. Angostura bitters lend warmth and depth, keeping it from tasting candied. Served tall over ice, it is a lively, refreshing drink for warm afternoons.

cocktails.name: Midnight Stinger
cocktails.shortDescription: Sam Ross's digestivo sour of bourbon and Fernet-Branca with lemon and sugar, served over crushed ice with mint.
instructions: Shake all ingredients with ice.
Strain into an old fashioned glass filled with crushed ice.
Garnish with a bouquet of mint sprigs.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the Midnight Stinger is adapted from a drink created by Sam Ross at Attaboy in New York City. Ross's original used equal parts bourbon and Fernet-Branca with three-quarters of an ounce each of lemon juice and 1:1 sugar syrup; Difford's version switches to a richer 2:1 syrup and reduces it slightly. Difford's presents it as a digestivo for after a hearty meal and lists it in its Cocktail Hall of Fame.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bracing, minty and surprisingly refreshing. Fernet-Branca brings intense bitter herbs, menthol and liquorice, softened by bourbon's vanilla and caramel. Lemon and sugar turn it into a balanced sour, and crushed ice plus a mint bouquet make it cool and aromatic. The first sips can be challenging for fernet newcomers, but it soon becomes easy to drink. A stomach-settling after-dinner drink.

cocktails.name: Milano Torino
cocktails.shortDescription: Equal parts Campari and sweet vermouth over ice: the 1860s Milanese aperitivo that led to the Americano and Negroni.

ingredients.note: preferably a large cube or block ice

instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass.
Stir both ingredients with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass, ideally over a large cube.
Garnish with an orange slice or wedge.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the Milano Torino was created in the 1860s by Gaspare Campari at his Caffè Campari on Milan's Piazza del Duomo. The name reflects where its two ingredients came from: Campari from Milan and rosso vermouth, traditionally from Turin. It is said that adding soda water to the Mi-To produced the Americano, and that adding gin later turned it into the Negroni, making this simple mix the ancestor of two of the world's best-known aperitivi.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet, aromatic and simple. Campari brings bitter orange, rhubarb and gentian, and sweet vermouth answers with vanilla, dark fruit and herbs. Without gin or soda it is richer than an Americano and lighter in alcohol than a Negroni. An orange slice adds a fresh citrus aroma. Sip it slowly over a large ice cube as a classic Italian pre-dinner aperitivo.

cocktails.name: Mimosa
cocktails.shortDescription: Sparkling wine and orange juice in a flute: the light, fruity brunch staple often credited to the Paris Ritz.
instructions: Pour the orange juice into a flute.
Gently pour in the Prosecco.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The Mimosa is often credited to Frank Meier, the bartender at the Ritz Hotel in Paris, with dates given as either the early 1920s or 1925. Meier's 1936 book is the first known publication to list it, calling it the 'Mimosa or Champagne Orange' and serving it over ice in a large wineglass. Oddly, the book does not mark it with the symbol Meier used for his own creations, so his authorship is uncertain.

Its close cousin, the Buck's Fizz, is believed to have been created around 1921 at Buck's Club in London and appears in print earlier, in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book. The two are nearly the same mix of orange juice and sparkling wine; traditionally the Buck's Fizz uses more wine, while the Mimosa was the version served with ice. The IBA notes the two names are used interchangeably.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, fruity and gently fizzy. Fresh orange juice provides sweet, juicy citrus with a little tang, while dry Prosecco adds crisp bubbles, a touch of green apple and pear, and a refreshing lift. Equal parts keep it low in alcohol and easy to drink, more like sparkling juice than a strong cocktail. The result is bright, breezy and soft, a natural fit for brunch.

sources.title: Buck's Fizz & Mimosa cocktails – history & recipes

cocktails.name: Mint Julep
cocktails.shortDescription: A cold, aromatic Southern serve of bourbon, mint and sugar packed with crushed ice.
instructions: Gently muddle the mint with the sugar and water in a julep cup.
Fill the cup with cracked ice.
Add the bourbon and stir until the cup is well frosted.
cocktails.history:
The word 'julep' goes back to the Persian 'gulab', a rosewater syrup, which passed into Arabic and Latin and was later used in Europe for herbal medicinal syrups. The earliest verified reference to the American drink comes from John Davis's 1803 account of his travels, describing Virginians taking a morning dram of spirit steeped with mint. At that point juleps could be based on rum, brandy or whiskey.

Jerry Thomas's 1862 guide offered cognac, gin and whiskey versions, and by about 1900 whiskey had become the usual base. The bourbon julep is now tied to the Kentucky Derby at Churchill Downs: it became the race's official drink in 1938, and from 1939 the track commissioned souvenir glasses after many of its glasses were taken home. Around 120,000 are sold over the race weekend.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Cold, aromatic and strong. A heap of crushed ice chills and slowly dilutes the bourbon, whose caramel, vanilla and oak notes come through softly. Fresh mint adds a cool, green perfume that hits the nose before each sip, and a little sugar smooths the spirit's heat. It is simple and sweet-edged rather than sour, with the frosty cup making it feel especially refreshing on a hot day.

cocktails.name: Missionary's Downfall
cocktails.shortDescription: Donn Beach's frozen 1930s tiki drink blending white rum, peach brandy, lime, honey, fresh mint and pineapple.

ingredients.note: half a cup of crushed ice

cocktails.garnish: Mint sprig and a slice of pineapple
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a blender with about half a cup of crushed ice.
Blend until smooth.
Pour into a large goblet.
Garnish with a mint sprig and a slice of pineapple.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Missionary's Downfall to Donn Beach, who created it in the late 1930s at his Don the Beachcomber restaurant in Hollywood, California. Wikipedia describes Beach as the founding father of tiki culture: he opened his first Hollywood bar when Prohibition ended in 1933, and his menus came to feature dozens of exotic rum drinks. The IBA recipe blends fresh mint and pineapple with crushed ice into a frosty, almost slushy drink, and PUNCH has published a granita version of it.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Cool, minty and tropical. Fresh mint and pineapple dominate, giving a bright, green, fruity flavour, while peach brandy adds soft stone-fruit sweetness and honey a floral roundness. White rum keeps the base light and lime adds tang. Blending with crushed ice makes it frosty and smooth, like a tropical Mojito slush. Perfect for hot afternoons and poolside drinking.

cocktails.name: Mojito
cocktails.shortDescription: Cuba's minty highball of white rum, lime, sugar and fresh mint, topped with soda.
instructions: Muddle the mint with the sugar and lime juice in the glass.
Add a splash of soda water and fill the glass with ice.
Pour in the rum and top with soda water.
Stir gently to combine.
cocktails.history:
The Mojito's exact origins are unclear. One popular theory links it to the Draque, a medicinal mix of crude cane spirit, sugar, lime and mint said to be named after Sir Francis Drake, who menaced Havana in 1586. Once rum replaced the rough cane spirit in the 1800s, the drink is said to have taken the Mojito name, possibly with encouragement from Bacardi. Another theory points to American visitors bringing the Mint Julep to Cuba.

The earliest known recipe, a 'Mojo Criollo', appears in a Cuban book from 1927, and the name 'Mojito' turns up on a Sloppy Joe's Bar menu in 1931–32. The famous link to Hemingway and La Bodeguita del Medio in Havana rests on a framed note in the bar, but nothing in Hemingway's known writing mentions the drink.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fresh, minty and thirst-quenching. Light white rum keeps things clean and gently sweet, while lime juice brings a sharp, zesty tang. Muddled mint releases a cool herbal fragrance that runs through every sip, and the sugar balances the sourness without making it heavy. Topped with soda and lots of ice, it is long, bubbly and light, tasting more like a herbal limeade with a rum backbone.

cocktails.name: Monkey Gland
cocktails.shortDescription: Harry MacElhone's Paris cocktail of gin and orange juice with grenadine and absinthe, named after a notorious rejuvenation treatment.
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history: The Monkey Gland was created by Harry MacElhone of Harry's New York Bar in Paris. Its name refers to the experiments of Dr Serge Voronoff, who believed he could rejuvenate elderly men by grafting monkey glands onto them. Difford's Guide reports that the 'Monkey's Gland Cocktail' first appeared in MacElhone's 1922 Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails. His 1923 edition gives a dash of absinthe and a teaspoon of grenadine with equal parts orange juice and Gordon's gin, described as invented by the author and named after Voronoff's experiments in rejuvenation.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, aromatic and gently sweet. Orange juice gives a soft, juicy body and gin adds juniper and spice, while grenadine brings a red-fruit sweetness and a sunset colour. Absinthe weaves through with anise and herbal notes that make the drink more interesting than a simple gin and juice. Light and approachable, it suits brunch or a relaxed early evening.

cocktails.name: Monte Carlo
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey stirred with Bénédictine and Angostura over ice: a honeyed, Manhattan-like nightcap first printed by David Embury in 1948.
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice, ideally one large cube.
Stir the rye, Bénédictine and bitters with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
The Monte Carlo first appears in print in David Embury's 1948 book The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, as one part Bénédictine to two parts rye with a dash or two of Angostura, shaken with cracked ice. Embury, a tax lawyer with a notably dry palate, found it a little sweet and suggested adding lemon juice and more rye.

Difford's Guide prefers it stirred and served on the rocks, describing it as a Manhattan with Bénédictine in place of vermouth. Served straight up it belongs to the Scaffa family, and relatives include the bourbon-based Kentucky Colonel and the Monte Cassino.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A strong, warming sipper with a honeyed herbal sweetness. Spicy, high-proof rye provides the backbone, Bénédictine adds honey, baking spice and a soft herbal depth, and a dash of aromatic bitters ties them together. The lemon twist brightens the nose. Fuller and sweeter than an Old Fashioned yet still spirit-led, it suits the end of an evening as an after-dinner drink or nightcap.

cocktails.name: Morning Glory Fizz
cocktails.shortDescription: A frothy 1884 Scotch whisky fizz with lemon, lime, sugar, egg white, a dash of absinthe and soda.

ingredients.note: Speyside single malt, from the freezer
for shaking only; served without ice

instructions: Shake the first six ingredients with ice, then strain back into the shaker.
Dry shake without ice to emulsify.
Pour two-thirds of the mix from a height into a chilled empty highball glass while pouring soda at the same time.
Let it settle for at least a minute, ideally somewhere cold.
Slowly pour in the rest of the mix so the head rises, then garnish with a lime wheel.
cocktails.history: The Morning Glory Fizz appears in two books published in 1884: George Winter's How to Mix Drinks and O. H. Byron's The Modern Bartenders' Guide. Byron insisted that it be drunk immediately or its effect would be lost, and described it as a morning beverage, a tonic and a nerve quieter. Difford's Guide notes that the drink was traditionally considered a restorative pick-me-up, a hair of the dog for the morning after.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fresh, frothy and aromatic. Scotch whisky gives malty, honeyed depth, lemon and lime provide a sharp sour edge, and sugar balances them. The dash of absinthe adds an anise perfume, while egg white and soda create a light, soufflé-like head and a lively, sparkling texture. Served without ice and drunk quickly, it is a classic brunch restorative.

cocktails.name: Moscow Mule
cocktails.shortDescription: Vodka, lime and spicy ginger beer from the 1940s, traditionally served in a copper mug.
instructions: Combine the vodka and ginger beer in a mule cup or rocks glass with ice.
Add the lime juice.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The Moscow Mule appeared sometime between 1941 and 1946, though where and when exactly is disputed. In 1939 John G. Martin had acquired the Smirnoff vodka rights for Heublein, while his friend Jack Morgan, owner of the Cock 'n' Bull pub on Hollywood's Sunset Strip, was struggling to sell his own ginger beer. One legend has the pair combining their slow-selling products, with a squeeze of lime, during a meeting in New York.

A rival version, reported in a 2007 Wall Street Journal article, credits Cock 'n' Bull head bartender Wes Price, who supposedly invented it to clear surplus ginger beer. The engraved copper mug, linked to a friend of Morgan's who had inherited a copper business, became the drink's trademark, and Martin promoted it by photographing bartenders with Smirnoff and the mug using an early Polaroid camera.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, spicy and refreshing. Vodka stays neutral in the background, letting the ginger beer take the lead with its peppery heat, gentle sweetness and lively fizz. A splash of fresh lime adds a bright, tart edge that keeps the drink from tasting sugary. Served over ice, traditionally in a chilled copper mug, it feels cold, zesty and easygoing, with a warming ginger tingle on the finish.

cocktails.name: Naked and Famous
cocktails.shortDescription: A modern equal-parts mezcal sour with yellow Chartreuse, Aperol and lime, created in 2011 by Joaquín Simó.
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Naked and Famous to Joaquín Simó, who created it in 2011. It is best known from Death & Co. in Manhattan, but it first appeared on the opening menus of Candelaria in Paris and Teardrop Lounge in Portland, Oregon. Simó's original called for Del Maguey Chichicapa mezcal. The drink follows the equal-parts template of the Last Word, swapping in smoky mezcal, honeyed yellow Chartreuse and bittersweet Aperol. Its name comes from a lyric in 'Tricky Kid', a song on Tricky's 1996 album Pre-Millennium Tension.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smoky, bittersweet and tangy. Mezcal brings earthy smoke and roasted agave, yellow Chartreuse adds honey, saffron and gentle herbs, and Aperol contributes orange and rhubarb bitterness with a bright orange colour. Lime ties everything together with clean acidity. The four equal parts create a surprisingly balanced, layered drink that is lively rather than heavy, ideal before dinner.

cocktails.name: Negroni
cocktails.shortDescription: Equal parts gin, Campari and sweet vermouth: the bold, bittersweet Florentine aperitivo said to date from 1919.
instructions: Pour all ingredients directly into a chilled old fashioned glass filled with ice.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The usual story places the Negroni in Florence around 1919. Count Camillo Negroni, a regular at the Casoni bar, is said to have asked for a stronger Americano, and bartender Fosco Scarselli swapped the soda water for gin. Other customers began ordering 'the Count's drink', and the name stuck. The Americano itself descends from the Milano-Torino, a mix of Milanese Campari and Turin vermouth.

The tale has its doubters. A descendant of the Negroni family has questioned whether Camillo was ever a count and has promoted a French general, Pascal Olivier de Negroni, as the true inventor. Equal-parts gin, Campari and vermouth also appears as the 'Campari Mixte' in a 1929 French cocktail book, while the earliest recipes under the Negroni name date only from the late 1940s and 1950s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bold, bittersweet and aromatic. Campari leads with bitter orange, rhubarb and gentian, while sweet vermouth adds plummy fruit, vanilla and herbal sweetness. Gin's juniper and botanicals give structure and a dry, piney lift. Equal parts keep the three in tension, so the drink feels rich and slightly syrupy at first, then finishes long, dry and pleasantly bitter. Orange on the side brightens the aroma.

cocktails.name: Negroni Sbagliato
cocktails.shortDescription: A "mistaken" Negroni from Milan's Bar Basso, with sparkling wine replacing gin alongside Campari and sweet vermouth.
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice.
Pour in all ingredients.
Stir briefly.
Garnish with an orange wheel.
cocktails.history: Sbagliato means "mistaken" in Italian. Difford's Guide says the drink was created in the late 1980s by Mirko Stocchetti at his Bar Basso in Milan, when he reached for a bottle of spumante instead of gin while making a Negroni. Bar Basso still serves it, with spumante rather than prosecco, often in the huge stemmed glasses Stocchetti designed. Long known mainly to bartenders, the drink became a social-media sensation in 2022 after an HBO TikTok video for House of the Dragon, in which actor Emma D'Arcy named it as their drink, "with prosecco in it".
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, bittersweet and bubbly. Campari brings bitter orange and herbal notes, sweet vermouth adds vanilla, spice and dark fruit, and sparkling wine replaces the gin with crisp fizz and a gentler alcoholic kick. Lighter and fresher than a Negroni, it is easy to sip, and the orange wheel adds a juicy aroma. A great aperitivo for warm early evenings.

cocktails.name: New York Sour
cocktails.shortDescription: A whiskey sour with a float of dry red wine on top, giving a striking two-tone look.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon or orange zest and a cherry
instructions: Add the whiskey, simple syrup, lemon juice and egg white to a shaker.
Shake vigorously with ice.
Strain into a chilled rocks glass filled with ice.
Float the red wine on top.
Garnish with a lemon or orange zest and a cherry.
cocktails.history: According to Difford's Guide, the drink probably began with a Chicago bartender in the 1880s. Over the following decades it was sold as the Continental Sour, the Southern Whiskey Sour, the Brunswick Sour and the Claret Snap. The New York name most likely stuck once a Manhattan bartender adopted it and turned it into a local favourite. The drink first appears in print under its current name in the 1934 Mr. Boston Bartender's Guide. Its signature is the float of red wine, which sits as a separate layer on top of the sour.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tart, rich and fruity, with a dramatic layered look. The whiskey sour base is bright with lemon and softened by sugar, while a little egg white gives a silky texture. The red wine float adds dry, dark-berry fruit and a touch of tannin that gradually mixes into the drink. Spicy from rye or rounder with bourbon, it is a sophisticated evening sour.

cocktails.name: Nuclear Daiquiri
cocktails.shortDescription: A fierce modern Daiquiri twist of overproof Jamaican white rum, green Chartreuse, lime and falernum, created in London in 2005.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a lime wedge on the rim.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Nuclear Daiquiri to the late Gregor de Gruyther, who created it in 2005 at LAB bar in London. It keeps the basic Daiquiri idea of rum, lime and sweetener, but the sugar is replaced by falernum, a large measure of green Chartreuse joins the mix, and the rum is an unaged, high-strength Jamaican style. Difford's now ranks it among its modern classics and Cocktail Hall of Fame drinks.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Explosive and herbal. Overproof Jamaican rum brings a funky, fruity punch and plenty of heat, and green Chartreuse adds a wave of alpine herbs, mint and pepper. Lime sharpens the drink while falernum contributes gentle sweetness with clove and almond. The result is bright green, strong and surprisingly well balanced. Sip one slowly at the end of a night out rather than as a first drink.

cocktails.name: Oaxaca Old-Fashioned
cocktails.shortDescription: Phil Ward's 2007 agave Old Fashioned of reposado tequila and mezcal, sweetened with agave syrup and bittered.

ingredients.note: preferably a large cube or block ice

instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass, ideally over a large cube.
Express a flamed orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the Oaxaca Old-Fashioned was created in 2007 by Phil Ward at Death & Co in Manhattan, New York City. Ward's original recipe combined reposado tequila with a smaller measure of mezcal, agave syrup and a dash of Angostura Aromatic Bitters. Over time the recipe evolved, with chocolate bitters and more recently cocoa bitters now favoured by many bartenders in place of the aromatic bitters, as in Difford's current version.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smooth, earthy and gently smoky. Reposado tequila gives cooked agave, vanilla and light oak, while a measure of mezcal adds a wisp of smoke that depends on the brand chosen. Agave syrup rounds it with soft sweetness, and cocoa bitters add a dark chocolate depth. The flamed orange twist lends a caramelised citrus aroma. A slow evening sipper.

cocktails.name: Obituary
cocktails.shortDescription: Old Tom gin stirred with bianco vermouth and a splash of absinthe: a 1940s New Orleans twist on the Martini.
instructions: Stir the Old Tom gin, bianco vermouth, absinthe and chilled water with ice.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a skewered green olive.
cocktails.history: The Obituary is an absinthe-laced Dry Martini that was popularised during the 1940s at Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop in New Orleans, and it is regarded as one of the Crescent City's own cocktails. The traditional recipe uses dry gin and dry vermouth. Difford's Guide prefers Old Tom gin, which it finds sits much better with absinthe, and bianco vermouth in place of dry, but also gives a version with freezer-cold dry gin, dry vermouth and absinthe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A potent, aromatic Martini with a twist of anise. Old Tom gin brings rounded juniper and a hint of sweetness, bianco vermouth adds soft floral and herbal notes, and a small measure of absinthe threads liquorice and wormwood through every sip. A little water opens up the botanicals. Bracing and complex, it suits Martini lovers looking for something different before dinner.

cocktails.name: Old Cuban
cocktails.shortDescription: Audrey Saunders' festive modern classic: an aged-rum Mojito shaken with bitters and topped with Champagne.
instructions: Add the mint, aged rum, lime juice, simple syrup and bitters to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Top with the sparkling wine.
Garnish with mint sprigs.
cocktails.history:
The Old Cuban was created by the New York bartender Audrey Saunders. Difford's Guide dates it to 2004, while Wikipedia gives 2001. According to PUNCH, she began working on it at Beacon and finished it at Tonic, with the working title El Cubano.

Saunders was reworking the Mojito: she swapped white rum for aged rum, called it the Old Cuban, then topped it with Champagne to make it festive. PUNCH calls it a Mojito Royale and says it is probably found on more menus worldwide than any of her other creations, particularly in London.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Elegant, minty and celebratory. Aged rum gives caramel, vanilla and oak depth, fresh mint adds a cool herbal lift, and lime with sugar syrup keeps it bright and balanced. A couple of dashes of Angostura add warm spice, and the sparkling wine on top brings a dry, fizzy finish. Like a refined Mojito, it suits parties and celebrations.

cocktails.name: Old Fashioned
cocktails.shortDescription: Whiskey, sugar, bitters and a little water: the original 'cock-tail' formula, rich, mellow and whiskey-led.

ingredients.note: a few dashes of plain water

cocktails.garnish: Orange slice or zest and a cocktail cherry
instructions: Place the sugar cube in an old fashioned glass and saturate it with bitters.
Add a few dashes of plain water and muddle until the sugar dissolves.
Fill the glass with ice and add the whiskey.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The Old Fashioned is a direct descendant of the earliest definition of a 'cock-tail', printed in 1806 as spirit, sugar, water and bitters. Aromatic bitters date back to a London apothecary around 1690, and by the late 1700s Americans were mixing them with whiskey to make the Whiskey Cocktail, served without ice. During the 1800s bartenders dressed it up into 'Fancy' and 'Improved' versions with absinthe, curaçao and other liqueurs.

Drinkers who wanted the plain original began asking for an 'Old-Fashioned' Whiskey Cocktail, and the name stuck along with the heavy tumbler now called an old fashioned glass. During Prohibition, muddled orange and cherry crept in, possibly to hide rough spirit. The cocktail revivals in London in the 1990s and later in the US brought back the simpler, unfruited style.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, mellow and whiskey-led. The bourbon or rye shows caramel, vanilla, oak and spice, softened by a little dissolved sugar that rounds out the alcohol. Angostura adds warm clove and cinnamon notes plus a faint bitterness, and the dilution from stirring over ice opens up the spirit. The citrus garnish brings a fresh orange-oil aroma, so the drink feels both comforting and quietly complex.

cocktails.name: Old Friend
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, pink grapefruit, red bitter aperitivo and elderflower liqueur: a tart, bittersweet modern aperitif by Jim Meehan.
instructions: Shake the gin, pink grapefruit juice, red bitter liqueur and elderflower liqueur with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a grapefruit zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: The Old Friend was created by Jim Meehan in 2012 for the cocktail menu at Chef's Club in Aspen, Colorado. Difford's Guide publishes an adapted version: Meehan's original used 7.5 ml of elderflower liqueur, which Difford's first doubled in 2020 after reader feedback and then settled at 10 ml in 2022 in search of a balance that would please the widest range of palates.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tart, dry and gently bitter. Pink grapefruit and gin give a bright, zesty core, the red bitter aperitivo adds orange-peel bitterness and colour, and a small measure of elderflower liqueur lends floral sweetness that softens the edges and draws you back for another sip. Light and crisp, it works best as an aperitif on a warm summer evening.

cocktails.name: Old Hickory
cocktails.shortDescription: Sweet and dry vermouth stirred with Peychaud's and orange bitters: a low-strength New Orleans aperitif tied by legend to Andrew Jackson.
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice.
Stir the sweet and dry vermouths with both bitters and ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Express a grapefruit zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
The Old Hickory appears in Stanley Clisby Arthur's 1937 Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em, made with equal measures of French and Italian vermouth, orange bitters and Peychaud's. Arthur repeats a hoary, unsubstantiated tradition that it was the favourite drink of General Andrew Jackson, nicknamed Old Hickory, while he helped win the Battle of New Orleans in the winter of 1814-15.

Difford's Guide adapts a 2017 riff by Maxwell Britten at Maison Premiere in Brooklyn, which leans towards sweet vermouth and adds extra Peychaud's. Jackson's nickname came from the tough discipline he showed on an 1812 march, before he became the seventh US president.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A light, aromatic and low-strength aperitivo. Rich Italian vermouth leads with vanilla, dried fruit and bittersweet herbs, while dry vermouth adds a crisp, winey contrast. Generous dashes of Peychaud's bitters bring anise and cherry-like spice, and orange bitters add zest. The grapefruit twist gives a fresh, bitter-citrus perfume. Easy-drinking yet complex, it is ideal before dinner or whenever a lighter drink is wanted.

cocktails.name: Old Pal
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey stirred with red bitter aperitivo and dry vermouth: a 1927 Paris relative of the Boulevardier and Negroni.
instructions: Stir the rye whiskey, red bitter liqueur, dry vermouth and bianco vermouth with ice.
Strain into an old fashioned glass over fresh ice, ideally one large cube.
Garnish with an orange wheel.
cocktails.history:
The Old Pal first appears in Harry MacElhone's 1927 Barflies and Cocktails, not in the main recipe list but in a chapter by Arthur Moss, the New York Herald's Paris "Around the Town" columnist, about drinks made by or for regulars of Harry's Bar. In a tongue-in-cheek tale set on "30th February 1878", Moss credits the recipe of Canadian Club, Italian vermouth and Campari to his friend William "Sparrow" Robinson, sports editor of the paper.

Difford's Guide notes that MacElhone is often wrongly taken to be the "writer" in the story, and therefore the drink's creator, when the narrator was in fact Moss, the author of that chapter. It describes the Old Pal as a rye whiskey-based version of the Boulevardier, and the drink is also known as the Rye Negroni.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A dry, bitter, Negroni-style sipper built on rye. The whiskey gives spice and grip, the red bitter aperitivo adds orange peel and gentian bitterness, and dry vermouth keeps it lean and herbal. Difford's split of dry and bianco vermouth adds just a little extra sweetness and softness to tame the classic equal-parts version. Bracing and complex, it is an excellent aperitif.

cocktails.name: Painkiller
cocktails.shortDescription: A navy-rum tiki drink from the British Virgin Islands with pineapple, orange and cream of coconut, dusted with nutmeg.

ingredients.note: cream of coconut such as Coco Lopez

cocktails.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and a pineapple wedge
instructions: Pre-chill a tiki mug or collins glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Dust with freshly grated nutmeg and garnish with a pineapple wedge.
cocktails.history: The Painkiller comes from the Soggy Dollar Bar at White Bay on Jost Van Dyke in the British Virgin Islands. Difford's Guide explains the bar's name: there is no dock, so sailors swim ashore and pay with wet banknotes. Wikipedia dates the drink to the 1970s and says it is often credited to Daphne Henderson, though previous owners George and Marie Myrick are also named. In 1989 Pusser's Rum filed a US trademark on the name and recipe, and its later legal action against a New York bar of the same name led to a bartender boycott.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, creamy and tropical. Pineapple leads, backed by orange juice and the rich vanilla-coconut of cream of coconut, while full-strength navy rum gives the drink enough weight to stop it from becoming cloying. Nutmeg on top adds a warm, spicy aroma with every sip. Long, cold and easy-going, it is a beach or poolside drink, a slightly drier and spicier cousin of the Piña Colada.

cocktails.name: Paloma
cocktails.shortDescription: Mexico's favourite tequila highball: tequila, lime and grapefruit soda with a pinch of salt.
instructions: Pour the tequila into a highball glass and squeeze in the lime juice.
Add ice and a pinch of salt.
Top with pink grapefruit soda.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
Despite being one of Mexico's favourite tequila drinks, the Paloma has a surprisingly thin paper trail. It almost certainly depends on grapefruit soda: Squirt was created in Arizona in 1938 and began reaching Mexico in the 1950s, and historian David Wondrich suggests the drink took shape around then. However, researchers have not found the Paloma name in print until the late 1990s, with a 1999 trade publication and a 2000 cocktail book among the earliest references.

Two popular origin stories have been challenged. A widely quoted 1953 pamphlet by 'Evan Harrison' appears to have been an invention added to Wikipedia as a joke, and Don Javier of La Capilla bar in the town of Tequila, often named as the creator, reportedly denied inventing it. The name means 'dove' in Spanish.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Zesty, salty and easy-drinking. Agave tequila provides an earthy, peppery base, while pink grapefruit soda brings sweet-tart citrus with a pleasantly bitter pith note and plenty of fizz. A squeeze of lime sharpens it, and a pinch of salt makes the grapefruit taste brighter and juicier. Long, cold and lightly sweet, it is a more casual and refreshing alternative to the Margarita.

sources.title: Paloma History – Tracing the Facts and Fiction about this Tequila Cocktail's History

cocktails.name: Paper Plane
cocktails.shortDescription: A modern equal-parts sour of bourbon, Amaro Nonino, Aperol and lemon, created by Sam Ross in 2007.
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide describes the Paper Plane as a riff on the Last Word, created in 2007 by Sam Ross for The Violet Hour in Chicago. He first made it with Amaro Nonino Quintessentia and Campari, but soon replaced the Campari with a less bitter aperitivo when he began serving it at Milk & Honey in New York.

Ross has said the name comes from an M.I.A. track that was blasting on repeat during the summer he and his colleagues worked on the drink. The IBA now lists the Paper Plane in its New Era category, made with equal parts bourbon, Amaro Nonino, Aperol and lemon juice.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet, bright and perfectly balanced. Bourbon brings vanilla and caramel warmth, Amaro Nonino adds orange peel, honey and gentle herbal bitterness, and Aperol contributes zesty orange and rhubarb notes. Fresh lemon keeps it tangy and lively. The equal-parts build makes it smooth and very drinkable, a great choice before dinner or for anyone curious about amaro.

cocktails.name: Paradise
cocktails.shortDescription: A simple 1920s cocktail of gin, apricot brandy and orange juice, shaken and served straight up.
instructions: Add the gin, apricot brandy and orange juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history: According to Difford's Guide, the Paradise Cocktail first appeared in Harry MacElhone's 1922 Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails as equal parts dry gin, apricot brandy and orange juice. It reappeared with a better-balanced formula in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, which used half gin, a quarter each of orange juice and apricot brandy, and a dash of lemon juice, shaken and strained into a cocktail glass. The IBA lists it among its Unforgettables.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, soft and sunny. Apricot brandy gives a rich, sweet stone-fruit flavour, orange juice adds juicy freshness, and gin provides a botanical backbone that keeps the drink from being too sweet. Without much acidity, it is smooth and rounded rather than sharp. An easy, cheerful drink for brunch or early evening, and a good introduction to vintage cocktails.

cocktails.name: Pegu Club
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin shaken with orange curaçao, lime and two bitters: the 1920s house cocktail of a British colonial club in Rangoon.
cocktails.garnish: Lime zest twist (expressed and discarded) and a lime wedge on the rim
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the gin, curaçao, lime juice, lime cordial, syrup, water and both bitters with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lime zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a lime wedge on the rim.
cocktails.history:
The Pegu Club is named after an expatriate gentlemen's club in British colonial Rangoon, Burma, where it is said to have been created in the 1920s. It first appears in print in Harry McElhone's 1923 ABC of Mixing Cocktails, made with gin, orange curaçao, Rose's lime juice and two bitters, and Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book called it the club's favourite cocktail, asked for around the world.

A recipe published months before Craddock's by Jimmy of Ciro's in London used fresh lime rather than cordial, closer to most modern versions. Difford's Guide argues that, as with the Gimlet, lime cordial is part of the drink's DNA, so its recipe keeps a little cordial alongside fresh lime and balances a dry, strong curaçao with a touch of sugar syrup.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A crisp, citrus-driven gin cocktail with a bitter-orange core. Dry gin forms the backbone, dry curaçao adds rich, zesty orange, and the mix of fresh lime and lime cordial brings both bright acidity and a slightly cooked, candied lime note. Angostura and orange bitters add depth and spice. Bracing and refreshing, with only a touch of sweetness, it makes an excellent aperitif or warm-weather drink.

cocktails.name: Penicillin
cocktails.shortDescription: Sam Ross's 2005 modern classic of Scotch, lemon, honey and ginger, finished with a smoky Islay float.
instructions: Muddle the fresh ginger in a shaker.
Add the remaining ingredients except the Islay single malt.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake.
Fine-strain into a chilled old fashioned glass with ice.
Float the Islay single malt on top.
cocktails.history:
Sam Ross created the Penicillin in 2005 at Milk & Honey, the influential New York bar. Starting from the Gold Rush, a bourbon, lemon and honey sour already popular at the bar, he switched to blended Scotch, added honey and ginger syrup, and finished the drink with a float of smoky Islay single malt. His original was garnished with crystallised ginger.

The drink travelled quickly through the Milk & Honey family of bars and on to cocktail bars in the US and London, becoming one of the best-known modern classics of the 21st-century cocktail revival. It was later added to the IBA's official list in the New Era category. Its name plays on the idea of a soothing, medicinal-sounding mix of honey, lemon and ginger.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Warming, spicy and gently smoky. The blended Scotch base gives malt and honeyed grain, lifted by fresh lemon's sour brightness and smoothed by rich honey. Fresh ginger adds a peppery bite that tingles on the tongue. The float of Islay whisky lands first on the nose, wrapping the drink in peat smoke and sea-spray notes, while the body underneath stays balanced, soothing and lightly sweet.

cocktails.name: Picante de la Casa
cocktails.shortDescription: Soho House's spicy Margarita: reposado tequila, lime and agave shaken with muddled chilli and fresh coriander.

ingredients.note: one deseeded slice of red chilli (jalapeño or fresno)

instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass.
Muddle the chilli and coriander in the base of a shaker.
Add the other ingredients and shake with ice.
Fine strain into the ice-filled glass.
Garnish with chilli slices.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits this drink to Chris Ojeda at Soho House in West Hollywood, where it was served as the club's "House Tonic". It went on to become the best-selling cocktail across Soho Houses worldwide and a popular contemporary classic in other bars. Structurally it is a Tommy's-style Margarita, with agave syrup in place of orange liqueur, lifted by coriander and chilli, and Difford's calls it the "Spicy Margarita" that led the trend.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, herbal and gently fiery. Reposado tequila gives cooked agave with a hint of vanilla and wood, lime brings sharp citrus, and agave syrup rounds the edges. Muddled chilli adds a building warmth that lingers on the finish, while coriander contributes a fresh, green, slightly peppery note. Served over ice, it is refreshing and moreish, perfect with Mexican food or on a hot day.

cocktails.name: Piña Colada
cocktails.shortDescription: Puerto Rico's national drink: white rum, coconut cream and pineapple juice, creamy and tropical.

ingredients.note: fresh; 4 slices of fresh pineapple can be used instead

instructions: Blend all ingredients with ice in an electric blender.
Pour into a large glass.
Serve with straws.
cocktails.history:
Puerto Rico regards the Piña Colada as its national drink, but three bartenders have claimed it. Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero said he first made it at the Caribe Hilton's Beachcomber Bar in San Juan in 1952, while the hotel itself gives 1954; he used the then-new Coco López cream of coconut. Ricardo Garcia, another Caribe Hilton bartender, also claimed it, and Ramón Portas Mingot said he created it in 1963 at Barrachina in Old San Juan.

Difford's Guide suggests all three may have played a part, with the Caribe Hilton the most likely birthplace. The name, meaning 'strained pineapple', is older: a 1922 Travel magazine piece describes a Cuban Piña Colada of rum, pineapple, lime and sugar with no coconut. The modern drink only reached cocktail books in the late 1960s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Creamy, sweet and tropical. Coconut cream gives a lush, velvety texture and toasted-coconut richness, while pineapple juice adds juicy, tangy fruit that keeps it from feeling too heavy. Light rum sits quietly underneath, adding gentle warmth and a hint of sugarcane. Blended with ice into a frosty, smooth slush, it tastes like a holiday dessert in a glass, with a mellow, fruity finish.

cocktails.name: Piña Verde
cocktails.shortDescription: Green Chartreuse blended with pineapple, cream of coconut and lime: Erick Castro's herbal San Diego twist on the Piña Colada.

ingredients.note: cream of coconut, e.g. Coco Lopez

instructions: Chill a Collins glass.
Blend the Green Chartreuse, pineapple juice, cream of coconut and lime juice with a scoop of crushed ice.
Pour into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a bouquet of mint sprigs.
cocktails.history: Piña Verde means 'green pineapple' in Spanish. The drink was created by Erick Castro at his Polite Provisions bar in San Diego, California, where staff nicknamed it the Greenya Colada. According to PUNCH, it grew out of Castro's unorthodox habit of adding Green Chartreuse to Piña Coladas; when rum and then gin failed to give the herbal richness he wanted, he dropped the base spirit altogether and let the liqueur carry the drink.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A herbal twist on the Piña Colada. Green Chartreuse takes the lead with its intense, sweet, alpine-herb character and generous warmth, while pineapple juice and cream of coconut provide a lush, tropical, creamy body. Fresh lime adds a bright, tart edge that keeps it from becoming cloying. Blended with crushed ice it is cold, frothy and surprisingly refreshing, a fun choice for hot days and tiki fans.

cocktails.name: Pink Lady
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin and applejack shaken with lemon, grenadine and egg white: a foamy, blush-pink sour first recorded in 1913.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the gin, applejack, lemon juice, syrup, grenadine and egg white with ice.
Strain back into the shaker and dry shake without ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
The first known reference to the Pink Lady is in Jacques Straub's 1913 Manual of Mixed Drinks, which mixed equal parts lime juice, gin and applejack with grenadine. Later recipes, including Harry Craddock's in The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, dropped the applejack, which was hard to find in Britain, and added egg white for a fluffier drink.

The name probably honours actress Hazel Dawn, star of the 1911 Broadway musical The Pink Lady, who kept the nickname for life. The creator is not recorded, though the drink is sometimes attributed to actress and decorator Elsie de Wolfe. Ted Haigh jokingly calls it The Secret Cocktail.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A tasty, foamy sour that is neither sweet nor weak despite its pink colour. Gin and high-proof applejack give a spicy, spirituous backbone with a hint of orchard fruit, fresh lemon brings sharp acidity, and a little grenadine adds subtle red-fruit sweetness and the signature blush. Egg white creates a soft, silky foam. Elegant and balanced, it works well as an aperitif or celebration drink.

cocktails.name: Pink Squirrel
cocktails.shortDescription: Crème de noyaux, white crème de cacao and cream shaken together: a pink, almond-and-chocolate dessert drink from 1941 Milwaukee.
cocktails.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and a line of Creole-style (Peychaud's) bitters across the surface
instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Shake the crème de noyaux, white crème de cacao and cream with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Dust with grated nutmeg and finish with a line of Creole-style bitters.
cocktails.history:
The Pink Squirrel was created in 1941 by Bryant Sharp at Bryant's Cocktail Lounge in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The original reportedly used ice cream rather than cream, and Difford's Guide suggests it may have begun life before Repeal as a spirit-spiked milkshake. Difford's credits Michael Lazar, known as Mr. Manhattan, for researching the drink's origins.

In the 1960s Bryant's second owner, Pat Malmberg, judged the crème de cacao unnecessary and removed it, and Bryant's still makes its Pink Squirrels that way. Difford's keeps the cacao, noting that some prefer heavy cream or equal parts of each ingredient.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light pink, sweet and creamy. Crème de noyaux brings a toasted almond, marzipan-like flavour and its signature rosy colour, while white crème de cacao adds soft milk-chocolate notes. Whipping cream gives a smooth, silky body, and the nutmeg and line of Creole bitters add warm spice and a faint anise lift. Indulgent and dessert-like, it is best enjoyed after dinner or as a festive treat.

cocktails.name: Pisco Punch
cocktails.shortDescription: San Francisco's legendary Bank Exchange drink: pisco with pineapple, lemon, clove-spiced syrup and a splash of white wine.

ingredients.note: whole cloves, mashed with the syrup

instructions: Gently mash the cloves with the simple syrup in a shaker.
Add the pisco, pineapple juice and lemon juice.
Shake vigorously with ice and double strain into a large goblet.
Add the white wine on top and stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The Pisco Punch was made famous at the Bank Exchange, a lavish San Francisco saloon that opened in 1853 and closed with Prohibition in 1919. Difford's Guide says the recipe was a closely guarded secret, and its creation has been credited variously to Professor Jerry Burns, to early owner John Torrence and to the last proprietor, Duncan Nicol.

Rudyard Kipling drank it there and in his 1889 From Sea to Sea described it as made from the shavings of cherubs' wings. Difford's also notes that steamships calling at Peru on their way to San Francisco kept the city supplied with pisco, pineapples and lemons.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, aromatic and deceptively easy. Pisco gives a floral, grapey brightness, pineapple adds tropical sweetness, and lemon keeps it fresh and zesty. Clove-infused syrup brings warm spice, and the white wine on top lightens and lengthens the drink with a dry, crisp finish. Smooth and highly drinkable, it suits warm afternoons and gatherings, though it is stronger than it tastes.

cocktails.name: Pisco Sour
cocktails.shortDescription: Peru's frothy classic of pisco, lemon, sugar and egg white, finished with drops of bitters.
cocktails.garnish: A few dashes of Amargo bitters on the foam
instructions: Shake all ingredients with ice.
Strain into a chilled goblet.
Add a few dashes of Amargo bitters on top of the foam.
cocktails.history:
The Pisco Sour has long been credited to Victor Morris, an American from Salt Lake City who moved to Peru in 1903 to work for a railway company. Family lore says he swapped whiskey for pisco when supplies ran short at a railway celebration. On 1 April 1916 he opened Morris' Bar in Lima, where his Pisco Sours became famous; a Peruvian magazine credited 'Mister Morris' with the drink in 1921.

After the bar closed in 1929, former staff carried the recipe to Lima's Hotel Bolívar and Country Club, and Mario Bruijet is sometimes credited with adding the bitters. However, a 1903 Lima cookbook already contains a pisco, lime, sugar and egg-white 'cocktail', suggesting the drink predates Morris. Peru and Chile both claim it, though Difford's Guide concludes it is Peruvian.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Silky, tart and aromatic. Pisco brings a fragrant, grapey and slightly floral spirit character, cut by bright lemon and softened by sugar syrup. Shaking with egg white creates a thick, velvety foam that makes the drink feel smooth and almost creamy. The drops of Amargo bitters on top add a warm, spicy perfume with every sip, balancing the fresh sourness with a gentle bitter edge.

cocktails.name: Planter's Punch
cocktails.shortDescription: A Jamaican rum punch of dark rum, lime and sugar cane juice, built over ice and diluted to taste.

ingredients.note: dilution to taste; may be water, ice or fresh juices

instructions: Pour the rum, lime juice and sugar cane juice directly into a small tumbler or terracotta cup.
Add ice, water or fresh juice to dilute to taste.
Garnish with an orange zest.
cocktails.history:
Planter's Punch is a rum punch that Wikipedia traces to Jamaica, built on the classic punch proportions of one part sour, two sweet, three strong and four weak. Wikipedia notes that a recipe was printed in the September 1878 issue of the London magazine Fun, and that the IBA now specifies Jamaican rum, lime and sugar cane juice.

Difford's Guide links the drink to Fred L. Myers, founder of Myers's rum, whose 'Old Plantation formula' on the back of each bottle uses the classic proportions. Difford's own recipe instead follows David Embury's 1948 ratio of one sweet, two sour, three strong and four weak.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, fruity and refreshing. Jamaican rum brings bold molasses, banana and spice, fresh lime gives a sharp citrus lift, and sugar cane juice adds a fresh, grassy sweetness. Dilution with water, ice or juice makes it long and easy to drink, and the balance can be adjusted to taste. A classic hot-weather punch that suits beaches, barbecues and lazy afternoons.

cocktails.name: Poet's Dream
cocktails.shortDescription: A Prohibition-era stirred drink of gin, Bénédictine and dry vermouth, first printed in a 1931 Waldorf-Astoria bar book.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide traces the Poet's Dream to Albert Stevens Crockett's 1931 book Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Days, which gave it as equal thirds of Bénédictine, French vermouth and dry gin, with lemon peel squeezed over the top. The same formula was repeated in later books, including the 1949 edition of Esquire's Handbook for Hosts. Difford finds the equal-parts version a little rich, so his modern recipe trims the Bénédictine to below the gin and vermouth measures.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Honeyed, herbal and smooth. Bénédictine brings honey, saffron and baking spice, dry vermouth adds herbal, slightly bitter dryness, and gin supplies a firm juniper backbone. The lemon twist brightens the aroma and cuts the richness. It is soft and rounded rather than sharp, with a silky texture, and makes a good slow sipper before or after dinner.

cocktails.name: Porn Star Martini
cocktails.shortDescription: Douglas Ankrah's 2002 London hit of vanilla vodka, passion fruit and vanilla sugar, served with a Champagne shot alongside.

ingredients.note: served on the side as a shot

cocktails.garnish: Half a passion fruit dusted with sugar
instructions: Add the vanilla vodka, passion fruit liqueur, passion fruit purée and vanilla sugar to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Double strain into a large chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with half a passion fruit and serve with a shot of Champagne on the side.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Porn Star Martini to Douglas Ankrah, who created it in 2002 at the Townhouse bar in Knightsbridge, London. Ankrah, who also founded London's LAB bar, is closely associated with the drink. In his 2004 book Shaken & Stirred, Ankrah called it the Maverick Martini or Porn Star Martini, saying it was named after a Cape Town nightclub he used to visit. He recalled that on the first night he made it at Townhouse, the whole bar was ordering it by closing time. His original served the Champagne shot on the side.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, tangy and indulgent. Passion fruit purée and liqueur give an intense tropical tartness, while vanilla vodka and vanilla sugar add a smooth, sweet, creamy aroma. Shaking gives a light froth. The shot of Champagne alongside offers a dry, fizzy contrast that can be sipped separately or poured in. Bright and fun, it is a classic party and celebration drink.

cocktails.name: Port of Spain
cocktails.shortDescription: Mezcal, orgeat and lime with a full half ounce of Angostura: a bold, spicy 2013 San Francisco sour named after Trinidad's capital.
cocktails.garnish: Lime wheel (preferably dehydrated) floated on top
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the mezcal, orgeat, lime juice and Angostura bitters with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Float a lime wheel on the surface.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide adapts this drink from a recipe created in 2013 by Dominic Alling at Beretta, a restaurant and bar in San Francisco. It is named after Port of Spain, the capital of Trinidad, which is home to Angostura bitters, and the recipe pays tribute by calling for a full half ounce of the bitters rather than the usual few dashes alongside smoky mezcal, orgeat and lime.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bold and spice-driven, yet surprisingly easy to drink. The large measure of Angostura floods the glass with clove, cinnamon and bitter orange, while mezcal adds an earthy smoke beneath it. Orgeat brings nutty almond sweetness and body, and lime keeps it lively and balanced. The result is rich, aromatic and gently tart, best enjoyed as an after-dinner digestive.

cocktails.name: Porto Flip
cocktails.shortDescription: A rich, velvety flip of tawny port and brandy shaken with egg yolk and dusted with nutmeg.
instructions: Add the brandy, tawny port and egg yolk to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Grate fresh nutmeg on top.
cocktails.history: Flips are among the oldest mixed drinks. Wikipedia explains that the word was first used in 1695 for a hot mix of beer, rum and sugar heated with a red-hot iron, and that over time egg was added, beer was dropped and the drink came to be served cold. Jerry Thomas's 1862 How to Mix Drinks was the first bar guide to include flips. Difford's Guide reports that a 'Port Wine Flip' first appears in the 1887 edition of Thomas's Bartender's Guide. The IBA lists the Porto Flip among its Unforgettables.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, silky and warming. Tawny port provides nutty, raisin and caramel flavours, brandy adds warmth and depth, and the egg yolk gives a velvety, custard-like texture when shaken hard. Fresh nutmeg on top adds a fragrant spice. Low in strength but rich in body, it is a perfect after-dinner or winter drink, like a lighter, boozy eggnog.

cocktails.name: Queen's Park Hotel Super Cocktail
cocktails.shortDescription: Gold rum, sweet vermouth, lime, grenadine and Angostura shaken and served up: a 1932 Trinidadian take on the Daiquiri.
instructions: Shake the rum, sweet vermouth, lime juice, grenadine, sugar syrup and bitters with ice.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lime zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
This recipe comes from If Crab No Walk: A Traveller in the West Indies, a 1932 book by the British travel writer Owen Rutter. Describing the Queen's Park Hotel in Port of Spain, Trinidad, he praised its cooking, ballroom and band, and its "Long Bar with the Brass Rail", where guests could order the Queen's Park Hotel Super Cocktail.

According to Rutter, the drink was originally made with a Trinidad gold rum, Canning's Caroni Rum. Difford's Guide calls it a Trinidadian Daiquiri, because of its generous dose of Angostura bitters. Difford's serves it straight up in a coupe, with a lime twist to finish.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A fruity, spiced Daiquiri with extra depth. Golden rum provides a smooth, lightly oaked base, lime juice brings bright sourness, and grenadine adds red-fruit sweetness and a rosy colour. Sweet vermouth contributes herbal, wine-like richness, and three dashes of Angostura give warm clove and cinnamon spice. Well balanced and aromatic, it is an excellent aperitif or a tropical evening sipper.

cocktails.name: Queen's Park Swizzle
cocktails.shortDescription: Golden rum, lime, brown sugar, mint and Angostura swizzled over crushed ice: Trinidad's Queen's Park Hotel signature drink.
instructions: Gently muddle the mint in the base of a collins glass to bruise it, then rub it up around the inside of the glass.
Add the rum, lime juice, brown sugar syrup and bitters.
Two-thirds fill the glass with crushed ice and swizzle.
Top with more crushed ice and churn briefly.
Garnish with a lime wedge and mint sprigs and serve with a straw.
cocktails.history:
The Queen's Park Swizzle was created at the Queen's Park Hotel in Port of Spain, Trinidad, which opened on 15 January 1895; the drink probably appeared soon after. The luxury hotel drew Hollywood stars and wealthy holidaymakers, who spread the fame of its tall, swizzled signature drink.

Trader Vic Bergeron called it "the most delightful form of anesthesia given out today" in his 1946 Book of Food and Drink, and included it in his 1947 Bartender's Guide with Demerara rum, lime, mint, Angostura and syrup. His 1972 revision used a blend of three rums.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Like a drier, more complex Mojito. Golden rum provides smooth sugar-cane and vanilla notes, lime brings sharp freshness, and brown sugar syrup adds a soft caramel sweetness. Bruised mint perfumes every sip without dominating, and Angostura swizzled through the drink adds warm spice and a rosy tint. Frosty with crushed ice and long, it is a perfect hot-weather refresher.

cocktails.name: Rabo de Galo
cocktails.shortDescription: Brazil's 'rooster tail': cachaça stirred over ice with sweet vermouth and Cynar, a 1950s São Paulo classic.
instructions: Pour the cachaça, sweet vermouth and Cynar into a rocks glass.
Add the Angostura if using.
Add ice and stir briefly.
Garnish with an orange twist.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide describes Rabo de Galo as one of Brazil's best-known drinks. It appeared in the mid-1950s, after a Cinzano factory opened in São Paulo and sweet vermouth began to be mixed with local cachaça. The name translates as 'rooster tail', a play on the word cocktail.

It was first served as a shot in simple Brazilian bars, with proportions varying from place to place, usually about two-thirds cachaça to one-third vermouth. In São Paulo, Cynar is now often used alongside or instead of the vermouth, and modern bars serve it on the rocks.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet, herbal and robust. Cachaça brings grassy, vegetal and slightly funky cane flavours, sweet vermouth adds rich dried-fruit sweetness and spice, and Cynar contributes earthy artichoke bitterness and a bittersweet finish. Served over ice, it is like a Brazilian cousin of the Manhattan or Negroni. A strong, satisfying aperitif or after-work drink.

cocktails.name: Ramos Gin Fizz
cocktails.shortDescription: New Orleans' famously long-shaken 1888 fizz of gin, citrus, cream, egg white and orange flower water.
instructions: Add all ingredients except the soda water to a shaker with ice and shake for two minutes.
Double-strain, return the liquid to the shaker and shake hard without ice for one minute.
Strain into a highball glass.
Top with soda water.
cocktails.history:
Henry Charles Ramos created this drink in 1888 at the Imperial Cabinet Saloon on the corner of Gravier and Carondelet Streets in New Orleans, first calling it the New Orleans Fizz. It needed so much shaking that his bar reportedly employed teams of 'shaker boys' passing shakers down the line, and at the 1915 Mardi Gras even dozens of them reportedly struggled to keep up. In 1907 Ramos moved to the larger Stag Saloon.

When Prohibition arrived in 1919, Ramos closed his bar and the recipe stayed secret until a newspaper published it shortly after his death in 1928. Whether vanilla belonged in the original is still argued over. In 1935 the Roosevelt Hotel, now the Fairmont, bought the rights to the name, and Louisiana governor Huey P. Long famously had one of its bartenders train staff in New York.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, frothy and cloud-like. Long shaking whips cream and egg white into a tall, airy foam that rises above the glass, giving a texture somewhere between a milkshake and a soufflé. Underneath, gin's botanicals meet a lively mix of lemon and lime, sweetened just enough to taste like citrus meringue. Orange flower water adds a delicate floral perfume, and soda keeps the whole thing surprisingly fresh and bright.

cocktails.name: Ranch Water
cocktails.shortDescription: Blanco tequila, lime, a little triple sec and agave topped with salty sparkling water: the Texan highball from Austin.

ingredients.note: or slightly salty sparkling mineral water such as Topo Chico

instructions: Pour the tequila, lime juice, triple sec, agave syrup and saline solution into a collins glass and stir to combine.
Add the soda water (or sparkling mineral water).
Fill the glass with ice.
Garnish with a lime wedge or wheel.
cocktails.history: Kevin Williamson is widely credited with creating Ranch Water, now something of a staple across Texas. He says it has been on the menu at his Ranch 616 restaurant in Austin since it opened in 1998. The White Buffalo Bar at the Gage Hotel in Marathon, Texas, is also linked to the drink's origins, though Williamson says his own team introduced it there. The original is made with a slightly salty Mexican mineral water, Topo Chico.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, light and thirst-quenching. Blanco tequila gives clean, peppery agave, lime brings a sharp citrus zing, and small amounts of triple sec and agave syrup add just enough sweetness to round it out. Soda water with a few drops of saline mimics the slightly salty mineral water of the original, giving lively bubbles and a savoury edge. Ideal for hot Texan afternoons.

cocktails.name: Rattlesnake
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey, lemon, sugar and egg white with a few dashes of absinthe: a frothy 1930 Savoy whiskey sour.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist (discarded) and dashes of aromatic bitters drawn through the foam in a snake shape
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice, then strain the liquid back into the shaker.
Dry shake without ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Drag a few dashes of aromatic bitters through the foam to resemble a snake.
cocktails.history: The Rattlesnake first appeared in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book as a recipe for six people: rye whisky, egg whites, sweetened lemon juice and a few dashes of absinthe, shaken hard and strained through a fine sieve. Craddock joked that it was so called because it would either cure a rattlesnake bite, kill rattlesnakes, or make you see them. Difford's Guide notes that its modern revival owes much to an adaptation by Will Elliott at Maison Premiere in Brooklyn.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A rich, frothy whiskey sour with an anise twist. Spicy rye gives warmth and backbone, lemon and sugar make it crisp and balanced, and the egg white creates a dense, silky foam. A few dashes of absinthe add a herbal, aniseed perfume that lingers on the finish, while the bitters on top lend aroma. It is a satisfying early evening drink for whiskey lovers.

cocktails.name: Rebujito
cocktails.shortDescription: Fino sherry lengthened with lemon-lime soda over ice: a light, refreshing Andalusian highball famous at Seville's April Fair.
instructions: Fill a chilled collins glass with ice.
Pour in the lemon-lime soda and fino sherry.
Stir gently.
Garnish with lemon and lime wheels.
cocktails.history: The Rebujito takes its name from the Spanish verb arrebujar, meaning to mix. Difford's Guide explains that the recipe changes from region to region in Spain and is often as simple as equal parts of fino sherry and soda water, or of fino and a lemon-lime soda such as Sprite or 7-Up. It is popular in Seville and across the south of Spain, especially during the Feria de Abril, Seville's April Fair, and Difford's own long version uses roughly five parts fino to seven parts lemon-lime soda.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, crisp and thirst-quenching. Dry fino sherry brings its distinctive nutty, saline and yeasty character, which the sweet lemon-lime soda softens and brightens. The result is low in alcohol, gently sweet, very fizzy and refreshing, a little like a sophisticated shandy. Served long over plenty of ice with citrus wheels, it is an ideal drink for hot afternoons and outdoor gatherings.

cocktails.name: Red Hook
cocktails.shortDescription: A Manhattan-like Brooklyn riff of rye whiskey, Punt e Mes and maraschino, named after a Brooklyn neighbourhood.
instructions: Pre-chill a coupe or similar small glass.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide describes the Red Hook as a riff on the classic Brooklyn Cocktail, created between 2003 and 2005 by Vincenzo "Enzo" Errico at Milk & Honey in Manhattan, New York City, and named after a neighbourhood of Brooklyn. It is one of several contemporary drinks named after Brooklyn districts. Difford's calls it a rightly recognised contemporary classic and updated its own recipe in November 2023, trimming the rye and maraschino from earlier measures of 60 ml and 15 ml.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bold, bittersweet and spicy. Rye whiskey gives peppery grain and warmth, Punt e Mes adds a bitter-edged, red-fruit vermouth richness, and maraschino brings a subtle cherry-almond sweetness. The result is a Manhattan-like drink with more bitterness and complexity. Smooth and spirit-forward, it is good straight up or on the rocks as an evening sipper.

cocktails.name: Remember the Alimony
cocktails.shortDescription: Fino sherry, Cynar and gin stirred and served over ice: Dan Greenbaum's 2012 bittersweet, low-strength riff from New York.

ingredients.note: For stirring, plus a large cube in the glass

instructions: Chill an old fashioned glass and add a large ice cube.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the glass over the ice.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: Remember the Alimony was created in 2012 by Dan Greenbaum at The Beagle, a bar in New York City, and Difford's Guide lists it among its Modern Classics. The drink is built on equal parts of dry fino sherry and Cynar, the Italian artichoke-based amaro, with a smaller measure of gin, making it lower in alcohol than a classic Negroni-style stirred drink while keeping a similar bittersweet profile.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet, nutty and savoury. Fino sherry gives a dry, saline and almond-like character, Cynar adds earthy bitterness with caramel and herbal notes, and a measure of gin brings a juniper backbone. Served over a large cube, it stays cold and dilutes slowly, and the orange twist adds brightness. Lighter than most stirred drinks, it is an excellent aperitif.

cocktails.name: Remember the Maine
cocktails.shortDescription: A rich Manhattan-style drink of rye, sweet vermouth and cherry liqueur in an absinthe-rinsed glass, from 1930s Havana.
instructions: Pour the absinthe into a coupe and swirl to coat the inside, then discard the excess.
Add the rye, sweet vermouth and cherry brandy to a mixing glass three-quarters full of ice.
Stir until well chilled.
Strain into the absinthe-rinsed glass.
Garnish with a lemon zest.
cocktails.history: The recipe comes from Charles H. Baker Jr.'s 1939 The Gentleman's Companion, where he remembers drinking it in Havana during the unrest of 1933, with bombs going off on the Prado. Difford's Guide explains that the name comes from the slogan 'Remember the Maine, to Hell with Spain', which blamed Spain for the sinking of the USS Maine off Cuba in 1898. That slogan helped provoke the Spanish-American War. Some link the cocktail to the very similar McKinley's Delight, recorded in Albert Stevens Crockett's 1931 Old Waldorf Bar Days.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, spicy and complex. Rye whiskey gives a peppery, robust base, sweet vermouth adds dark fruit and herbal sweetness, and cherry liqueur brings a deep, cherry-stone note. The absinthe rinse adds a fragrant anise aroma that hovers over each sip without overpowering. Smooth and strong, it is a great evening drink for Manhattan lovers.

cocktails.name: Revolver
cocktails.shortDescription: Bourbon stirred with coffee liqueur and orange bitters under a flamed orange twist: Jon Santer's 2004 San Francisco classic.
instructions: Stir the bourbon, coffee liqueur, sugar syrup (if using) and orange bitters with ice.
Strain into a chilled Nick and Nora or small cocktail glass.
Flame a coin-sized orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Jon Santer created the Revolver in 2004 at Bruno's in San Francisco. He named it after the Beatles album Revolver following an argument with a musician at the bar about the band's best song, and the name doubly suited a drink originally made with Bulleit bourbon. It caught on after Santer moved across town to Bourbon & Branch. Difford's Guide adds a little sugar syrup, as some coffee liqueurs leave the drink rather dry.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Spirit-forward and smooth, like a coffee-scented Manhattan. Bourbon leads with vanilla, oak and spice, while coffee liqueur adds roasted coffee and a gentle sweetness without turning it into a dessert drink. Orange bitters and a flamed orange twist bring bright citrus oils and a slightly smoky aroma that lifts the dark flavours. Strong and warming, it is an ideal after-dinner sipper.

cocktails.name: Right Hand
cocktails.shortDescription: Aged rum stirred with sweet vermouth, red bitter aperitivo and mole bitters: a rum Negroni from Milk & Honey, New York.
cocktails.garnish: Orange zest twist or orange wheel
instructions: Stir the rum, sweet vermouth, red bitter liqueur and mole bitters with ice.
Strain into an old fashioned glass over fresh ice, ideally one large cube.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish, or garnish with an orange wheel. It can also be served straight up in a coupe.
cocktails.history: The Right Hand was created in 2007 or 2008 by Michael McIlroy at Milk & Honey in New York City, and the recipe in Difford's Guide is adapted from his. It is essentially a Negroni built on aged rum rather than gin, with chocolate (mole) bitters added. McIlroy serves it without ice in a coupe; Difford's Guide pours it over ice in a rocks glass instead, which softens its intensity.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A rich, bittersweet rum Negroni. Aged rum lends molasses, dried fruit and caramel, which meet the herbal sweetness of red vermouth and the bitter orange of the red aperitivo. Mole bitters add a subtle cocoa and spice note that ties everything together. Rounder and softer than a gin Negroni yet still firmly bitter, it is a fine aperitif or a slow sipper after dinner.

cocktails.name: Rob Roy
cocktails.shortDescription: Blended Scotch stirred with sweet vermouth and aromatic bitters: the Scotch Manhattan, linked to an 1894 Broadway operetta.

ingredients.note: Abbott's-style bitters; or 1 dash Angostura plus 1 dash Peychaud's

cocktails.garnish: Orange zest twist (expressed and discarded) and a maraschino cherry
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir the Scotch, sweet vermouth and bitters with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a skewered maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Rob Roy is usually linked to the operetta Rob Roy, about the Scottish outlaw Robert Roy MacGregor, which opened on Broadway in October 1894 near the old Waldorf Astoria. The story goes that the hotel's bar swapped Scotch for American whiskey in a Manhattan to honour the show. Cocktail historian David Wondrich later found an unrelated Rob Roy cocktail described by bartender Edward F. Barry in 1873.

A Scotch-based Manhattan was printed in London by Charlie Paul in 1884 without the Rob Roy name, while the first Scotch recipe actually called Rob Roy appears in James C. Maloney's 1900 guide, made with French vermouth and lemon. Today it is known as the Scotch Manhattan.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Scotch whisky's answer to the Manhattan. Blended Scotch brings malt, honey and a whisper of smoke, softened and sweetened by rich Italian vermouth with its notes of dried fruit, vanilla and bitter herbs. The bitters are essential, adding spice and complexity that knit the two together. Smooth, silky and warming, it is an elegant pre-dinner drink or a fireside sipper on a cold evening.

cocktails.name: Rome With a View
cocktails.shortDescription: Campari, dry vermouth, lime and sugar shaken and lengthened with soda: Michael McIlroy's 2008 bittersweet highball.
instructions: Chill a collins glass and fill it with ice.
Shake the Campari, dry vermouth, lime juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Top with soda water.
Garnish with an orange slice.
cocktails.history: Rome With a View was created in 2008 by Michael McIlroy at Milk & Honey in Manhattan, the influential New York bar where many modern classics were born. Difford's Guide reports that McIlroy was inspired by a drink called the Triumph of Pompeii, which was itself inspired by another called Rome is Burning. The result is a light, Campari-based highball that reads like a cross between an Americano and a Collins.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet, tart and refreshing.
