Campari leads with bitter orange and herbal notes, dry vermouth adds a crisp, wine-like dryness, and plenty of lime juice with a little sugar turns it into a lively sour. Soda water lengthens it into a light, sparkling drink that stays bright to the last sip. Low in strength, it is perfect as an afternoon aperitif on a warm day.

cocktails.name: Rosita
cocktails.shortDescription: Reposado tequila stirred with Campari, sweet and dry vermouth and bitters: a bittersweet, Negroni-like drink traced to 1974.
instructions: Stir the tequila, red bitter liqueur, dry and sweet vermouths, bitters and saline solution with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled old fashioned glass.
Express a grapefruit zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
The Rosita's origin is unknown, but its revival is credited to Gary "gaz" Regan. A friend showed him the recipe in 2005, taken from an article by drinks writer Terry Sullivan. In 2007 Sullivan finally recalled the source: The Bartender's Bible, published in 1991 and written by Regan himself.

Regan's working notes revealed that he had taken the recipe from a 1988 Mr. Boston Official Bartender's Guide, adding a dash of bitters and a little more tequila. The drink has since been traced back to a 1974 edition of the Mr. Boston guide, which stirred tequila, Campari and both vermouths over cracked ice.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bittersweet, earthy and Negroni-like. Reposado tequila provides agave, pepper and gentle oak, red bitter liqueur adds orange-peel bitterness, and the split of sweet and dry vermouth gives herbal depth without too much sugar. A dash of aromatic bitters and a grapefruit twist sharpen the aroma. Complex and satisfying, it is a fine aperitif for anyone who loves a Negroni.

cocktails.name: Royal Bermuda Yacht Club
cocktails.shortDescription: Gold rum, lime, falernum and a little orange curaçao shaken and served up: a spiced Daiquiri named after a Bermuda club.
instructions: Shake the rum, falernum, orange curaçao, lime juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wedge on the rim.
cocktails.history:
The drink is named after, and said to have been created at, the Royal Bermuda Yacht Club, founded in Bermuda in 1844 and popular with British Army officers. It first appears in print in Crosby Gaige's 1941 Cocktail Guide and Ladies' Companion as the favourite of Mary Mabon, a writer for Harper's Bazaar, who discovered it at the club in Hamilton.

Gaige's recipe combined Barbados rum, lime juice, falernum or sugar syrup and a dash of Cointreau or brandy. Difford's Guide adapts its version from Trader Vic's 1972 Bartender's Guide, which also calls for Barbados rum, lime, falernum and a dash of Cointreau.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A full-flavoured, tangy take on the Daiquiri. Light golden rum gives soft vanilla and sugar-cane notes, lime keeps it bright and sour, and falernum adds a subtle clove and almond spice along with sweetness. A splash of orange curaçao rounds out the fruit. Crisp, aromatic and elegant served straight up, it is a fine aperitif or a lively summer evening drink.

cocktails.name: Royal Hawaiian
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin shaken with pineapple, lemon and orgeat: a fruity, almond-tinged 1948 Waikiki gin sour first printed in Ted Saucier's Bottoms Up.
cocktails.garnish: Skewered pineapple wedge (or dehydrated pineapple wheel) and maraschino cherry
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the gin, pineapple juice, lemon juice and orgeat with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge or wheel and a cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Royal Hawaiian was created in 1948 at the Moana Hotel on Waikiki Beach, Hawaii, and first appeared in print in Ted Saucier's 1951 Bottoms Up, credited to the hotel. That recipe shook gin with equal pineapple juice, a little lemon and a teaspoon of orgeat, served in a chilled champagne glass.

In 1953 the Moana's bungalows across the road were demolished to make way for the Princess Kaiulani Hotel, named after the last heir apparent to the Hawaiian throne, and the cocktail appears to have re-emerged there as the new hotel's signature drink.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A fruity, almond-scented gin sour. London dry gin provides crisp juniper and botanicals, pineapple juice adds tropical sweetness and a soft, frothy texture when shaken, and lemon brings a bright, tart balance. Orgeat lends a gentle nutty, floral richness that recalls a Mai Tai. Served straight up, it is light and elegant, a lovely aperitif or summer drink for gin lovers who enjoy tiki flavours.

cocktails.name: Royal Smile
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin and calvados shaken with lemon and grenadine: a balanced, apple-scented sour from David Embury's 1948 classic book.
instructions: Shake the gin, calvados, lemon juice, sugar syrup and grenadine with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide adapts the Royal Smile from David A. Embury's seminal 1948 book The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks. Embury's recipe called for four parts each of gin and apple brandy, two parts lemon juice and one part grenadine, shaken with cracked ice. He noted that the balance of gin and applejack could be adjusted to taste and that some recipes added an egg white for every two drinks. Difford's version adds a little sugar syrup.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A balanced sweet-and-sour drink with a fruity apple heart. Calvados brings baked-apple and orchard aromas, gin adds crisp juniper and botanical lift, and lemon juice keeps it bright. A little grenadine lends a pink blush and red-fruit sweetness, supported by a touch of sugar syrup. Smooth and cheerful, it makes a lovely aperitif, especially in autumn.

cocktails.name: Rum Old Fashioned
cocktails.shortDescription: Aged and overproof rums stirred with falernum, sugar and bitters: a 2009 Berlin rum Old Fashioned by Gonçalo de Sousa Monteiro.
instructions: Stir the aged rum, overproof rum, falernum, sugar syrup and bitters with ice.
Strain into an old fashioned glass over fresh ice, ideally one large cube.
Express an orange (or lime) zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide adapts this Rum Old Fashioned from a recipe created in 2009 by Gonçalo de Sousa Monteiro in Berlin, Germany. Difford's notes that there are many rum riffs on the Old Fashioned, but singles out this version as the one that made the drink both special and famous. Its signature is a measure of white overproof rum alongside the aged rum, together with spiced falernum in place of most of the sugar.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, spirit-forward and fragrant. Aged rum provides molasses, toffee and oak, while a splash of white overproof rum adds punchy, funky character and intensity. Falernum brings clove, lime zest and almond spice, a touch of syrup rounds it out, and Angostura deepens the warm spice notes. Strong and smooth over a large cube, it is an ideal slow sipper after dinner.

cocktails.name: Rum Punch
cocktails.shortDescription: Overproof rum, lime, sugar syrup, bitters and water built on the old sour-sweet-strong-weak formula: Jamaica's classic punch.
cocktails.garnish: Skewered orange wheel and maraschino cherry
instructions: Shake the overproof rum, lime juice, sugar syrup, bitters and chilled water with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled collins glass (or over crushed ice for extra dilution).
Garnish with a skewered orange wheel and maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history: The Rum Punch follows a traditional formula of one part sour (lime juice), two parts sweet (sugar syrup), three parts strong (rum) and four parts weak, whether water, juice or cold tea. Difford's Guide builds its recipe around those classic proportions. It calls Jamaica the spiritual home of the drink. There, overproof rum is the preferred spirit, and many drinkers like their punch served over crushed ice to dilute and tame its considerable strength.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, sour and potent. Fiery white overproof rum gives a bold, grassy and slightly funky base, lime cuts through with a sharp citrus tang, and generous sugar syrup balances the acidity. Chilled water and plenty of ice soften the alcohol, while a couple of dashes of Angostura add warm spice. Long and refreshing but deceptively strong, it suits beach days and summer parties.

cocktails.name: Rum Runner
cocktails.shortDescription: Two rums shaken with banana and blackberry liqueurs, pineapple, lime and grenadine: a fruity Florida Keys tiki-bar classic.
instructions: Chill a hurricane glass and fill it with crushed ice.
Shake both rums, the banana liqueur, crème de mûre, pineapple juice, lime juice and grenadine with ice.
Strain into the glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Holiday Isle Tiki Bar in Islamorada in the Florida Keys claims to be the home of the Rum Runner. The bar opened in 1969 as The Hapi Hula Hut and was renamed in 1971. According to the bar's own account, which it presents as legend, manager John 'Tiki John' Elber needed to use up surplus rum and liqueurs before new stock arrived, so he mixed banana liqueur, Myers's rum, brandy and grenadine.

He named the result after the rum runners, the liquor smugglers who used the Florida Keys as their base during the early twentieth century. Difford's Guide's version moves away from that improvised mix, pairing Jamaican and Cuban rums with banana and blackberry liqueurs, pineapple, lime and grenadine.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, rounded and tropical with a touch of rum funk. Jamaican rum adds rich molasses and ripe fruit, while light Cuban rum keeps the base clean. Banana liqueur gives a lush, sweet banana note and crème de mûre brings dark blackberry depth. Pineapple and lime make it juicy and tart, and grenadine adds colour and sweetness. Served over crushed ice, it is a cheerful beach-bar drink for hot days.

cocktails.name: Rum Swizzle
cocktails.shortDescription: Aged rum, falernum, lime, lemon and brown sugar swizzled with crushed ice: a spicy Caribbean long drink with 19th-century roots.
instructions: Pour the rum, falernum, lime and lemon juices, brown sugar syrup and bitters into a chilled collins glass.
Two-thirds fill the glass with crushed ice and swizzle.
Fill with more crushed ice and swizzle again.
Garnish with an orange wheel and mint sprigs and serve with a straw.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide traces the Rum Swizzle to the early 1800s in Guyana, where British expatriates drank it on the terrace of the Georgetown Club. The swizzle as a style is older and widespread: Wikipedia cites references to iced rum swizzles from the mid-18th century onwards, from New York to St Kitts and Barbados, and notes an early 20th-century claim that the drink began on St Kitts.

Those early swizzles were often little more than rum diluted with water and whisked to a froth by spinning a forked swizzle stick between the palms. Today the Rum Swizzle is also celebrated as Bermuda's national drink, though recipes vary widely.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Long, rich and spicy. Dark aged rum and brown sugar syrup give deep molasses and caramel flavours, while falernum adds clove, cinnamon and lime-zest spice. Lime and lemon juices freshen everything, and a dash of aromatic bitters adds depth. Swizzled with plenty of crushed ice, it arrives frosty cold and dilutes gently as you sip, making it ideal for hot, lazy afternoons.

cocktails.name: Russian Spring Punch
cocktails.shortDescription: Dick Bradsell's 1980s London party drink of vodka, lemon and crème de cassis topped with sparkling wine over ice.
cocktails.garnish: Blackberries and, optionally, a lemon slice
instructions: Add the vodka, lemon juice, crème de cassis and sugar syrup to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled tall glass filled with ice.
Top up with sparkling wine.
Garnish with blackberries and, if you like, a lemon slice.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide credits the Russian Spring Punch to Dick Bradsell, who created it in London in the 1980s, before his daughter was born in 1988. He made it for friends who wanted to host a cocktail party but could not afford much drink, so each guest brought a bottle of bubbly to top glasses already filled with vodka, lemon, sugar and cassis.

Bradsell later described it as a spiked Kir Royal over ice, following the punch formula with sparkling wine replacing the usual weak element. He named it after the Russian vodka and the fact that a Collins or Fizz is a spring drink.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, tart and sparkling. Crème de cassis gives a deep blackcurrant sweetness and purple-red colour, lemon brings bright acidity, and vodka adds a clean kick. Topped with sparkling wine, it is long, lively and festive, like a stronger Kir Royal on ice. Easy to drink and dangerously so, it suits parties, celebrations and summer gatherings.

cocktails.name: Rusty Nail
cocktails.shortDescription: Scotch whisky and Drambuie over ice: a smooth, sweet and warming two-ingredient after-dinner drink.
instructions: Pour both ingredients directly into an old fashioned glass filled with ice.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
Scotch and Drambuie make an obvious pairing, and the Rusty Nail's exact birth is hazy. Drambuie, a whisky liqueur sweetened with honey and spices, was first produced commercially in Edinburgh in 1908, so the combination may have been tried long before anyone recorded it. Cocktail historian David Wondrich traced the mix back to 1937, when a drink called the B.I.F. was made for the British Industries Fair.

Other accounts say the drink was created at a bar in Hawaii in 1942 for the artist Theodore Anderson. What is clearer is that it became fashionable in the 1950s at New York's 21 Club, and its two-ingredient simplicity has kept it on back bars ever since. Proportions vary widely according to taste.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smooth, sweet and warming. Scotch whisky provides malt, oak and a touch of smoke, while Drambuie adds honey, heather, herbal spice and a rich liqueur sweetness. Stirred over ice, the two blend into a mellow, rounded sipper with a soft, syrupy texture. A twist of lemon zest lifts the aroma and keeps the sweetness from feeling cloying, leaving a long, honeyed finish.

cocktails.name: San Francisco (Café Royal)
cocktails.shortDescription: Sloe gin stirred with equal parts sweet and dry vermouth and two bitters: a fruity 1937 Café Royal aperitif.
instructions: Stir the sloe gin, dry and sweet vermouths and both bitters with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled Nick and Nora or small cocktail glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history: This San Francisco was first published in William James "Billy" Tarling's 1937 Café Royal Cocktail Book, which gives the drink its bracketed name. Tarling's recipe is simple: equal thirds of sloe gin, Martini sweet vermouth and French vermouth, with a dash each of orange and Angostura bitters, mixed and served with a cherry. Difford's Guide keeps those proportions, serving the drink in a small Nick and Nora glass, and names it one of its favourite sloe gin cocktails.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, aromatic and complex, yet light in alcohol. Sloe gin provides tart plum and berry flavours with gentle sweetness, while equal measures of sweet and dry vermouth add herbal, wine-like depth and keep the sugar in check. Orange and aromatic bitters lend zest and spice to the finish. Small and elegant, it is a charming aperitif or an easy early-evening sipper.

cocktails.name: Sangaree
cocktails.shortDescription: Red wine, brandy, curaçao, orange and lemon topped with soda: the single-serve, nineteenth-century American forerunner of sangria.
cocktails.garnish: Strawberry slices, orange and lemon wheels and a bouquet of mint
instructions: Chill a goblet.
Stir the brandy, curaçao, red wine, orange juice, lemon juice and both syrups with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled goblet.
Top with soda water.
Garnish with strawberry slices, orange and lemon wheels and mint sprigs.
cocktails.history:
The Sangaree is the single-serve forerunner of Spanish sangria. Difford's Guide notes that this version was popular in nineteenth-century America and differs mainly in being made by the glass rather than in batches. According to Wikipedia, the sangaree probably originated in the West Indies and reached mainland America in the colonial era, where it was served hot or cold.

The drink had largely disappeared in the United States by the early twentieth century. Spanish restaurants and Hispanic Americans reintroduced iced sangria in the late 1940s, and it gained wider popularity through the 1964 World's Fair in New York. Difford's single-glass recipe uses Rioja, Spanish brandy and dry curaçao, nodding to the drink's Spanish cousin.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Summer in a glass. Fruity Rioja forms the base, its tannins softened and sweetened by orange juice, curaçao and a touch of sugar, while brandy adds warmth and body. Lemon keeps it fresh, a hint of cinnamon syrup brings gentle spice, and a splash of soda lightens the whole drink. Served over ice with plenty of fruit, it is a refreshing, low-key drink for warm afternoons and outdoor meals.

cocktails.name: Satan's Whiskers (Straight)
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, sweet and dry vermouth, orange juice and Grand Marnier shaken and served up: a 1930 Savoy relative of the Bronx.
instructions: Shake the gin, dry and sweet vermouths, Grand Marnier, orange juice and orange bitters with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: The recipe is adapted from Harry Craddock's 1930 The Savoy Cocktail Book, which lists Satan's Whiskers in a "straight" form: equal parts Italian vermouth, French vermouth, gin and orange juice, with half a part of Grand Marnier and a dash of orange bitters, shaken and strained. Difford's Guide describes it as a variation on the classic Bronx, which shares its base of gin, both vermouths and orange juice, with the orange liqueur and bitters adding extra depth.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry and citrusy with real complexity. Fresh orange juice and Grand Marnier give a bright, layered orange character, while the two vermouths bring herbal, wine-like notes and just a little sweetness. Piney gin runs underneath, and a dash of orange bitters sharpens the finish. Lighter in alcohol than many classics, it is a lively aperitif or a good brunch alternative to a Mimosa.

cocktails.name: Sazerac
cocktails.shortDescription: New Orleans' aromatic signature: cognac, sugar and Peychaud's bitters in an absinthe-rinsed glass.

ingredients.note: used to rinse the glass; excess discarded
crushed ice to chill the glass; ice for stirring

instructions: Rinse a chilled old fashioned glass with the absinthe, add crushed ice and set aside.
Stir the cognac, sugar cube and Peychaud's bitters over ice in a mixing glass.
Discard the ice and excess absinthe from the prepared glass.
Strain the drink into the glass.
cocktails.history:
The Sazerac grew out of New Orleans' brandy cocktail culture. Pharmacist Antoine Amédée Peychaud, who arrived in the city as a refugee in 1795, created the bitters that still define the drink. Around the 1850s Sewell T. Taylor became local agent for Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac, and a cocktail of that cognac, Peychaud's bitters and sugar became the house drink at the Exchange Coffee House, later renamed the Sazerac Coffee House.

When phylloxera devastated French vineyards from the late 1860s, Thomas Handy, who took over the bar and the bitters, is said to have switched to American rye whiskey, and an absinthe rinse was added around this time. Historian David Wondrich has questioned this traditional account, suggesting it began as a bottled whiskey cocktail. In 2008 it was named the official cocktail of New Orleans.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bold, aromatic and layered. The cognac base offers dried fruit, vanilla and a soft, rounded warmth, sweetened lightly by the dissolved sugar cube. Peychaud's bitters bring bright anise, cherry and floral notes along with their signature red tint. The absinthe rinse leaves a haunting licorice and herbal aroma that hits before the first sip, and the lemon oil adds a fresh citrus lift over a long, dry finish.

cocktails.name: Scorpion
cocktails.shortDescription: Light rum and cognac blended with orange, lemon and orgeat: Trader Vic's fruity tiki classic, also served as a sharing bowl.

ingredients.note: Lightly aged Cuban rum (Havana Club Añejo 3 Años)

cocktails.garnish: Orange wheel, mint sprigs and ideally an edible gardenia or white rose; serve with a straw
instructions: Chill a double old fashioned glass.
Blend the rum, cognac, orange juice, lemon juice and orgeat briefly without ice (Difford's optionally adds a little xanthan gum).
Add half a scoop of crushed ice and blend again.
Pour into the chilled glass.
Garnish with an orange wheel, mint and a flower, and serve with a straw.
cocktails.history: The Scorpion is one of the signature drinks of Victor Bergeron, the restaurateur better known as Trader Vic. Difford's Guide credits him with creating it around the 1950s and bases its recipe on his 1972 revised Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide. That book gives two versions: an individual serve of light Puerto Rican rum, brandy, orange and lemon juice and orgeat, blended with shaved ice and decorated with a gardenia, and a larger batch poured into a scorpion bowl for three or four people to share.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, nutty and deceptively easy to drink. Orange juice gives a juicy sweetness, lemon adds a sharp edge, and orgeat lends a creamy almond note that rounds everything out. Light rum keeps it clean while the cognac adds a warmer layer of dried fruit and oak. Blended with crushed ice, it is cold, frothy and refreshing, ideal for summer parties and especially fun served from a communal bowl.

cocktails.name: Screaming Orgasm
cocktails.shortDescription: A 1980s creamy dessert drink of vodka, coffee liqueur, amaretto, Irish cream, cream and milk over crushed ice.
instructions: Shake all ingredients with ice.
Strain into a hurricane glass filled with crushed ice.
Dust with cocoa powder.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide calls the Screaming Orgasm one of the best-known cocktails of the 1980s. It is the vodka-spiked version of the Orgasm, which Wikipedia describes as a drink with many versions, commonly built on equal parts amaretto, coffee liqueur and Irish cream, sometimes with cream. Wikipedia notes that the Screaming Orgasm is often made with vodka, coffee liqueur, amaretto and Irish cream lengthened with milk, and that the Orgasm was dropped from the IBA official list in 2011.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, sweet and creamy like a boozy milkshake. Coffee liqueur brings roasted coffee and caramel, amaretto adds marzipan, and Irish cream contributes chocolate and whiskey notes. Cream and milk make it smooth and velvety, while the vodka gives a hidden kick. Served over crushed ice with a dusting of cocoa, it is an indulgent dessert drink for parties.

cocktails.name: Sea Breeze
cocktails.shortDescription: A light, tart highball of vodka with cranberry and grapefruit juices, popular since the cranberry-juice boom.
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the vodka, cranberry juice and grapefruit juice.
Garnish with an orange zest and a cherry.
cocktails.history: Wikipedia says a drink called the Sea Breeze existed in the late 1920s, but it was quite different, made with gin and grenadine. The modern version grew out of the efforts of the cranberry growers' cooperative that became Ocean Spray, which promoted cranberry juice as a mixer, first with gin and later with vodka, creating the Cape Codder and a family of related 'breeze' drinks. Difford's Guide notes that the Sea Breeze may date from the 1980s or even the 1960s, and that marketing by Absolut vodka and Ocean Spray drove its popularity through the 1990s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, tart and refreshing. Cranberry juice gives a dry, tangy red-berry flavour and a bright pink colour, grapefruit adds a zesty, slightly bitter edge, and vodka provides a clean kick without changing the fruit character. Light and not too sweet, it is easy to make in quantity and ideal for summer afternoons, beach days and casual parties.

cocktails.name: Sex on the Beach
cocktails.shortDescription: A fruity 1980s vodka highball with peach schnapps, orange and cranberry juice, built over ice.
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the vodka, peach schnapps, orange juice and cranberry juice.
Garnish with half an orange slice.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide describes Sex on the Beach as an infamous cocktail of the 1980s with many different recipes. Wikipedia notes that two main versions exist: the IBA build of vodka, peach schnapps, orange juice and cranberry juice, and an alternative in the 2008 Mr. Boston Official Bartender's Guide that uses raspberry and melon liqueurs with pineapple and cranberry juices. Related drinks include the Woo Woo, which leaves out the orange juice, and alcohol-free versions served under milder names.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, fruity and easy-going. Peach schnapps adds a soft, sweet peach flavour, orange juice brings juicy citrus, and cranberry juice provides tartness and a sunset red colour. Vodka sits quietly in the background, so the alcohol is well hidden. Long and light, it is a classic holiday and party drink for those who prefer fruit over bitterness.

cocktails.name: Shaft
cocktails.shortDescription: Cold brew coffee, vodka, Irish cream and coffee liqueur shaken over ice: a Canadian caffeinated shot turned creamy sipper.
instructions: Shake the cold brew coffee, vodka, Irish cream liqueur and coffee liqueur with ice.
Fine strain into an ice-filled old fashioned glass.
Serve without garnish.
cocktails.history:
The Shaft takes its name from John Shaft, the private detective hero of the 1971 film Shaft. Difford's Guide credits its creation, around 2000, to Mark Smith at The Living Room restaurant in Calgary, Canada, where it was a built caffeinated shot of espresso, a splash of coffee liqueur and skimmed milk.

The drink became a fixture in Victoria, British Columbia, so much so that many locals assumed it was invented there. On its way west it seems to have picked up vodka, with Irish cream often replacing the milk and cold brew coffee frequently standing in for espresso.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A creamy, coffee-driven pick-me-up. Cold brew coffee gives a smooth, roasted backbone, coffee liqueur adds sweetness and depth, and Irish cream contributes a soft, mocha-like richness that rounds out the vodka. Lower in alcohol than it tastes, it can be sipped over ice or knocked back as a shot, and suits late nights when an energy boost is wanted.

cocktails.name: Sherry Cobbler
cocktails.shortDescription: America's most fashionable 1830s drink: sherry shaken with sugar and citrus, served over crushed ice with a straw.

ingredients.note: 45 ml amontillado plus 45 ml palo cortado
half an orange wheel, cut in quarters
half a lemon wheel, cut in quarters
for shaking; crushed ice to serve

cocktails.garnish: Fresh berries and a quarter wheel each of orange and lemon; serve with straws
instructions: Add the sherries, sugar and two quarter wheels each of orange and lemon to a shaker with ice.
Shake briskly.
Strain into a julep cup filled with crushed ice.
Garnish with fresh berries and quarter wheels of orange and lemon, and serve with straws.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide reports that the Sherry Cobbler emerged in the 1830s and soon replaced the Mint Julep as America's favourite tavern drink. Historian David Wondrich found the earliest known reference in the 1838 diary of Katherine Jane Ellice, who enjoyed one while touring resorts in upstate New York.

Its fame spread abroad, encouraging 'American bars' to open in cities around the world, and it appears in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit and Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon. Wondrich argues that the Cobbler, served over ice, is what brought the drinking straw into common use.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, nutty and refreshing. Sherry provides dry, savoury notes of almond, dried fruit and salinity, while a little sugar and shaken citrus wheels add sweetness and a fresh orange-lemon zest. Served over a mound of crushed ice, it is very cold, low in alcohol and gently diluted as you sip. A perfect hot-weather drink and a great introduction to sherry.

cocktails.name: Sidecar
cocktails.shortDescription: An elegant post-First World War sour of cognac, orange liqueur and lemon, tart and warming.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Sidecar emerged around the end of the First World War, and its creator is uncertain. David Embury wrote in 1948 that a friend invented it at a Paris bistro during the war, naming it after the motorcycle sidecar that carried a captain there; many assume he meant Harry's New York Bar. Yet the first printed recipe, in Robert Vermeire's 1922 book, credits Pat MacGarry, bartender at Buck's Club in London.

Harry MacElhone's own book from the same year also first credited MacGarry, though later editions seem to claim the drink for himself. Difford's Guide's best reading is that MacGarry created it in London and MacElhone popularised it in Paris. Early recipes used equal parts brandy, triple sec and lemon; the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book doubled the brandy, and the sugared rim came later.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Elegant, tart and warming. Cognac gives a rich base of dried fruit, vanilla and oak, while triple sec adds sweet orange peel and a little extra body. Fresh lemon juice cuts through with a crisp sourness that keeps the drink lively. Served very cold and straight up, it balances brandy depth with citrus brightness, finishing dry and slightly bittersweet, like a refined brandy-based relative of the Daiquiri.

cocktails.name: Siesta
cocktails.shortDescription: Blanco tequila shaken with lime, pink grapefruit, sugar and a little Campari: Katie Stipe's bittersweet mid-2000s tequila sour.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a grapefruit zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Siesta to Katie Stipe, who created it around 2006 at the Flatiron Lounge in Manhattan, New York City. Built like a tequila Daiquiri, it takes blanco tequila, lime and sugar and adds pink grapefruit juice and a small measure of Campari for a bittersweet edge and a blush of colour. It has since become one of the drinks listed among Difford's Modern Classics.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, tart and lightly bitter. Blanco tequila gives a fresh, peppery agave base, lime and pink grapefruit bring zesty citrus with a hint of pith, and a small dose of Campari adds bitter orange and a pale pink colour. Sugar syrup rounds off the sharp edges so it finishes clean and balanced. Light and refreshing, it is ideal on a warm afternoon.

cocktails.name: Silk Stocking
cocktails.shortDescription: Tequila shaken with white crème de cacao, cream and grenadine: a silky, chocolatey after-dinner drink dating from the early 1980s.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the tequila, white crème de cacao, grenadine and cream with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Dust with freshly grated nutmeg.
cocktails.history:
The Silk Stocking emerged in the late 1970s or early 1980s. The earliest book reference Difford's Guide has found is Helen Spence's 1982 Cocktails For Two, where Silk Stockings is a blended drink of tequila, white crème de cacao, fresh cream and grenadine, dusted with cinnamon and finished with a cherry.

Difford's shaken recipe comes from Ryan Chetiyawardana, who shared it in 2009 at The Cabinet Room in London during the UK final of that year's World Class bartending competition. His version swaps the blender for the shaker, keeps the tequila, cacao, cream and grenadine core, and finishes the drink with nutmeg instead of cinnamon.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Remarkably smooth and creamy, yet with a clear tequila bite. Blanco tequila brings peppery, vegetal agave notes that cut through the richness, white crème de cacao adds a gentle milk-chocolate sweetness, and a little grenadine contributes a hint of red fruit and a soft pink colour. Whipping cream gives a silky, dessert-like texture and nutmeg adds warm spice. A perfect after-dinner indulgence.

cocktails.name: Singapore Sling
cocktails.shortDescription: A long, pink gin drink with cherry liqueur, Bénédictine, pineapple and lime, created at the Raffles Hotel, Singapore.
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a hurricane glass.
Garnish with pineapple and a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide says the weight of evidence credits the Singapore Sling to Ngiam Tong Boon, a Chinese-born bartender at the Long Bar of the Raffles Hotel in Singapore. That dates it to between 1899, when he started at the hotel, and 1915, when he died.

The original name and recipe are debated. Gin Slings were popular in Singapore at the time, a pink sling is mentioned in a local newspaper in 1903, and early books list both Singapore and Straits Slings. Robert Vermeire still called it the Straits Sling in 1922, and the Singapore name seems to have settled by the early 1930s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, complex and refreshing. Pineapple juice gives a juicy, frothy body, cherry liqueur adds dark-fruit sweetness and the drink's pink colour, while Bénédictine and orange liqueur bring honeyed herbs and orange peel. Gin and lime keep it fresh, and a dash of bitters adds spice. Long and tropical, it is a celebratory, holiday-style drink with plenty of depth.

cocktails.name: Slow Comfortable Screw Against The Wall
cocktails.shortDescription: Vodka, Southern Comfort and orange juice with sloe gin and a Galliano float: the cheekily named 1980s Slow Screw variation.
instructions: Stir the vodka, Southern Comfort and orange juice with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled collins glass.
Drizzle the sloe gin around the surface so it bleeds into the drink.
Float the Galliano on top and garnish with an orange wheel.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide explains that the Slow Screw, a Screwdriver riff with sloe gin in place of vodka, emerged in the 1980s, when cocktails with suggestive names were at the height of their popularity. Adding Southern Comfort made it the Slow Comfortable Screw, and a whole family followed, each named after what was added.

In this version, "Slow" is the sloe gin, "Comfortable" the Southern Comfort, "Screw" the orange juice of the Screwdriver, and "Against the Wall" the Galliano borrowed from the Harvey Wallbanger. Difford's counts it among its most viewed cocktails and says it is far better than its name suggests when made with fresh juice.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A long, fruity and gently herbal drink. Fresh orange juice dominates, backed by clean vodka and the peachy, spiced sweetness of Southern Comfort. Sloe gin bleeds through the top with tart plum and berry notes, while a float of Galliano adds vanilla, anise and a hint of peppermint on the first sips. Light and easy to drink, it makes a fun brunch or summertime option.

sources.title: Slow Comfortable Screw Against The Wall
Slow Comfortable Screw Against The Wall

cocktails.name: South Side
cocktails.shortDescription: A crisp gin sour shaken with fresh mint, lemon and sugar, served straight up; a Prohibition-era favourite.
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well, or vigorously if using egg white.
Double strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with mint sprigs.
cocktails.history:
The origins of the South Side are uncertain. PUNCH notes that New York's 21 Club claims it as part of its Prohibition-era menu, while some historians place it decades earlier at the Southside Sportsmen's Club on Long Island, where wealthy Manhattanites went to hunt, fish and drink Mint Juleps.

Wikipedia adds another story, linking the name to Chicago's South Side and Al Capone's gang, whose rough gin needed sweetening to be palatable. Difford's Guide describes the cocktail as the straight-up version of the vintage South Side Fizz, which adds soda water.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fresh, zesty and cooling. Gin gives a crisp botanical base, lemon juice adds a bright sourness, and sugar syrup rounds the edges. Shaken mint brings a cool, green lift that makes it taste like a cross between a Gimlet and a Mojito. A little egg white, if used, adds a silky texture. Light and elegant, it suits summer afternoons and garden parties.

cocktails.name: South Side Rickey
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, lime, sugar and mint shaken and lengthened with soda over ice: the classic South Side served as a rickey.
instructions: Shake the gin, lime juice, sugar syrup and mint leaves with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled collins glass.
Top with soda water.
Garnish with a lime wedge and mint sprigs.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide describes the South Side Rickey as the classic South Side Fizz served in rickey style: fizzes are served in a highball glass without ice, while rickeys come over cracked ice. Its recipe is credited to the bartender Meaghan Dorman, several of whose drinks Difford's also features.

The origins of the South Side itself are uncertain. Wikipedia reports that its name has been linked to Chicago's South Side or to the Southside Sportsmen's Club on Long Island, and repeats a popular story that it was favoured by Al Capone's gang, whose rough gin needed plenty of sweetening.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Think of a gin-based Mojito: bright, minty and very refreshing. Gin brings juniper and botanical depth, plenty of fresh lime gives a lively sourness, and rich sugar syrup balances it. Mint leaves shaken with the drink release a cool, green aroma, and soda water adds sparkle and length. Easy-drinking and crisp, it is a superb choice for summer afternoons and garden parties.

cocktails.name: South Slope
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, Aperol-style aperitivo, Lillet Blanc, dry curaçao and lemon shaken: Michael Madrusan's bittersweet 2007 sour.
instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The South Slope was created in the summer of 2007 by Michael Madrusan, the bartender later known for The Everleigh in Melbourne. He named it after the South Slope area of Brooklyn, New York, where he was living at the time. The recipe reached a wider audience through Jim Meehan's 2011 PDT Cocktail Book, which is the version Difford's Guide follows, and it is now listed among Difford's Modern Classics.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, bittersweet and summery. Gin gives a juniper backbone, the Aperol-style aperitivo adds orange, rhubarb and a light bitterness, and Lillet Blanc brings honeyed citrus and floral wine notes. Dry curaçao reinforces the orange theme, and lemon juice keeps the finish crisp and clean. The texture is light and lively, making it an excellent aperitif or a warm-weather drink.

cocktails.name: Spicy Fifty
cocktails.shortDescription: Salvatore Calabrese's London modern classic of vanilla vodka, elderflower, lime and honey with a kick of red chilli.

ingredients.note: 2 thin slices of red chilli pepper

instructions: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Double strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with a red chilli pepper.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide reports that Salvatore Calabrese created the Spicy Fifty in 2004 or 2005 for his London bar Fifty, which opened in February 2005 with the drink on its first menu. Calabrese later called it one of his best-selling and most famous drinks, and said it was inspired by chilli-led dishes on Jean-Georges Vongerichten's menu for the Rama restaurant in the same building. Difford's places it in a period when vanilla vodka, elderflower cordial and chilli were all fashionable in London bars, noting that bartender Myles Cunliffe had created a similar drink for a 2004 competition.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, spicy and aromatic. Vanilla vodka brings a smooth, creamy sweetness, elderflower cordial adds a floral lift, and honey rounds the body, while lime keeps everything fresh and tangy. Slices of red chilli give a gentle but building heat that lingers on the finish. Balanced and fun, it is a lively pre-dinner drink for anyone who likes a little fire.

cocktails.name: Spritz
cocktails.shortDescription: The Veneto's bubbly aperitivo of prosecco, Aperol and soda: light, bittersweet and low in alcohol.

ingredients.note: Campari, Cynar or Select are used in other versions

instructions: Build all ingredients into a wine glass filled with ice.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The Spritz traces back to the Veneto in north-eastern Italy, which was part of the Austrian Empire in the 1800s. Austrian soldiers stationed there found the local wines strong and often diluted them with water, giving rise to the white wine and soda Spritzer. The name is linked to the German verb 'spritzen', meaning to splash or spray, and in Venetian dialect it is pronounced 'spriss'.

In time, Venetians added local bitter liqueurs such as Aperol, Campari, Select or Cynar, creating the Spritz al Bitter, also called the Spritz Veneziano. Gruppo Campari estimates that around 300,000 are drunk every day in the Veneto alone. The drink's international boom came much later, with the Aperol version becoming a worldwide favourite in the 2010s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, bubbly and bittersweet. Aperol brings bright orange and rhubarb flavours with a gentle bitterness and a vivid orange colour, while Prosecco adds crisp fruit and lively fizz. A splash of soda stretches it into a long, low-alcohol drink, and plenty of ice keeps it cool. Easy and refreshing, it balances sweetness against a soft bitter finish, ideal as an early-evening aperitivo.

cocktails.name: Stinger
cocktails.shortDescription: Cognac and crème de menthe from 1890s New York: a cool, smooth and boozy after-dinner drink.
instructions: Add both ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Stinger's roots lie in 1890s New York. According to PUNCH, a shaken mix of cognac and crème de menthe was served around 1890 at a hotel by Madison Square Park as the Bartholdi Cocktail; at the Holland House, George Kappeler added Angostura and called it the Brant. The Stinger name appears around 1910 in a handwritten addition to William Boothby's American Bartender, credited to a San Francisco bar.

Jacques Straub printed it in his 1913 bartender's manual, and the drink became a society favourite in the 1920s thanks largely to Reginald Vanderbilt, who mixed them for friends at his New York mansion. It remained a popular after-dinner order through the 1940s and has been revived by several New York bars in recent years.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Cool, smooth and boozy. Cognac provides warmth, dried fruit and a mellow oak depth, while white crème de menthe adds a clean, sweet peppermint flavour that cools the palate. Stirred and served very cold, the two combine into a silky, spirit-forward drink that tastes like a grown-up after-dinner mint. It is sweet but not cloying, with a fresh, minty finish over the brandy's lingering warmth.

sources.title: The Stinger: cocktail history and New York recipes

cocktails.name: Strawberry Daiquiri (Frozen)
cocktails.shortDescription: Rum, lime, sugar and ripe strawberries blended with crushed ice: the frozen fruit Daiquiri, first published in 1952.

ingredients.note: Lightly aged Cuban rum (Havana Club Añejo 3 Años)

cocktails.garnish: Half a strawberry (or a lime wedge) on the rim
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Blend the rum, lime juice, sugar syrup and strawberries without ice to break down the fruit (Difford's optionally adds a little xanthan gum).
Add crushed ice and blend at slow to medium speed until smooth.
Pour into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a strawberry on the rim.
cocktails.history: Nobody knows who first blended strawberries into a Daiquiri. Difford's Guide reports that the earliest published recipe is said to be in Electric Blender Recipes, a 1952 book by the home economist Mabel Stegner, which places the drink in the era when electric blenders were entering home kitchens. Wikipedia lists it among the many frozen Daiquiri variations: rum, lime and sugar whizzed in a blender with whole strawberries until smooth.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, fruity and icy. Ripe strawberries give a jammy berry flavour and a vivid pink colour, while lime keeps the sweetness lively and fresh. Light rum sits in the background, adding a gentle sugar-cane warmth. Blended with crushed ice, the texture is thick and slushy, close to a sorbet. It is a crowd-pleasing poolside or summer party drink.

cocktails.name: Suffering Bastard
cocktails.shortDescription: A wartime Cairo hangover cure of brandy and gin with lime, bitters and ginger beer, served long.
cocktails.garnish: Mint sprig and, optionally, an orange slice
instructions: Add the cognac, gin, lime juice and bitters to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Pour unstrained into a Collins glass or Suffering Bastard mug.
Top up with ginger beer.
Garnish with a mint sprig and, if you like, an orange slice.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Suffering Bastard to Joe Scialom, who created it in 1942 at the Shepheard's Hotel in Cairo, Egypt. Wikipedia relates that he was trying to make a hangover cure for Allied troops who complained about the poor local liquor, and that the drink became so popular that soldiers at the front reportedly asked for gallons of it. PUNCH quotes Martin Cate describing it as the drink that fortified Montgomery's forces against Rommel in North Africa. A different, rum-based drink of the same name was later served by Trader Vic.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Spicy, zesty and refreshing. Brandy and gin form an unusual but harmonious base, combining fruity warmth with botanical brightness. Lime juice adds tang, Angostura brings warm spice, and ginger beer lengthens it with a fiery, fizzy bite. Served long over ice, it is far more refreshing than its name suggests, and works well for afternoon sipping or the morning after.

cocktails.name: Sunflower
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, triple sec, elderflower liqueur and lemon in an absinthe-rinsed glass: Sam Ross's floral 2008 riff on the Corpse Reviver No. 2.
instructions: Chill a coupe glass, then rinse it with the absinthe and discard the excess.
Shake the gin, triple sec, elderflower liqueur and lemon juice with ice.
Fine strain into the absinthe-rinsed glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide adapts the Sunflower from a recipe created in 2008 by Sam Ross at Milk & Honey in New York City. It is a riff on the classic Corpse Reviver No. 2, keeping that drink's equal parts of gin, orange liqueur and lemon juice and its absinthe-rinsed glass, but replacing the aromatised wine with elderflower liqueur. Difford's notes that this swap makes the bitter oils from the lemon zest twist crucial to balancing the drink's floral, citrusy character.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Floral, citrusy and bright. Equal parts gin, triple sec, elderflower liqueur and lemon create a well-balanced sour in which juniper and orange meet lush elderflower sweetness. The absinthe rinse adds a faint anise perfume, and the bitter oils from the lemon twist are key to keeping the floral notes in check. Light and elegant, it is a lovely aperitif or a spring and summer afternoon drink.

cocktails.name: Takumi's Aviation
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, maraschino, a little violet liqueur and lemon: Takumi Watanabe's 2010 World Class version of the Aviation.

ingredients.note: Parfait Amour (violet liqueur); his 2010 original used crème de violette

instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history:
Takumi Watanabe, representing Japan, first presented this version of the Aviation at the 2010 Diageo World Class global final in Athens, where 24 finalists competed for Bartender of the Year; the title went to Erik Lorincz of London's Connaught Hotel. In the Cocktail Mastery challenge Watanabe first stirred the gin on its own to open its aromas, then carefully balanced the violet liqueur, maraschino and lemon.

The judge, Gary Regan, called it the best Aviation he had ever tasted, and Difford's Guide's account of the moment helped turn it into a contemporary classic. In 2017 Watanabe adjusted his recipe after Marie Brizard reformulated its Parfait Amour, raising the maraschino and lemon in proportion to the gin.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Delicate, floral and precise. The gin's botanicals lead, maraschino adds a dry, nutty cherry sweetness, and just a touch of violet liqueur gives a pale lilac tint and a perfumed edge without becoming soapy. A small amount of lemon keeps it bright but less tart than many Aviations. Clean and silky, it is an elegant aperitif for gin lovers.

cocktails.name: Tequila Sunrise
cocktails.shortDescription: A colourful 1970s highball of tequila and orange juice with grenadine sinking to the bottom to create a sunrise.
cocktails.garnish: Half an orange slice or an orange zest
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the tequila and orange juice.
Slowly add the grenadine so it sinks and creates a sunrise effect; do not stir.
Garnish with half an orange slice or an orange zest.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide credits this version of the Tequila Sunrise, a reworking of an earlier 1930s drink of the same name, to Bobby Lozoff, a 22-year-old bartender at the Trident in Sausalito, California, in 1970. In June 1972 the Trident hosted a party to launch the Rolling Stones' American tour, and Lozoff made one for Mick Jagger.

Jagger loved it, and the band took it on tour; Keith Richards later wrote that the 1972 tour was nicknamed the Cocaine and Tequila Sunrise tour. The recipe was printed on Jose Cuervo bottles, and in 1973 the Eagles released their song 'Tequila Sunrise'.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, fruity and sunny. Orange juice provides a juicy, refreshing base, tequila adds an earthy, peppery agave note, and grenadine sinks to the bottom, giving red-fruit sweetness and the famous gradient from red to gold. As you drink, the layers blend and it becomes sweeter. Simple and cheerful, it is a classic brunch, beach or party drink.

cocktails.name: The Business
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin shaken with lime juice and honey syrup: Sasha Petraske's simple, lime-driven cousin of the Bee's Knees from Milk & Honey.

ingredients.note: 3 parts honey to 1 part water by weight

instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lime zest twist over the drink and use it as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The Business was created by Sasha Petraske at Milk & Honey, his famous bar in Manhattan, New York City. Difford's Guide adapts its recipe from the 2016 book Sasha Petraske: Regarding Cocktails, by Georgette Moger-Petraske, which collects his recipes and methods. The book's version calls for two ounces of gin, one ounce of fresh lime juice and three-quarters of an ounce of honey syrup, shaken hard over a single large ice cube and strained into a chilled coupe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Clean, tart and honeyed. Gin provides a crisp juniper and botanical base, a full measure of lime juice brings sharp, zesty acidity, and rich honey syrup balances it with floral sweetness and a rounder, silkier texture than plain sugar would give. Simple and bracing, it is a refreshing sour for any time of year, especially before dinner.

cocktails.name: The Conference
cocktails.shortDescription: Bourbon, rye, calvados and cognac stirred with demerara syrup and bitters: Brian Miller's four-spirit Old Fashioned from Death & Co.

ingredients.note: For stirring, plus a large cube in the glass

instructions: Chill an old fashioned glass and add a large ice cube.
Stir all ingredients with ice.
Strain into the glass over the ice.
Express lemon and orange zest twists over the drink and use them as a garnish.
cocktails.history: The Conference was created by Brian Miller at Death & Company in New York City, and Difford's Guide lists it among its Modern Classics. The drink is built in the style of an Old Fashioned, but instead of a single base spirit it splits equal measures between four: bourbon, rye whiskey, calvados and cognac. A small amount of demerara syrup and two kinds of bitters tie them together.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, layered and warming. Bourbon brings vanilla and caramel, rye adds pepper and spice, calvados contributes baked apple, and cognac offers dried fruit and oak, so each sip shifts between them. Demerara syrup gives a gentle molasses sweetness, while Angostura and mole bitters add spice and a hint of chocolate. Strong and slow-sipping, it is an ideal after-dinner or winter drink.

cocktails.name: Three Dots and a Dash
cocktails.shortDescription: Donn Beach's WWII-era tiki drink of rhum agricole and aged rum with falernum, allspice, honey, lime and orange.
cocktails.garnish: Three cherries and a rectangular chunk of pineapple on a pick
instructions: Add all the ingredients to a blender with about 12 ounces (350 ml) of crushed ice.
Flash blend for a few seconds.
Pour into a footed glass.
Top with more crushed ice.
Garnish with three cherries and a chunk of pineapple on a pick.
cocktails.history: Three Dots and a Dash was created during the Second World War by Donn Beach at his Don the Beachcomber restaurant. Its name is the Morse code for the letter V, standing for victory. Difford's Guide adapts its recipe from Jeff 'Beachbum' Berry's book Sippin' Safari. Wikipedia notes that Berry rediscovered the long-lost drink, and that it gave its name to a celebrated tiki bar in Chicago's River North, where PUNCH reports owner Paul McGee replaces the orange juice with dry curaçao.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, spicy and tropical. Grassy rhum agricole and aged rum give depth and character, honey and orange juice add a rounded fruity sweetness, and lime keeps it bright. Falernum and allspice dram bring the signature tiki spice of clove, allspice and lime zest, with a dash of bitters for warmth. Flash-blended with crushed ice, it is frosty, complex and celebratory.

cocktails.name: Three Storms Flip
cocktails.shortDescription: Light rum, falernum and peated whisky shaken with a whole egg, salt and pepper: Ryan Chetiyawardana's 2015 London flip.

ingredients.note: Lightly aged Cuban rum (Havana Club Añejo 3 Años)
Saline solution or a pinch of salt

instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake all ingredients hard with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Dust with freshly grated nutmeg.
cocktails.history: Three Storms Flip was created in 2015 by Ryan Chetiyawardana at Dandelyan, his bar in London, and is listed by Difford's Guide among its Modern Classics. It updates one of the oldest families of mixed drinks. Wikipedia notes that the word flip was first used in 1695 for a heated mix of beer, rum and sugar; over time egg was added, the beer dropped out, and the drink came to be served cold.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, velvety and spiced. The whole egg gives a creamy, custard-like texture, and light rum provides a clean base. Falernum adds lime zest, clove and almond sweetness, while a small measure of peated whisky brings a gentle wisp of smoke. Salt, black pepper and orange bitters sharpen the flavours, and nutmeg adds warmth on the nose. It is a satisfying after-dinner or winter drink.

cocktails.name: Ti Punch
cocktails.shortDescription: Rhum agricole, cane syrup and a squeezed disc of lime: the small, punchy national cocktail of Martinique and Guadeloupe.

ingredients.note: a disc cut from the side of the lime, squeezed and dropped in
one or two large cubes, optional

instructions: Pour the rhum agricole and cane syrup into an old fashioned glass.
Squeeze a disc of lime peel and flesh between finger and thumb over the drink, then drop it in.
Stir, adding one or two large ice cubes if desired.
Serve with a small spoon if liked, so the drinker can press more juice from the lime.
cocktails.history:
Ti is Creole for the French petit, so Ti Punch literally means a small punch. Unlike most rum punches it is not lengthened with water or juice, and it is often served without ice despite the warm climate. It is the national cocktail of Martinique and Guadeloupe and is also popular in Réunion, Mauritius, Haiti, French Guiana and other French-speaking Caribbean islands.

On the islands it is often chased with a large glass of chilled water, called a crase in Martinique. The earliest known written mention, as 'yon Ti Punch', appears in an 1890 book by the travel writer Lafcadio Hearn, recounting the years he spent living in Martinique.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Punchy, grassy and deceptively simple. Unaged rhum agricole, traditionally bottled at 50% abv, brings vivid fresh sugar cane, green and slightly vegetal notes. Cane syrup softens the spirit and adds a rich, rounded sweetness, while the squeezed lime disc releases fragrant peel oils and a touch of juice. With little or no dilution it is strong but very pleasing, a great sundowner or aperitif.

cocktails.name: Tia Mia
cocktails.shortDescription: Mezcal and aged rum shaken with dry curaçao, orgeat and lime: Ivy Mix's smoky 2010 New York riff on the Mai Tai.

ingredients.note: Havana Club Añejo 7; original used Appleton Jamaican rum

cocktails.garnish: Spent lime shell, mint sprigs and a pineapple and cherry fruit stick
instructions: Fill a double old fashioned glass with crushed ice.
Shake the mezcal, rum, dry curaçao, orgeat and lime juice with ice.
Strain into the crushed-ice-filled glass.
Garnish with a lime shell, a bouquet of mint and a fruit stick.
cocktails.history:
The Tia Mia was created around 2010 by Ivy Mix in New York City as a riff on the Mai Tai, splitting the base between mezcal and aged rum. Her original recipe used Del Maguey Chichicapa mezcal and Appleton Estate Reserve Jamaican rum, with Ferrand Dry Curaçao, orgeat and fresh lime.

The drink is also known as the Mezcal Mai Tai. Difford's Guide notes that swapping the rum for añejo tequila turns it into a Mexican Mai Tai, and its own spec uses a Cuban añejo rum alongside Del Maguey Vida mezcal.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A smoky, tropical take on the Mai Tai. Mezcal brings earthy smoke and agave, aged rum adds molasses, vanilla and dried fruit, and dry curaçao supplies bitter orange. Orgeat's almond sweetness gives body while lime keeps the finish bright and tart. Served over crushed ice it is cold, refreshing and dangerously easy to drink, a good choice for summer evenings or anyone who enjoys tiki drinks with a savoury edge.

cocktails.name: Tipperary
cocktails.shortDescription: A rich, herbal stirred drink of Irish whiskey, sweet vermouth and green Chartreuse, first printed in 1916.
instructions: Pour all the ingredients into a mixing glass with ice.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with a slice of orange.
cocktails.history: The Tipperary first appeared in Hugo R. Ensslin's 1916 Recipes for Mixed Drinks as equal parts Bushmills Irish whiskey, Chartreuse and Italian vermouth. Difford's Guide notes that Harry MacElhone's 1922 ABC of Mixing Cocktails gave a heavier whiskey ratio, while Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book returned to equal parts and added a second, unrelated Tipperary. A third version, based on sloe gin and dry vermouth, appears in Albert Stevens Crockett's 1931 Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book. Most modern recipes, including the IBA's, follow MacElhone's whiskey-forward proportions.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, herbal and warming. Irish whiskey gives a smooth, gently fruity and malty base, sweet vermouth adds dark fruit and spice, and green Chartreuse contributes an intense herbal, minty, slightly peppery character. Bitters tie the flavours together. Stirred and served cold, it is complex and fairly strong, suiting cooler evenings or a thoughtful pre-dinner drink.

cocktails.name: Tokyo Iced Tea
cocktails.shortDescription: A green Long Island Iced Tea variation with melon liqueur, five spirits, lime and lemon-lime soda.
instructions: Shake the first seven ingredients with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled sling or highball glass.
Top with lemon-lime soda and stir briefly.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and serve with a straw.
cocktails.history: Who first added green melon liqueur to a Long Island Iced Tea to make the Tokyo Iced Tea is unknown. Simon Difford associates the drink with TGI Fridays in the mid-1990s, when the chain was known for the professionalism of its bartenders and was very influential. It does not appear in his cocktail books from the 1980s, and its first appearance in print is credited to Paul Knorr's 2007 book 10,000 Drinks. A related drink with blue curaçao is known as the Adios.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sweet, fruity and deceptively strong. Five spirits combine into a neutral, boozy base, while melon liqueur gives a bright green colour and a candied honeydew flavour. Triple sec adds orange, lime juice brings sharpness, and lemon-lime soda lengthens it with sweet fizz. Despite the mix, the melon shows through clearly. A party drink to be sipped slowly through a straw.

cocktails.name: Tom Collins
cocktails.shortDescription: The original tall gin sour of lemon, sugar and soda, traced to London in the early 1800s.
cocktails.garnish: Orange wheel and maraschino cherry on a skewer
instructions: Pre-chill a Collins glass.
Shake the gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Top with soda water and stir briefly.
Garnish with an orange wheel and cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Collins is usually traced to John Collins, head waiter at Limmer's Hotel on Conduit Street in London, whose coffee house was known for its Gin Punch in the early 1800s. Difford's Guide suggests the Collins evolved from that punch. Harry Johnson's 1882 manual listed a John Collins with Dutch genever and a Tom Collins made with Old Tom gin, a lightly sweetened style of gin.

Other explanations abound, including a bartender at a New York tavern and American claims from San Francisco to New Jersey. In 1874 the 'Great Tom Collins Hoax' swept New York, a prank in which people were told a man called Tom Collins had insulted them and could be found in a nearby bar. Over time the base spirit shifted from genever to Old Tom to London dry gin.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tall, crisp and lemony. Old Tom gin brings soft juniper and botanicals with a slightly rounder, sweeter texture than London dry. Fresh lemon juice gives a clean sour tang, balanced by sugar syrup into something like a sparkling, grown-up lemonade. A generous top of soda and plenty of ice keep it light and effervescent, and the orange and cherry garnish adds a touch of fruity aroma.

cocktails.name: Tommy's Margarita
cocktails.shortDescription: A modern San Francisco Margarita that swaps orange liqueur for agave syrup to let 100% agave tequila shine.
instructions: Add the tequila, lime juice and agave nectar to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled rocks glass filled with ice.
Garnish with a lime slice.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide credits Tommy's Margarita to Julio Bermejo, who created it around 1987 or 1988 and named it after his family's Mexican restaurant and bar in San Francisco. Tommy's was opened by his parents, Tomas and Elmy Bermejo, in 1965, and the whole family is involved in the business.

Bermejo replaced the triple sec of a classic Margarita with agave syrup and used hand-squeezed Persian limes, so the flavour of 100% agave tequila comes through. Tommy's became known for one of America's largest agave spirit selections, and the drink now appears on menus worldwide.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Clean, bright and agave-forward. Without orange liqueur, the earthy, peppery and vegetal flavours of 100% agave tequila take centre stage. Fresh lime gives a sharp, juicy acidity, and agave syrup adds a soft, honeyed sweetness that echoes the spirit. Served on the rocks, it is crisp, simple and refreshing, ideal with Mexican food or on a hot day.

cocktails.name: Toreador
cocktails.shortDescription: Blanco tequila, apricot liqueur and lime shaken and served up: a 1937 Café Royal precursor of the Margarita.
instructions: Shake the tequila, apricot liqueur, lime juice, sugar syrup and saline solution with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wedge on the rim.
cocktails.history: The Toreador, a variation on the Margarita template, was first published in W. J. "Billy" Tarling's 1937 Café Royal Bar Book as half tequila with a quarter each of apricot brandy and lime or lemon juice, shaken. The same book lists a Picador that is identical to today's Margarita, a reminder that Tarling's recipes appeared 16 years before the first written reference to a cocktail called the Margarita. Difford's updated its own recipe in January 2025.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, tangy and fruity. Clean blanco tequila gives fresh, peppery agave, lime keeps it sharp and lively, and apricot liqueur replaces the usual orange liqueur with a softer, stone-fruit sweetness. A spoon of sugar syrup and a couple of drops of saline round and sharpen the flavours. Familiar yet different, it is a great choice for Margarita lovers on a warm evening.

cocktails.name: Toronto
cocktails.shortDescription: Canadian whisky stirred with Fernet-Branca, maple syrup and bitters: a bold, bittersweet 1920s classic revived in Seattle in 2006.

ingredients.note: chilled; omit if using wet ice

cocktails.garnish: Orange zest twist (expressed and discarded) and a skewered maraschino cherry
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir the whisky, Fernet-Branca, maple syrup, bitters and water with ice.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a skewered maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Toronto's earliest printed form is the Fernet Cocktail in Robert Vermeire's 1922 Cocktails: How to Mix Them, made with Fernet-Branca and cognac or rye and noted as a favourite of Canadians in Toronto. David Embury listed it under the name Toronto in his 1948 Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, with Canadian whisky, Fernet-Branca and sugar syrup.

The drink was largely forgotten until Jamie Boudreau revived it in Seattle in 2006. In 2010 Marian Beke adapted it for the opening menu of London's Nightjar, where a coffee- and pecan-infused version became the bar's best seller. Difford's swaps the sugar syrup for maple, following a reader's suggestion.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A bracing, Manhattan-style drink dominated by Fernet-Branca. Smooth Canadian whisky gives a gentle grain sweetness, but the fernet takes over with menthol, saffron, bitter herbs and a long, dry finish. Maple syrup tames the bitterness while adding a rounded, woody sweetness that suits the whisky, and a dash of aromatic bitters adds spice. Bold and warming, it makes a fine digestif or cold-weather sipper.

cocktails.name: Trinidad Sour
cocktails.shortDescription: An IBA sour that uses a full measure of Angostura bitters as its base, softened with orgeat, lemon and rye.
instructions: Pour all ingredients into a cocktail shaker.
Shake well with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide credits the Trinidad Sour to Giuseppe Gonzalez, who created it in 2009 at the Clover Club in Brooklyn, inspired by the competition-winning Trinidad Especial by Valentino Bolognese. Wikipedia adds that Gonzalez's drink flopped in the competition it was entered for, failing to reach the top ten, yet it slowly earned a reputation as a modern classic and later joined the IBA list. What makes it unusual is the role of Angostura: rather than a few dashes for seasoning, the bitters form the largest single ingredient, with rye whiskey reduced to a supporting measure.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Intensely spiced and surprisingly balanced. The large dose of Angostura gives clove, cinnamon and bitter bark, while orgeat rounds it out with almond sweetness and a silky texture. Lemon keeps the drink lively and the small measure of rye adds a dry, peppery backbone. The colour is a deep garnet. It is a bold after-dinner sour for drinkers who already enjoy bitter, aromatic flavours.

cocktails.name: Turf Club
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin and dry vermouth stirred with maraschino, orange bitters and absinthe: Harry Johnson's dry, Martini-like 1900 Turf Club.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist (expressed and discarded) and a maraschino cherry
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir the gin, dry vermouth, maraschino, orange bitters and absinthe with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and discard it.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
Harry Johnson did not include the Turf cocktail in the 1882 or 1888 editions of his Bartenders' Manual, but added it as the final drink of his revised 1900 edition. Reflecting changing tastes, he called for Plymouth gin rather than old tom, stirred with French vermouth, orange bitters, maraschino and absinthe, and garnished with an olive.

Robert Vermeire repeated Johnson's formula in 1922 and credited him as its creator, and Harry McElhone printed a near-identical Turf Club the same year. Harry Craddock also reproduced Johnson's recipe in The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930. Other, differing Turf Club recipes exist from the 1880s and 1890s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A dry, punchy Martini-style drink. Equal parts gin and dry vermouth give a crisp, winey and botanical base, while a touch of maraschino adds a subtle floral, nutty cherry note rather than sweetness. Orange bitters and a dash of absinthe add aromatic complexity and a hint of anise, and lemon oils brighten the nose. Clean and bracing, it makes an elegant aperitif.

cocktails.name: Tuxedo
cocktails.shortDescription: A stirred Martini relative of Old Tom gin and dry vermouth, seasoned with maraschino, absinthe and orange bitters.
instructions: Pour all ingredients into a mixing glass with ice cubes.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled martini cocktail glass.
Garnish with a cherry and lemon zest.
cocktails.history:
The Tuxedo belongs to the Martini family and takes its name from the Tuxedo Club in Tuxedo Park, Orange County, New York, where it is said to have been first mixed. Wikipedia dates it to the 1880s and notes that the same club gave its name to the dinner jacket.

The earliest recipe Difford's Guide knows of is in Harry Johnson's Bartenders Manual of 1900: equal parts Old Tom gin and dry vermouth with a dash each of maraschino and absinthe. Similar versions followed in books by Grohusko (1910), Mahoney (1912) and MacElhone (1927), most using orange bitters.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry, aromatic and layered. Old Tom gin is slightly rounder and sweeter than London dry, and the equal measure of dry vermouth makes the drink softer and more wine-like than a modern Martini. A touch of maraschino adds a faint cherry-almond note, absinthe gives a whisper of anise and the orange bitters tie everything together. It is an elegant pre-dinner sipper.

cocktails.name: Twentieth Century
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, white crème de cacao, quinine aperitif wine and lemon shaken and served up: a 1937 Café Royal classic.
instructions: Shake the gin, white crème de cacao, Americano bianco, lemon juice and saline solution with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history:
The Twentieth Century was first published in Billy Tarling's 1937 Café Royal Cocktail Book, which credits it to "C. A. Tuck": two parts gin to one each of crème de cacao, Lillet and lemon juice. Bartending legend says it was named after the 20th Century Limited express train between New York and Chicago, although the train's famous streamlined Art Deco makeover came a year after the book.

Charles A. Tuck was a noted London bartender who worked at the Hyde Park Hotel's Buttery Bar and later at the Piccadilly Hotel. He also chaired the UK Bartenders' Guild. His own book, Cocktails and Mixed Drinks, published in 1967, includes the Twentieth Century, but he makes no claim to it or to any other recipe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A beautifully balanced, sophisticated sour. Dry gin gives structure and botanical lift, lemon adds bright acidity, and white crème de cacao brings a surprising, subtle chocolate richness. The quinine-tinged aromatised wine adds bittersweet, herbal complexity that ties it all together. Silky and elegant, it is an intriguing aperitif or an excellent drink for an evening of classic cocktails.

cocktails.name: Ultima Palabra
cocktails.shortDescription: Mezcal, green Chartreuse, maraschino, pineapple and lime shaken equal parts: a smoky London riff on the Last Word.
instructions: Shake the mezcal, green Chartreuse, maraschino liqueur, pineapple juice, lime juice and chilled water with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a thyme sprig.
cocktails.history: The Ultima Palabra is a riff on the Last Word created by Simone De Luca at the High Road House club in Chiswick, London. Its name is a direct Spanish translation of "Last Word", which explains why mezcal replaces the gin of the original equal-parts recipe. De Luca also added pineapple juice to the classic line-up of green Chartreuse, maraschino and lime. Difford's Guide credits Gary Regan's Ardent Spirits as the source of the recipe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smoky, herbal and fruity in equal measure. Mezcal brings earthy smoke, green Chartreuse adds intense herbal and minty sweetness, and maraschino lends a floral cherry note. Pineapple juice gives tropical fruitiness and a softer body, while lime keeps everything sharp and refreshing. Complex but well balanced, it rewards slow sipping before dinner or as a lively evening drink.

cocktails.name: Vancouver
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin stirred with Bénédictine, dry and sweet vermouth and orange bitters: a herbal 1925 classic from Vancouver's About Town Cocktail Book.
cocktails.garnish: Orange zest twist and/or a skewered maraschino cherry
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Stir the gin, Bénédictine, both vermouths and the orange bitters with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish, with or without a cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Vancouver is adapted from the About Town Cocktail Book, a collection of popular food and drink recipes published in Vancouver in 1925 by Mitchell Publishing. Its recipe was half gin, with French vermouth and Bénédictine, a dash of orange bitters and an olive. The same book lists the Fitchett, an identical drink made with Italian vermouth, named after Joseph A. Fitchett, head bar steward of the Vancouver Club, who checked every recipe in the book.

Until a 2020 article in Scout Magazine drew attention to these entries, the accepted Vancouver recipe was in fact the Fitchett with sweet vermouth. Difford's Guide notes that the drink remains popular in the city it is named after, and its recipe splits the difference with a 'perfect' mix of equal dry and sweet vermouth.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A smooth, gently sweet and herbal gin drink. London dry gin gives juniper structure, Bénédictine adds honeyed sweetness with baking spice and herbs, and the blend of dry and sweet vermouth balances crisp wine notes with a richer, rounded body. Orange bitters and a twist of orange zest brighten the aroma. Silky and well-rounded, it suits an aperitif hour or a quiet nightcap.

cocktails.name: Venetian Spritz
cocktails.shortDescription: Prosecco and Campari-style red bitter lengthened with soda and garnished with an olive: the bittersweet aperitivo spritz of Venice.
cocktails.garnish: Orange zest twist (expressed and discarded) and a skewered green olive
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice.
Pour in the prosecco, red bitter liqueur and soda water.
Stir briefly so as not to lose the fizz.
Express an orange zest twist over the drink and discard it, then garnish with a skewered green olive.
cocktails.history:
The Spritz comes from northern Italy, especially Venice and the Veneto, where it is pronounced 'spriss' after the German spritzen, to splash. Difford's Guide traces it to the late nineteenth century, when Venice was part of the Austrian Empire and Austrian soldiers diluted the strong local wines with water, giving rise to the white wine and soda Spritzer.

In the Veneto the Spritz al Bitter, or Venetian Spritz, uses local Pinot Grigio, Soave or Prosecco with a bitter such as Campari, Aperol, Select or Cynar, garnished with orange or an olive. Wikipedia dates the pairing of spritz with local bitters to the 1920s and 1930s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Dry, bittersweet and very refreshing. Extra dry prosecco provides crisp orchard-fruit bubbles, while a generous splash of red bitter liqueur brings bold bitter orange, gentian and herbal notes with only light sweetness. Soda water lengthens it and keeps it lively. The expressed orange oils add brightness and the green olive lends a faintly savoury, salty nibble. Low in alcohol, it is the perfect aperitivo before an evening meal.

cocktails.name: Vesper
cocktails.shortDescription: James Bond's martini from fiction: gin, vodka and Lillet Blanc, crisp, dry and powerful.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Vesper comes from fiction rather than a bar. Ian Fleming wrote it into his first James Bond novel, Casino Royale, published in 1953. In the book Bond orders three measures of Gordon's gin, one of vodka and half a measure of Kina Lillet, shaken until ice-cold with a large slice of lemon peel, and announces he will name it once he finds a worthy title. He later names it after Vesper Lynd, who turns out to be a double agent.

Fleming drafted the novel at his Goldeneye home in Jamaica in early 1952, where he reportedly served guests a rum drink called 'Vespers'. Difford's Guide also notes the theory that Vesper Lynd was inspired by SOE agent Christine Granville. Because the original Kina Lillet is no longer made, modern versions such as the IBA's use Lillet Blanc.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, dry and powerful. Gin's juniper and botanicals lead, while the smaller measure of vodka softens and smooths the spirit without adding flavour of its own. Lillet Blanc contributes a gentle honeyed, citrusy and lightly bitter wine note that rounds the edges. Shaken very cold, the drink is clean and bracing, almost crystalline, and the lemon zest adds a bright, oily citrus aroma.

cocktails.name: Vieux Carré
cocktails.shortDescription: Created at New Orleans' Hotel Monteleone in 1938: rye, cognac, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine and bitters.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Vieux Carré was created in 1938 by Walter Bergeron, head bartender at the Hotel Monteleone in New Orleans, in the lounge now known as the Carousel Bar.
