He named it after the city's French Quarter, whose old French name translates as 'old square'. The recipe was published the same year in Stanley Clisby Arthur's book Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em.

Arthur's version combined equal measures of rye whiskey, cognac and Italian vermouth with a little Bénédictine and a dash each of Peychaud's and Angostura bitters, finished with a lemon twist. The drink draws on the city's love of rye and cognac seen in the Sazerac, mixed with the vermouth of a Manhattan, making it a true New Orleans signature.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, spicy and complex. Rye whiskey adds peppery grain, cognac brings soft fruit and roundness, and sweet vermouth contributes dark, wine-like sweetness. A small amount of Bénédictine layers in honey and herbal notes, while Peychaud's bitters add anise and cherry. Stirred and cold, it feels like a deeper, more herbal Manhattan, with a long, warming finish touched by orange from the garnish.

cocktails.name: Vodka Martini
cocktails.shortDescription: Ice-cold vodka stirred with a little dry vermouth, garnished with lemon or olive: the Vodkatini, first printed in 1935.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon zest twist and/or a skewered chilled green olive
instructions: Chill a martini glass.
Stir (or shake) the vodka and vermouth with ice; Difford's optionally adds a dash of ginseng bitters.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Express a lemon zest twist over the drink and/or add a skewered olive.
cocktails.history:
Vodka Martinis were being served in New York after Prohibition ended in 1933, and the first known printed recipe appears in a 1935 Smirnoff pamphlet: three parts vodka to one of dry French vermouth, stirred with lemon peel. The drink entered cocktail books with Lucius Beebe's 1946 Stork Club Bar Book, which notes that it was a favourite of the writer Dashiell Hammett.

Ted Saucier's 1952 Bottoms Up calls it the Vodkatini and credits it to Jerome Zerbe, society editor of Town and Country. Its popularity rose with vodka in the 1980s and 1990s, helped by James Bond's taste for vodka Martinis "shaken, not stirred".
cocktails.tasteProfile: Clean, cold and crisp. Freezer-chilled vodka gives a smooth, almost silky texture with little flavour of its own, so the small measure of dry vermouth shows through with subtle herbal and floral notes. A lemon twist adds bright citrus oil to the nose, while an olive brings a savoury, briny touch. Very strong and very dry, it is a classic pre-dinner drink.

cocktails.name: Ward Eight
cocktails.shortDescription: Rye whiskey shaken with lemon, orange juice and grenadine: a sweet-and-sour Boston classic named after a notorious voting ward.
cocktails.garnish: Skewered quarter orange slice and maraschino cherry
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the rye, lemon juice, orange juice, syrup and grenadine with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a skewered orange slice and cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Ward Eight is named after a Boston voting district notorious for political corruption. A 1951 Holiday Magazine article credited bartender Tom Hussion with creating it in November 1898 at the Locke-Ober Café, to honour Martin Lomasney's election campaign in Ward Eight. Difford's Guide notes Hussion apparently did not join Locke-Ober until 1900, and that another bartender, Billy Kane, may have mixed the first round.

A rival claim came from bartender Charlie Carter, who wrote in 1934 that he invented it for a 1903 Lomasney victory. The drink appears in print in the 1913 Cocktail Book and in Robert Vermeire's 1922 Cocktails: How to Mix Them.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A spirited sweet-and-sour whiskey drink. Spicy, high-proof rye provides a robust backbone, lemon juice brings a crisp tartness and orange juice adds rounder, juicier citrus sweetness. A small measure of grenadine contributes a subtle red-fruit note and a gentle blush. Bright and balanced, it is a fine aperitif and a good choice for anyone who enjoys a Whiskey Sour with a fruitier edge.

cocktails.name: Whiskey Collins
cocktails.shortDescription: Bourbon, lemon juice, sugar and bitters lengthened with soda: the whiskey cousin of the Tom Collins, also called the Colonel Collins.
cocktails.garnish: Orange wheel and maraschino cherry on a skewer
instructions: Fill a chilled Collins glass with ice.
Shake the bourbon, lemon juice, syrup and bitters with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass while pouring in the soda water.
Garnish with a skewered orange wheel and cherry.
cocktails.history: The Whiskey Collins is a classic variation on the Tom Collins, also known as the Colonel Collins when made with bourbon. In his 1948 book The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, David Embury remarked that the Collins family originally had only two brothers, Tom and John, but that numerous cousins had since appeared, among them the Colonel. Other members include the Jock or Sandy Collins with Scotch, the Mike Collins with Irish whiskey and the Pierre Collins with cognac.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A long, refreshing whiskey sour lengthened with soda. Bourbon brings vanilla, caramel and gentle oak, fresh lemon gives a bright tartness, and rich syrup rounds the edges. A couple of dashes of aromatic bitters add spice and depth, while soda water makes it light, lively and easy to sip. Served tall over ice, it is perfect for warm afternoons or for anyone who finds a straight whiskey drink too heavy.

cocktails.name: Whiskey Smash
cocktails.shortDescription: Bourbon shaken with lemon, sugar and fresh mint: a Jerry Thomas-era smash revived by Dale DeGroff as a minty whiskey sour.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon wheel and a bouquet of mint sprigs
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice.
Shake the mint leaves, bourbon, lemon juice and syrup hard with ice.
Fine strain into the ice-filled glass.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a bouquet of mint sprigs.
cocktails.history:
Smashes appeared in the American South in the 1840s and peaked in the following decade. Jerry Thomas printed a Whiskey Smash in his 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide, describing the smash as a small-scale julep, and refined his recipes for the 1887 edition. The style later faded and was largely forgotten for much of the twentieth century.

Dale DeGroff is credited with reviving it. His version muddles lemon quarters with mint and syrup before shaking with bourbon, and he says he created it for the opening menu of Bobby Flay's Bar Americain. Older recipes call for shaved or crushed ice, but Difford's notes that modern convention serves it over cubed ice.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A bright, minty cousin of the Whiskey Sour. Bourbon supplies vanilla, caramel and oak, fresh lemon gives a sharp citrus snap, and rich syrup rounds the edges. Shaking the mint with the other ingredients releases a cool, green freshness that runs through every sip. Served over ice it is refreshing and easy to drink, ideal for warm afternoons when a julep feels too strong.

cocktails.name: Whiskey Sour
cocktails.shortDescription: Bourbon, lemon and sugar, with optional egg white for a silky texture: the balanced, approachable classic sour.
cocktails.garnish: Half orange slice and maraschino cherry (or orange zest)
instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake well (a little harder if using egg white).
Strain into a cobbler glass, or into an ice-filled old fashioned glass to serve on the rocks.
cocktails.history:
Sours, combining spirit, citrus and sugar, are among the oldest families of mixed drinks, and the Brandy Sour may once have been the more popular member. The earliest known mention of a Whiskey Sour dates from 1870, though no individual creator is known. By 1883 a Chicago bartender was describing customers who expected a float of claret on their sours, a variation now known as the New York Sour.

The Whiskey Sour came into its own during Prohibition, when it became the best-loved sour of all. Adding egg white is also an old habit: Robert Vermeire's 1922 book recommended a few drops to improve any sour. The drink now even has its own day, celebrated on 25 August.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Balanced, tangy and approachable. Bourbon brings caramel, vanilla and oak, while fresh lemon juice adds a bright, mouth-watering sourness and sugar syrup smooths the edges. With a little egg white the texture turns soft and silky with a light foam on top. The result is sweet-tart and warming at once, with the whiskey's richness still clear and a gentle citrus finish.

cocktails.name: White Lady
cocktails.shortDescription: A clean, crisp gin sour of orange liqueur and lemon, associated with Harry MacElhone.
instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The first drink called a White Lady is credited to Harry MacElhone at Ciro's Club in London in 1919, but it was quite different: brandy, crème de menthe and Cointreau. His family later said he reinvented it with gin at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in 1929, though Difford's Guide finds no evidence for this. The Savoy instead credits Harry Craddock of its American Bar, whose 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book printed a gin version.

Difford's Guide favours Victor Cabrin of London's Grosvenor House as the most likely creator of the gin White Lady, citing a 1946 newspaper article that says he invented it in 1929. Early recipes had no egg white; it first appeared in a White Lady recipe in 1936 and in a specialist bar book a decade later.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Clean, crisp and citrusy. Gin gives a dry juniper and botanical backbone, while triple sec adds sweet orange and a smooth, slightly fuller body. Fresh lemon juice brings a sharp, refreshing sourness that keeps the drink bright. Served ice-cold and straight up, it tastes elegant and zesty, a gin-based cousin of the Sidecar, with a dry, lingering orange-lemon finish.

cocktails.name: White Negroni
cocktails.shortDescription: A pale Negroni twist of gin, gentian liqueur and Lillet Blanc, created by Wayne Collins in Bordeaux in 2001.

ingredients.note: saline solution or a pinch of salt

instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass and fill it with ice.
Pour in all ingredients.
Stir.
Express a pink grapefruit zest twist over the drink and use it as garnish.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide says the White Negroni was created in 2001 by Wayne Collins at VinExpo in Bordeaux, France, using Plymouth Gin, for Nick Blacknell, then the brand director of Plymouth Gin. Simon Ford, who was Plymouth's ambassador, later introduced the drink to Audrey Saunders in the early days of her Pegu Club in New York, where it became a hit on the menu. Collins originally used equal parts, like a classic Negroni, and specified a grapefruit twist.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bitter, floral and dry. Gentian liqueur provides an earthy, rooty bitterness with hints of citrus peel, Lillet Blanc softens it with honeyed orange and quince notes, and gin brings juniper and spice. A few drops of saline round the edges, and the grapefruit twist is essential for its bright aroma. Paler and more austere than a classic Negroni, it is an aperitif for bitter lovers.

cocktails.name: White Russian
cocktails.shortDescription: Vodka and coffee liqueur over ice, topped with a float of cream: a creamy classic made famous by The Big Lebowski.
instructions: Pre-chill an old fashioned glass.
Stir the vodka and coffee liqueur with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Lightly whip or shake the cream, then carefully float it on top.
Dust with freshly grated nutmeg.
cocktails.history: The White Russian is named for its colour and its vodka base, as vodka was associated with Russia at the time. It is a creamy relative of the Black Russian, whose origins are thought to date from 1949, but who first added cream is unknown. Difford's Guide finds the earliest printed mention in a 1965 Boston Globe advertisement for a long-gone coffee liqueur called Coffee Southern. The drink was popular in the 1970s disco era, faded in the 1980s, and was revived by the 1998 film The Big Lebowski, in which Jeff Bridges's character, The Dude, drinks it throughout.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smooth, sweet and creamy. Vodka provides a clean alcoholic base, coffee liqueur brings roasted coffee, caramel and vanilla, and the layer of cream adds a soft, silky richness that gradually blends in as you sip. A dusting of nutmeg gives a warm, spicy aroma. It is an easy-drinking, dessert-like after-dinner drink with a laid-back reputation.

cocktails.name: Widow's Kiss
cocktails.shortDescription: Calvados stirred with Bénédictine, Yellow Chartreuse and Angostura: an 1895 Holland House classic with a rich, herbal, apple-brandy core.
instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Stir the calvados, Bénédictine, Yellow Chartreuse and bitters with ice (or shake, as the original did).
Strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with two skewered cherries.
cocktails.history:
The Widow's Kiss is credited to George J. Kappeler, head bartender at the Holland House Hotel in New York City, who published it in his 1895 book Modern American Drinks. His recipe combined a pony of apple brandy with half a pony each of yellow Chartreuse and Bénédictine plus two dashes of Angostura, shaken and strained into a fancy cocktail glass.

Difford's Guide follows the classic split of Yellow Chartreuse and Bénédictine, while noting that the drink is also often made with green Chartreuse. Its modern spec reduces both liqueurs and stirs rather than shakes. Jim Meehan's contemporary version goes further, leaning harder on bonded calvados and using only a quarter ounce of each liqueur.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A rich, herbal after-dinner drink built on apple brandy. Calvados brings baked orchard fruit, while Bénédictine and Yellow Chartreuse layer honey, saffron, mint and a eucalyptus-like coolness on top. Two dashes of aromatic bitters add spice and keep the sweetness in check. The texture is silky and warming, and the drink suits a cold evening or the end of a meal when something complex and gently sweet is wanted.

cocktails.name: Yellow Bird
cocktails.shortDescription: Gold and white rum with banana liqueur, Galliano, orange, pineapple and lime: a sunny, lightly tiki drink named after a song.
cocktails.garnish: Banana carved into a bird, or a pineapple wedge with a maraschino cherry and half an orange slice
instructions: Shake the two rums, banana liqueur, Galliano and the orange, pineapple and lime juices with ice.
Fine strain into a chilled collins glass.
Garnish with a carved banana bird, or a skewered pineapple wedge, cherry and half orange slice.
cocktails.history:
The Yellow Bird may simply be named for its golden colour, or after the 19th-century Haitian song "Choucoune", which was given English lyrics as "Yellow Bird" in the mid-1950s. Norman Luboff and his choir first recorded that calypso-style version in 1957, and the Mills Brothers had a minor hit with it in 1959.

It was Hawaiian musician Arthur Lyman's recording, however, that reached number four on the Billboard charts in July 1961. Some say the record was played constantly at the Shell Bar in The Hawaii Village, inspiring bartenders there to create the cocktail.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sunny, fruity and lightly tropical. Two rums give a smooth sugar-cane base, while orange and pineapple juices bring juicy sweetness and a squeeze of lime adds freshness. The real character comes from the liqueurs: ripe banana from the banana liqueur and vanilla, anise and peppermint from Galliano. Bright and easy to drink, it is made for poolside afternoons and summer parties.

cocktails.name: Yellow Daisy
cocktails.shortDescription: Gin, dry vermouth and Grand Marnier with a dash of absinthe: a sweetened, aromatised Martini linked to Deadwood Dick.

ingredients.note: Grand Marnier or other cognac-based orange liqueur

instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake (or stir) all ingredients with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
cocktails.history:
Despite its name, the Yellow Daisy is not part of the daisy family of sours; Difford's Guide describes it as a sweetened, aromatised Martini that was popular in the early twentieth century. It appears in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book as a recipe for six, with a note calling it the favourite, and perhaps the invention, of Richard William "Deadwood Dick" Clark.

Clark was a larger-than-life Wild West figure: Craddock lists him as a Pony Express rider and stagecoach guard who inspired the Deadwood Dick dime novels and counted Buffalo Bill and Calamity Jane among his friends. He was buried overlooking Deadwood Gulch in South Dakota.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Aromatic, orange-scented and fairly strong. Gin and dry vermouth form a crisp, herbal Martini-style base, and Grand Marnier adds a rich, cognac-backed bitter orange sweetness that gives the drink its golden colour. A few dashes of absinthe add a subtle anise lift on the nose. Smooth and balanced, it works as an aperitif for those who find a Martini too dry.

cocktails.name: Zombie
cocktails.shortDescription: Donn Beach's potent 1934 tiki drink of three rums, lime, falernum, grapefruit, cinnamon and a hint of anise.

ingredients.note: 45 ml Jamaican dark rum plus 30 ml Demerara rum
part of Donn's Mix (2 parts grapefruit to 1 part cinnamon syrup)

instructions: Make Donn's Mix from 2 parts fresh grapefruit juice to 1 part cinnamon syrup.
Add all ingredients to an electric blender with about 170 g of cracked ice.
Pulse-blend for a few seconds.
Pour into a tall tumbler.
Garnish with mint leaves.
cocktails.history: Difford's Guide and Wikipedia both credit the Zombie to Donn Beach, who created it at his Don the Beachcomber restaurant in Hollywood in 1934. Legend says he mixed it to help a hung-over customer through a business meeting, and the customer later complained it had turned him into a zombie. The drink was so strong that the restaurants limited guests to two each. Beach kept his recipes in code, which did not stop a copy being served at the 1939 New York World's Fair. His original formulas were later recovered and published by tiki historian Jeff "Beachbum" Berry in Sippin' Safari.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fruity, spicy and deceptively strong. A blend of dark, gold and Demerara rums gives molasses, caramel and wood, while lime and grapefruit keep it bright. Falernum and cinnamon add warm spice, grenadine a touch of fruity sweetness, and drops of anise and bitters lift the aroma. Blended with ice it is cold and easy to drink, so treat it with respect at a summer party.
